label: H.R. 4930
title: To expand the sharing of information with respect to suspected violations of intellectual property rights in trade.
one: The bill lets U.S. Customs and Border Protection share more information, including nonpublic data from shipping and online-sales companies, with trademark and copyright owners and other interested parties when it reasonably suspects imported goods are counterfeit or pirated.
summary: Right now, if U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) suspects that imported goods copy a protected trademark or copyright, it can ask certain parties, such as the brand owner, for help. To let them check the goods, CBP shares information and images of the product, its packaging, and its labels. This bill changes that in four ways. First, CBP needs a "reasonable suspicion" instead of just a suspicion. That is a somewhat firmer standard. Second, CBP can also share information and images of packing materials and shipping containers. Third, CBP may share nonpublic information about the goods that came from online marketplaces, express delivery companies, freight forwarders, or any other business involved in selling or moving the goods, if CBP got that information. When it does, CBP must notify the person who receives it, following rules set by the Secretary of Homeland Security. Fourth, CBP's list of who it can ask for help grows to include "any other party with an interest in the merchandise," as the CBP Commissioner decides. The bill text does not say how the nonpublic data would be protected, whether the companies that supplied it would be told, or what limits apply to the new "other party" category. The bill passed the House and then the Senate, and the latest action was a message on the Senate action sent back to the House.
does: Changes CBP's trigger from "suspects" to "has a reasonable suspicion" of an IP violation.
who: Trademark and copyright owners

stage.stage_label: Sent to the President for signature
stage.last_action: Presented to President.

crs:
This bill expands the authority of U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) to provide information to certain persons (e.g., trademark or copyright owners) regarding suspected violations of intellectual property rights in trade. 
Under current law, if CBP suspects that merchandise is being imported in violation of certain trademark and copyright laws, it may request assistance from specified persons when determining whether the merchandise is imported in violation of these laws. To permit the party to conduct examination and testing, CBP must provide them with specified information that appears on the merchandise and its packaging and labels. 
This bill (1) expands the definition of 
person
 to allow CBP to request assistance from any other appropriate party with an interest in the imported merchandise, and (2) expands the scope of information that CBP is authorized to share with others to include information on and images of packing materials and containers.
The bill allows CBP to request this assistance if it has a reasonable suspicion (currently, suspects) that the merchandise being imported is in violation of certain trademark and copyright laws.
Additionally, CBP may provide a person with nonpublic information about the imported merchandise that was generated by an online marketplace or similar market platform, express consignment operator, freight forwarder, or any other entity that plays a role in the sale, importation, or facilitation of the merchandise into the United States and has been provided to, shared with, or obtained by CBP. CBP must provide the person with notification of the transmitted information.

transparency.reason: CBP may share nonpublic marketplace, shipping, and logistics data with private parties and expand who gets information, while the bill does not require public disclosure or explain how the data is protected, so government sharing of information becomes less visible to the public.

people_over_profit.reason: The bill gives brand owners and other private parties more access to nonpublic commercial data and examination of goods, which mainly serves rights holders' enforcement interests and may expose companies' business information to private parties.

label: H.R. 8552
title: Veterans’ Compensation Cost-of-Living Adjustment Act of 2026
one: Raises veterans' disability pay, dependent add-ons, clothing allowances, and survivor benefits on December 1, 2026, by the same percentage as the Social Security cost-of-living increase.
summary: This bill gives disabled veterans and the survivors of some veterans a yearly raise so their benefits keep up with rising prices. On December 1, 2026, the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) must raise several payments by the same percentage that Social Security benefits go up that same day. The payments covered are: disability compensation for veterans with service-connected disabilities, extra pay for veterans with dependents, the clothing allowance for certain disabled veterans, and Dependency and Indemnity Compensation (DIC), a monthly benefit paid to surviving spouses and children of certain veterans. The bill also lets the VA make matching adjustments for certain people covered under an older law (Public Law 85-857) who have not received compensation under the main veterans' disability chapter. The VA must publish the new payment amounts in the Federal Register, the government's official daily notice, by the date the Social Security increase figures must be published. The bill does not name a percentage because it depends on the Social Security calculation, which was not given in the material. It also does not give a cost estimate. This kind of bill is passed most years. The latest action listed is a message on Senate action sent to the House, so the final steps may still be pending.
does: Requires the VA to raise listed disability compensation rates on December 1, 2026.
Ties the raise to the same percentage as the Social Security cost-of-living increase effective that date.
Covers wartime disability compensation, extra pay for dependents, the clothing allowance, and survivor benefits (DIC) for spouses and children.
Lets the VA adjust rates for certain people under Public Law 85-857 who have not received compensation under the main disability chapter.
Requires the VA to publish the new amounts in the Federal Register by the Social Security publication deadline.
who: Veterans with service-connected disabilities
Veterans with dependents who receive extra compensation
Surviving spouses and children receiving DIC
Certain disabled veterans who get the clothing allowance
The VA, which must pay and publish the new rates
Federal taxpayers, who fund the benefits

stage.stage_label: Sent to the President for signature
stage.last_action: Presented to President.

crs:
Veterans' Compensation Cost-of-Living Adjustment Act of 2026
This bill requires the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) to increase the amounts payable for wartime disability compensation, additional compensation for dependents, the clothing allowance for certain disabled veterans, and dependency and indemnity compensation for surviving spouses and children. Specifically, the VA must increase the amounts by the same percentage as the cost-of-living increase in benefits for Social Security recipients that is effective on December 1, 2026. The act requires the VA to publish the amounts payable, as increased, in the Federal Register.
The VA is authorized to make a similar adjustment to the rates of disability compensation payable to persons who have not received compensation for service-connected disability or death.

life.reason: Annual cost-of-living increases help disabled veterans and survivors afford necessities like food, housing, and medical needs, which supports their health and wellbeing.

transparency.reason: The bill requires the VA to publish the new payment amounts in the Federal Register, making the adjusted rates publicly available.

no_bailouts.reason: This is a formula-based benefit adjustment for veterans, not a corporate bailout or ratepayer-funded tax break.

honesty_kindness.reason: Keeping veterans' and survivors' benefits in line with rising prices is a caring step that helps those who have sacrificed for the country maintain their standard of living.

label: H.R. 2302
title: Shingle Springs Band of Miwok Indians Land Transfer Act of 2025
short_title: Shingle Springs Band of Miwok Indians Land Transfer Act
one: Moves federal land and tribe-owned land in El Dorado County, California, into trust as part of the Shingle Springs Band of Miwok Indians' reservation, and bans casino-style gaming on it.
summary: This bill would give the Shingle Springs Band of Miwok Indians, in El Dorado County, California, more land to add to its reservation. First, it cancels an old 1964 federal order (Public Land Order 3309) that set aside certain land. The CRS summary says the order reserved the land as a Forest Service experiment station. The bill then moves control of that land to the Secretary of the Interior. Within 180 days of becoming law, the Secretary must put two areas of land "into trust" for the tribe. Trust means the U.S. government holds the legal title for the tribe's benefit. One area is federal land managed by the Bureau of Land Management. The other is land called Indian Creek Ranch, which the CRS says the tribe already owns. Both areas become part of the tribe's reservation. The Secretary must check whether a land survey is needed. If one is done, it must be kept on file where the public can view it. The bill also bans all gaming on this land, including casino-style gaming. The bill text gives the acreage as about 80 and 185 acres. The CRS summary gives about 85.3 and 118.84 acres, 204.14 in total. The bill relies on a map dated May 2, 2025, which I could not see. The bill says nothing about costs, environmental review, or local government input.
does: Revokes Public Land Order 3309 (from 1964) and transfers jurisdiction over that land to the Secretary of the Interior.
Requires the Secretary to place two parcels into trust for the tribe within 180 days, subject to valid existing rights.
Declares the trust land part of the tribe's reservation, managed under the usual rules for tribal trust land.
Requires a review of whether a survey is needed, and allows minor fixes to clerical or surveying errors.
Requires any survey to be kept on file for public inspection at the Bureau of Indian Affairs.
Bans Class II and Class III gaming on the land under the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act.
who: Shingle Springs Band of Miwok Indians
Residents and local governments in El Dorado County, California
Department of the Interior, Bureau of Land Management, and Bureau of Indian Affairs
Forest Service (if it currently manages the land, as the CRS describes)
Anyone holding existing rights on the land, such as easements

stage.last_action: Message on Senate action sent to the House.

crs:
Shingle Springs Band of Miwok Indians Land Transfer Act of 2025
This bill takes approximately 204.14 acres of specified lands in El Dorado County, California, into trust for the benefit of the Shingle Springs Band of Miwok Indians.
The bill revokes a specified public land order and administratively transfers the land from the Forest Service to the Department of the Interior. (In the public land order, the land was designated for use by the Forest Service as an experiment station.)
The bill directs Interior to take the following lands into trust for the benefit of the tribe: (1) approximately 85.3 acres of federal land managed by Interior's Bureau of Land Management (which includes the land transferred from the Forest Service), and (2) approximately 118.84 acres of fee land held by the tribe. These combined lands, approximately 204.14 acres, shall be part of the tribe's reservation. Further, the bill prohibits gaming on the land taken into trust.

transparency.reason: The bill requires surveys to be kept on file for public inspection, but it does not require public notice or comment, and the text relies on a map the public could not see here, so it gives the public less visibility into the land transfer.

local_say.reason: Putting federal land and fee land into trust and reservation status removes local government land-use authority and does not provide for input from El Dorado County or residents, though the gaming ban limits one type of local impact.

news.overall: Only two Lean Left headlines were provided, both about a California billionaire tax rather than the named federal bill, so the evidence for how this outlet group covers the Shingle Springs land transfer is essentially absent. The headlines do not include article descriptions, so the framing is inferred only from the headline wording. No other perspective groups were supplied, so no cross-perspective comparison is possible.

label: H.R. 2347
title: Survivor Justice Tax Prevention Act
one: The bill would make money that survivors of sexual acts or sexual contact receive through court judgments or settlements (other than punitive damages) tax-free, even without medical records or visible injuries, and would make it easier to prove that the money qualifies.
summary:
Under current law, money you get from a lawsuit or settlement for a physical injury or physical sickness is not taxed, unless it is punitive damages (money meant to punish the wrongdoer). The IRS usually reads "physical injury" to mean harm that can be seen, like bruises or cuts. That can leave some survivors of sexual assault or abuse facing a tax bill on their settlements if there is no visible injury or medical record.

This bill adds a new category to the tax exclusion. Damages (other than punitive) received because of any "sexual act" or "sexual contact" would not count as taxable income. It uses the definitions in an existing federal criminal law (18 U.S.C. 2246). The exclusion applies whether or not there are medical records or visible injuries.

The bill also helps survivors prove their case if the IRS questions it. If a court decision or settlement agreement says the money is for a sexual act or contact, that statement counts as credible evidence, and the taxpayer is treated as having met the related requirements. This shifts the burden to the IRS to show otherwise.

The Treasury Department must also run a public awareness program about the exclusion, working with the Justice Department's Office on Violence Against Women. The rules apply to decisions and agreements made after the bill becomes law. Agreements that only replace or revise earlier ones do not count as new.
does: Adds a new tax exclusion for non-punitive damages received because of a sexual act or sexual contact, as defined in federal criminal law.
States the exclusion applies whether or not there are medical records or observable injuries.

Treats a court decision or settlement statement that damages are for a sexual act or contact as credible evidence, and treats the taxpayer as meeting the related requirements, so the IRS must disprove it.
Applies to money from decisions and agreements made after the law is enacted; for court decisions, the date of the first payment counts.
Says agreements that replace or revise older agreements do not count as new, so they stay under old rules.
Says the bill should not be read to change how "physical injury" is interpreted in other cases.
Requires Treasury to run a public awareness program about the exclusion, in consultation with the DOJ Office on Violence Against Women.
who: Survivors of sexual assault, abuse, or unwanted sexual contact who win lawsuits or settle claims.
Attorneys and advocates who represent survivors.
The IRS, which would take on the burden of proof and the awareness program.
Defendants and insurers, who may see changes in how settlements are worded.
The Treasury and DOJ Office on Violence Against Women, which would run the awareness effort.

stage.last_action: Considered by Senate. (consideration: CR S5705)

crs:
Survivor Justice Tax Prevention Act
This bill excludes from gross income certain damages received by an individual due to any sexual act or sexual contact and establishes the applicable burden of proof in court proceedings regarding the characterization of such damages for federal tax purposes. 
Under current law, amounts received as damages (other than punitive damages) from a judgment, award, or settlement of a claim may be excluded from gross income and, thus, are not subject to federal income tax, if attributable to a personal physical injury or physical sickness. The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) generally interprets 
personal physical injury
 to require observable bodily harm (e.g., bruising, cuts, swelling, or bleeding).
Under the bill, amounts received as damages (other than punitive damages) from a judgment, award, or settlement due to any sexual act or sexual conduct, whether or not there are medical records or observable injuries of such act or contact, may be excluded from gross income.
Further, if a judgment, award, or settlement states that damages are due to any sexual act or sexual conduct, then the IRS has the burden of proving otherwise in court proceedings related to the tax liability associated with such damages. 
Finally, the bill requires the IRS to promote public awareness of the exclusion from gross income of damages related to any sexual act or sexual contact.

life.reason: It removes a tax burden on survivors of sexual assault or abuse, which supports their recovery and well-being, though it does not directly protect life or health.

people_over_profit.reason: Settlement money for survivors becomes untaxed, so more of the award goes to the injured person rather than being reduced by taxes, though defendants and insurers are not directly targeted.

no_bailouts.reason: It is a tax exclusion for individuals' damages, not a corporate bailout or ratepayer-funded tax break.

honesty_kindness.reason: It treats survivors more compassionately by not taxing settlements for harm that may lack visible injury, and it helps them prove their claims.

label: H.R. 2400
title: Pit River Land Transfer Act of 2026
short_title: Pit River Land Transfer Act of 2026
one: The bill moves about 557 acres of national forest land in Shasta County, California, to the Department of the Interior to be held in trust for the Pit River Tribe as part of its reservation, and it bans casino-style gaming on that land.
summary: This bill would move a piece of federal land called the Four Corners Property out of the Forest Service's care and give it to the Pit River Tribe. The land is about 557 acres in Shasta County, California. First, the Department of Agriculture (which oversees the Forest Service) would hand control of the land to the Department of the Interior. Interior would then hold the land "in trust" for the Tribe. Trust means the United States government holds legal title, and the Tribe gets the benefit and use of the land. Once in trust, the land becomes part of the Tribe's reservation. Any rights that other people already legally hold on the land would stay in place. About 87 acres of roads, highways, public rights-of-way, easements and special use permit areas are excluded from the transfer. Within 180 days of the bill becoming law, Interior must complete a survey of the land. Interior, Agriculture and the Tribe may agree to make small fixes to the boundaries or survey. The bill also bans all casino-style gaming (the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act's "class II" and "class III" gaming) on this land. The bill text does not describe any rules on public access, environmental review, or how the Tribe would manage the land. This version is the Senate's amendment. The latest recorded action is a message sent back to the House about that Senate action.

Residents and neighbors near the Four Corners Property in Shasta County

The Forest Service and the Department of the Interior, which would handle the transfer and survey
Members of the public who now use this national forest land for recreation

crs:
Pit River Land Transfer Act of 2026
This bill takes approximately 557 acres of specified federal land in Shasta County, California, into trust for the benefit of the Pit River Tribe.
The land, known as the Four Corners Property, is currently administered and managed by the Forest Service. Administrative jurisdiction over the land must be transferred to the Department of the Interior. Interior must then take the land into trust for the benefit of the Tribe. The land taken into trust shall be part of the Tribe's reservation.
The bill also prohibits gaming on the land taken into trust.

transparency.reason: Moving the land out of Forest Service management into trust status, with no stated public access, environmental review, or management-disclosure rules, reduces public visibility into how the land is used.

local_say.reason: Land becomes tribal reservation trust land, which removes the federal public-land process that local residents and recreation users currently can use to weigh in, though existing permits and easements are preserved and the Tribe itself gains a say over the land.

news.overall: Evidence is very limited: each perspective has only one headline and no article descriptions, so these readings rest on headlines alone. The Lean Left headline frames the bill as a Democratic move to restrict data centers on public lands, while the Lean Right headline frames the issue as public demand for a voice in data center decisions. Neither headline explicitly describes the bill's land-transfer provisions, so a fuller comparison would require the article text.

label: H.R. 5254
title: Gateway Partnership Act
one: Lets the National Park Service sign a one-time, up-to-five-year deal with the Gateway Arch Park Foundation to host private events at Gateway Arch National Park and its buildings, with fees to cover costs and a required report to Congress.
summary:
This bill would let the Secretary of the Interior, who oversees the National Park Service, make a single agreement with the Gateway Arch Park Foundation. The Foundation is a nonprofit that serves as the park's official philanthropic partner. The agreement could last up to five years. It would let the Foundation host private events, such as receptions, at Gateway Arch National Park in St. Louis. Events could use buildings such as the Arch Visitor Center and the Old Courthouse.

The agreement must set dates and times when the Foundation can be the only group holding a special event in certain buildings. It must also cap the number of events per month and set the National Park Service staffing needed for safety and resource protection. The Foundation must carry liability insurance that names the United States as an additional insured. The agreement must also say the federal government and its employees are not liable for injuries or deaths from the Foundation's use of the buildings.

Events must fit the park's purposes and must not harm its appearance or block public access. The Park Service must charge a fee for wear and tear. It may also recover its other costs, including utilities, security, and staff time. The authority ends seven years after enactment. Within four years, the Secretary must report to Congress on visitor access, security, staffing, and finances.

Requires the agreement to set exclusive-use dates and times, a monthly cap on events, and Park Service staffing levels for safety.

Keeps the Park Service's ability to host its own events and issue other permits.

crs:
Gateway Partnership Act
This bill authorizes the National Park Service (NPS) to enter into a one-time agreement with the Gateway Arch Park Foundation to host private events at the Gateway Arch National Park and its buildings for a period of up to five years. The NPS manages the park, located in St. Louis, Missouri, and its buildings, such as the Arch Visitor Center and the Old Courthouse.
The bill outlines the terms and conditions that must be included in the agreement. The bill also requires private events hosted at the park or its buildings to be consistent with the park's purposes and compatible with NPS programs. Such events may not (1) degrade the integrity, appearance, or purposes of the park; or (2) take place during times or in locations that prevent or disrupt public use or access to the park or its buildings.
The NPS must charge a fee to cover the cost of wear and tear resulting from the private events. The NPS may recover all costs incurred as a result of the private events, including maintenance, utilities, administrative expenses, security, and personnel costs.
The bill terminates the NPS's authority to enter and carry out an agreement with the foundation seven years after the enactment of this bill.

label: H.R. 7834
title: Safe Cloud Storage Act
one: The bill lets police and prosecutors hire cloud companies to store child sexual abuse evidence, shields those companies from most lawsuits and criminal charges, and requires strict security, audits, and reporting.
summary:
Police and prosecutors often have to keep huge amounts of child sexual abuse material (CSAM) as evidence. Many want to store it with cloud companies, but those companies could risk being sued or even charged with a crime for holding it. This bill would reduce that risk for "approved vendors," which are cloud companies that agree to security rules and are hired by a federal, state, tribal, or local law enforcement or prosecutor's office.

Under the bill, no civil lawsuit or criminal charge could be brought against an approved vendor over its work under the contract. There are exceptions. A case can go forward if the vendor acted intentionally wrong, was negligent, acted with actual malice or reckless disregard, or acted for a reason unrelated to its contract duties.

In return, vendors must follow federal cybersecurity standards and use end-to-end encryption. They must limit and keep a list of employees with access, and only open the material when the agency agrees. They must pass an independent audit every year and fix any problems found. Data must stay in the U.S. unless the agency approves moving it. Vendors must tell the Justice Department about each contract within 30 days. They must also report if an agency stops paying or ends the contract, and keep protecting the evidence until it is lawfully transferred. Agencies must follow FBI security policy and evidence retention rules. The bill also covers sexual images of identifiable minors, including digital forgeries.
does: Adds a new Section 202 to the PROTECT Our Children Act of 2008.
who: Child victims of sexual exploitation, whose images are held as evidence

stage.last_action: Message on Senate action sent to the House.

crs:
Safe Cloud Storage Act
This bill limits the civil and criminal liability of vendors that contract with law enforcement agencies to provide digital storage services (e.g., cloud-based storage) for storing, maintaining, and processing child sexual abuse material (CSAM) in investigations of online child sexual exploitation.
Under current law, the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC) receives reports of online child sexual exploitation via its CyberTipline, evaluates and prioritizes the reports, and refers the reports to law enforcement agencies to investigate. Currently, federal law limits the liability of vendors that contract directly with the NCMEC to store and transfer CSAM. However, federal law does not limit the liability of vendors that contract with law enforcement agencies to assist in investigations.
This bill establishes liability protections for vendors that contract with federal, state, and local law enforcement agencies to store, maintain, and process CSAM in investigations of online child sexual exploitation. Specifically, the bill prohibits a civil claim or criminal charge in federal or state court against such a vendor, so long as the vendor has not engaged in intentional misconduct or negligent conduct, acted with malice or reckless disregard, or acted for a purpose unrelated to its contractual duties.
The bill requires vendors to comply with cybersecurity requirements for CSAM that is stored, maintained, or processed. The bill also requires vendors to comply with storage requirements for CSAM that is retained as evidence.

life.reason: Stronger cybersecurity, encryption, and audit requirements for sensitive evidence about child victims help protect those children's privacy and safety, though the bill does not directly address abuse prevention.

transparency.reason: Vendors must report contracts to DOJ, but the bill shields vendors from lawsuits and limits public and court oversight of how CSAM is handled, and much of the security regime is not public.

people_over_profit.reason: Liability shields for private cloud companies reduce their legal risk and cost exposure, favoring vendor interests, though the security and audit duties partly offset this.

honesty_kindness.reason: The bill treats victims' images with protective handling and requires vendors to keep evidence secure until lawfully transferred, which reflects care for child victims.

label: H.R. 8454
title: To provide for the transfer of administrative jurisdiction over certain Federal land in the State of California, and for other purposes.
one: Swaps management of about 160 acres of Forest Service land (to Yosemite National Park) and about 170 acres of Park Service land (to Stanislaus National Forest) at Ackerson Meadow in Tuolumne County, California.
summary:
This bill trades management of two small pieces of federal land near Ackerson Meadow in California. About 160 acres now run by the Forest Service as part of Stanislaus National Forest would move to the Department of the Interior and become part of Yosemite National Park. About 170 acres now run by the National Park Service would move to the Department of Agriculture and become part of Stanislaus National Forest. The land stays public. Only the agency in charge changes.

According to the Congressional Research Service, cattle graze on the parcel now managed by the Park Service. Grazing happens mostly on Forest Service and Bureau of Land Management land. The Forest Service uses a "multiple-use" approach that fits with grazing. So the swap would let that land be managed under rules that allow it.

The bill lets the two agencies make minor fixes and survey corrections by mutual agreement. Those fixes take effect when a notice is published in the Federal Register, the government's public journal. The bill says it does not erase valid existing rights, permits, leases, easements or similar authorizations. The new managing agency would take over administering them. The bill does not mention money. It passed the House on September 14, 2026, and the Senate passed it without changes by unanimous consent on November 17, 2026.

Ranchers who graze cattle on the affected land
National Park Service and Forest Service staff

Protects existing rights, permits and leases, giving current users certainty.

Why 'hazardous wastes and toxic substances' appears among the subjects, since the text does not address it.
Whether there was local or tribal input.
The terms of any existing grazing permits on the parcel.

crs:
This bill exchanges administrative jurisdiction over specified parcels of federal land between Yosemite National Park and Stanislaus National Forest in California.
By way of background, cattle are grazing on the land currently managed by the National Park Service. However, grazing on federal lands primarily occurs on lands managed by the Bureau of Land Management or the Forest Service. The transfer would allow the land with cattle grazing to be managed by the Forest Service, which has a multiple-use management plan that is consistent with grazing.

life.reason: Adds about 160 acres to Yosemite National Park, though it removes about 170 acres from park protection, so the net effect is small.

label: S. 2677
title: A bill to expand the sharing of information with respect to suspected violations of intellectual property rights in trade.
one: Lets U.S. Customs and Border Protection share more information, including nonpublic business data from shippers and online platforms, with trademark and copyright owners and other interested parties when it reasonably suspects imported goods are counterfeit or pirated.
summary: When U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) thinks imported goods copy a protected trademark or copyright, current law lets it ask the rights holder for help and share some details, such as photos of the product, its packaging and labels. This bill widens that process in four ways. First, CBP would need a "reasonable suspicion" instead of just a "suspicion" before it starts this process. Second, CBP could share pictures and information about packing materials and shipping containers, not just the product and its packaging. Third, CBP could share nonpublic information about the goods that came from online marketplaces, express delivery companies, freight forwarders, or any other business involved in selling or importing the goods, if CBP already has that information. When CBP shares that kind of information, it would have to notify the person receiving it of what was sent, following rules the Homeland Security Secretary sets. Fourth, the group of people CBP can ask for help would grow to include any other party with an interest in the goods, as decided by the CBP Commissioner. The bill does not say what limits apply to how recipients may use the shared business information, and it does not add any new funding. The Senate passed it on August 7, 2026, and it is now with the House.
does: Changes the trigger from CBP "suspects" to CBP "has a reasonable suspicion" that imported goods violate certain trademark or copyright laws.
who: Trademark and copyright owners

stage.stage_label: Scheduled for House floor vote (second chamber)
stage.last_action: Held at the desk.

crs:
This bill expands the authority of U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) to provide information to certain persons (e.g., trademark or copyright owners) regarding suspected violations of intellectual property rights in trade. 
Under current law, if CBP suspects that merchandise is being imported in violation of certain trademark and copyright laws, it may request assistance from specified persons when determining whether the merchandise is imported in violation of these laws. To permit the party to conduct examination and testing, CBP must provide them with specified information that appears on the merchandise and its packaging and labels. 
This bill (1) expands the definition of 
person
 to allow CBP to request assistance from any other appropriate party with an interest in the imported merchandise, and (2) expands the scope of information that CBP is authorized to share with others to include information on and images of packing materials and shipping containers.
The bill allows CBP to request this assistance if it has a reasonable suspicion (currently, suspects) that the merchandise being imported is in violation of certain trademark and copyright laws.
Additionally, CBP may provide a person with nonpublic information about the imported merchandise that was generated by an online marketplace or similar market platform, express consignment operator, freight forwarder, or any other entity that plays a role in the sale, importation, or facilitation of the merchandise into the United States and has been provided to, shared with, or obtained by CBP.

life.reason: The bill concerns trademark and copyright enforcement in import trade and does not directly affect human, animal, or plant health or safety.

water.reason: The bill does not address water quality or water systems.

air.reason: The bill does not address air quality or emissions.

transparency.reason: Expanding CBP's authority to share nonpublic business information with outside parties, with no stated limits on recipients' use and no public disclosure requirements, reduces public visibility into government information sharing, though CBP must notify the recipient of what was sent.

people_over_profit.reason: Nonpublic business data from online marketplaces, carriers, and freight forwarders could be shared with rights holders for private enforcement, with no stated use limits, which tilts toward private commercial interests over the privacy of businesses and consumers.

local_say.reason: The bill does not change how communities or local residents participate in decisions affecting their area.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill does not involve bailouts, subsidies, or tax breaks, and it adds no new funding.

honesty_kindness.reason: The bill is a procedural information-sharing change for enforcement and does not clearly bear on honesty or kindness.

label: S. 3977
title: Bankruptcy Threshold Adjustment Act of 2026
one: Raises the debt limits that let small businesses use Subchapter V bankruptcy (to $7.5 million) and let individuals use Chapter 13 repayment-plan bankruptcy (to $2.75 million total debt), restoring higher limits that expired in 2024.
summary: This bill changes who can use two kinds of bankruptcy that are meant to be simpler and cheaper than the standard routes. The first is Subchapter V, a streamlined way for small businesses to reorganize their debts and keep operating. The bill sets the debt cap at $7.5 million. Today it is about $3.4 million, after a higher limit expired in 2024. The second is Chapter 13, where a person with regular income pays back debts over time through a court-approved plan. Today there are separate caps for secured debt (backed by property, like a mortgage) and unsecured debt (like credit cards), totaling roughly $2.1 million. The bill replaces them with one combined cap of $2.75 million. Public companies, their affiliates, and businesses whose main activity is owning a single piece of real estate stay excluded from Subchapter V. Affiliated groups are judged by their combined debt. The change would apply only to bankruptcy cases filed on or after the date the bill becomes law. It does not forgive debt, spend money, or change the rules of the bankruptcy process beyond who is eligible. The text does not say whether the higher limits are permanent. The CRS summary says the bill restores the limits that lapsed in 2024. The Senate passed the bill on August 3, 2026, and it was held at the desk on August 10, 2026, which is a procedural step in the House.
does: Raises the Subchapter V (small business) debt limit to $7,500,000 from about $3.4 million.
who: Small and mid-sized businesses with debts between about $3.4 million and $7.5 million

stage.stage_label: Scheduled for House floor vote (second chamber)
stage.last_action: Held at the desk.

crs:
Bankruptcy Threshold Adjustment Act of 2026
This bill restores changes that expired in 2024 applicable to debt limits for Subchapter V (small business reorganization) and Chapter 13 (the wage earner's plan) bankruptcies.
Specifically, the bill increases the debt limit under Subchapter V from approximately $3.4 million to $7.5 million and increases the cumulative debt limit under Chapter 13 from approximately $2.1 million to $2.75 million.
The bill also applies both secured and unsecured debt towards the Chapter 13 limit. (Currently, separate limits apply to secured and unsecured debt under Chapter 13 bankruptcy.)

people_over_profit.reason: Raising the Subchapter V cap lets larger businesses use a cheaper, streamlined reorganization route, which mainly benefits businesses and their creditors and owners rather than ordinary people, though it also helps keep workers' jobs in place.

label: S. 5600
title: Dennis John Benigno Traumatic Brain Injury Program Reauthorization Act of 2026
short_title: Traumatic Brain Injury Program Reauthorization Act of 2026
one: Renews federal traumatic brain injury (TBI) tracking, prevention, and state grant programs through fiscal year 2031, adds a focus on higher-risk groups, requires more public data sharing, and orders two reports to Congress.
summary:
This bill renews the federal government's traumatic brain injury (TBI) programs. Those programs track how many people have brain injuries, study what causes them, and give money to states and tribes for TBI services. The current funding authority covers 2020 through 2024. The bill extends it to 2027 through 2031. "Authorizing" funding means Congress allows the money to be spent. A separate spending law still has to provide the actual dollars.

The bill also updates how the programs work. The CDC would collect more data on groups at higher risk, such as people whose jobs raise their risk. It would also look at causes, risk factors, and long-term outcomes, which may include related mental health conditions. The CDC would have to post summary (aggregated) TBI and concussion information on its website, including prevention tips for higher-risk groups. The surveillance program would be renamed for the late Rep. Bill Pascrell, Jr.

State grants would explicitly include tribal governments and American Indian consortia. The bill also updates the legal definition of TBI. It lets the HHS Secretary revise that definition after talking with states and other groups.

Within two years, HHS must send Congress a report on higher-risk groups, such as survivors of domestic violence or sexual assault and public safety officers. HHS must also complete a study of long-term effects of TBI, including links to dementia and mental health conditions. If HHS does that study itself, it must post the report publicly.
does: Extends authorization for the CDC's TBI prevention and surveillance work through fiscal years 2027–2031.
Extends authorization for state TBI grants and protection and advocacy grants through fiscal years 2027–2031.
Adds "prevalence" tracking, causes, risk factors, and higher-risk groups (including occupation-related risk) to the CDC's data collection.
Requires the CDC to publish aggregated TBI and concussion information online, including prevention strategies tailored to higher-risk groups where feasible.
Renames the surveillance and registries program after Bill Pascrell, Jr.
Explicitly includes Tribal governments in state grant outreach language and updates the TBI definition, letting the HHS Secretary revise it after consulting states and others.
Requires an HHS report to Congress within 2 years on higher-risk groups, data gaps, and outreach.
Requires an HHS study and report within 2 years on long-term symptoms of TBI, including links to dementia and mental health. The report must be posted publicly if HHS does the study directly.
who: People who have had a TBI or concussion, and their families
Higher-risk groups: military and public safety workers, people in risky occupations, survivors of domestic violence or sexual assault
State and tribal governments and agencies that receive TBI grants
Protection and advocacy organizations for people with disabilities
CDC and HHS staff, who carry out the data collection, reports, and study
Researchers and health providers who use the data

stage.last_action: Held at the desk.

life.reason: Renewing TBI surveillance, prevention tips for higher-risk groups, and long-term outcome research supports preventing and treating brain injuries that can be life-altering or fatal.

transparency.reason: Requires CDC to post aggregated TBI and concussion information online and HHS to publicly post a study it conducts itself, and renames a program after a public official.

local_say.reason: Explicitly includes tribal governments and American Indian consortia in state grant outreach and lets states and others be consulted on the TBI definition revision.

news.overall: None of the provided headlines mention the Dennis John Benigno Traumatic Brain Injury Program Reauthorization Act of 2026, so this analysis cannot describe how any outlet framed the bill itself. The Lean Left group has five headlines on measles, immune function, brain data rights, and pain genetics, with the NYT brain-data piece the only one loosely near the topic of brain health; the Center group has a single UPI headline on a Java security issue, so evidence there is extremely thin. Coverage of the bill would need to be gathered separately to make a meaningful comparison.

label: S. 911
title: Chief Herbert D. Proffitt Act of 2025
short_title: Chief Herbert D. Proffitt Act of 2025
one: The bill would let certain retired law enforcement officers, or their families, get federal Public Safety Officers' Benefits if the officer is killed or permanently disabled in a targeted attack because of their police service.
summary: Right now, a federal program called the Public Safety Officers' Benefits (PSOB) program pays money to families of officers who die in the line of duty, and to officers who are permanently disabled on duty. This bill would widen that program to cover some retired law enforcement officers. To qualify, the person must have left their job in good standing at a public agency. They must also have died or become permanently and totally disabled as the direct result of an injury from a targeted attack. The attack must have happened because of the person's past work as a law enforcement officer. In other words, this is about retired officers who are singled out and attacked in revenge or retaliation for their service, not about general injuries or crimes. The bill would take effect once signed into law. It would apply to cases still pending at the Bureau of Justice Assistance, and to new claims. It also reaches back to cover events on or after January 1, 2012. The bill is named for Chief Herbert D. Proffitt. The text does not say who he was or give the case behind the name. It does not include a cost estimate or new funding amounts.

Defines a "retired law enforcement officer" as someone who left service in good standing at a public agency, with or without pay.
Makes such a retiree eligible for benefits if they die or become permanently and totally disabled as the direct result of a targeted attack because of their law enforcement service.
Takes effect on enactment and applies to pending matters before the Bureau of Justice Assistance and to later claims.
Applies to qualifying actions taken against retired officers on or after January 1, 2012.

This bill extends death and disability benefits under the Public Safety Officers’ Benefits (PSOB) program to certain retired law enforcement officers who die or become permanently and totally disabled as a direct and proximate result of a personal injury from a targeted attack based on the retired officer’s law enforcement service.
To be eligible for PSOB benefits under the bill, a retired law enforcement officer must have retired in good standing.
The bill applies retroactively to retired officers who die or become permanently and totally disabled on or after January 1, 2012.

label: S. 97
title: Securing Semiconductor Supply Chains Act
one: Requires the Commerce Department's SelectUSA program to gather input from state economic development groups and report to Congress on how to attract more foreign investment in U.S. semiconductor manufacturing, using no new money.
summary: This bill tells SelectUSA, a Commerce Department program that tries to attract business investment to the United States, to study how to bring more foreign investment into making computer chips (semiconductors) here. Within 180 days of the bill becoming law, SelectUSA's leader must ask state-level economic development organizations for comments. They would be asked what the federal government can do, what barriers exist, what opportunities states have found, and what resource gaps hold them back. They would also be asked for ideas on how SelectUSA can help and how to work with allied countries so that "foreign adversaries" do not benefit from the effort. Within two years, SelectUSA must send a report to the Senate and House commerce committees. The report would review the comments, describe what SelectUSA is already doing, and assess strategies it could use. The bill does not create new grants, tax breaks, or rules, and it does not authorize new money. SelectUSA must do the work with funds it already has. The bill passed the Senate on May 20, 2025, and is now waiting in the House. The text does not say anything about environmental, water, or air standards, or about public input beyond state organizations.

label: S. 1051
title: Historic Greenwood District—Black Wall Street National Monument Establishment Act
short_title: Black Wall Street National Monument Act
one: Creates a National Park System unit in Tulsa, Oklahoma, to preserve and teach the history of the Greenwood District, Black Wall Street, and the 1921 Tulsa Race Massacre, with a mostly descendant-led advisory commission.
summary: This bill would create the Historic Greenwood District–Black Wall Street National Monument in Tulsa, Oklahoma, as part of the National Park System. Its purpose is to preserve and explain the history of the Greenwood District, the thriving Black business community known as Black Wall Street, and the 1921 Tulsa Race Massacre. The monument would not officially exist until the Interior Secretary decides enough land has been acquired to make a manageable park. The Secretary could get land inside the mapped boundary only by donation, by buying from a willing seller, or by swapping land. The bill says it does not affect the rights of private property owners inside or next to the monument. The Secretary could also sign agreements with public or private groups for education, interpretation, and technical help. The National Park Service would run the site under normal park laws and write a management plan within 3 years after money is first made available. The bill also creates an 11-member advisory commission. Seven members would be descendants of people who lived or worked in Greenwood in 1921, three would have historic preservation expertise, and one would be recommended by Tulsa's mayor. Members serve without pay, though travel costs are covered. The commission would end 10 years after the monument is established. The bill exempts the commission from a federal advisory committee law (FACA), which normally sets open-meeting and record rules. It does not give a dollar amount.

label: S. 1377
title: Theodore Roosevelt National Park Wild Horses Protection Act
short_title: Theodore Roosevelt National Park Wild Horses Protection Act
one: Requires the Interior Department to keep a genetically diverse herd of at least 150 horses in the South Unit of Theodore Roosevelt National Park, limits when horses can be removed, and requires yearly public reporting on the herd.
summary:
This bill would change the 1947 law that governs Theodore Roosevelt National Park in North Dakota. It would require the Secretary of the Interior to keep a herd of horses in the park's South Unit. The herd must be genetically diverse, meaning varied enough to stay healthy over time, and must have at least 150 horses.

Within 120 days of becoming law, Interior must write a plan for managing the horses. The plan must be cost-effective and must make sure the park's natural resources, such as grasslands and wildlife habitat, are not harmed.

The bill also limits removing horses from federal land in the park. Removal is allowed only as part of a plan to keep the herd genetically diverse, in an emergency, or to protect public health and safety. As written, the text joins these conditions in a slightly unusual way, so how they fit together could be a question for the agency or courts.

Finally, each year Interior must monitor the herd and publish what it finds about the herd's size, makeup, and health. The bill does not add money. It does not say how many horses is too many, or what happens if the herd and the park's plants and wildlife come into conflict. The bill passed the Senate on June 11, 2026, and is now in the House Natural Resources Committee.

Requires the plan to be cost-effective and to avoid adverse impacts on the park's natural resources.
Bars removal of horses from federal land in the park except to maintain genetic diversity, in an emergency, or to protect public health and safety.
Requires annual monitoring and public release of findings on herd population, structure, and health.
Retitles section 5 of the 1947 park law and adds the new horse provisions as a subsection.

Theodore Roosevelt National Park Wild Horses Protection Act

title: Route 66 National Historic Trail Designation Act
short_title: Route 66 National Historic Trail Designation Act
one: Adds Route 66, about 2,400 miles from Chicago to Santa Monica, to the National Trails System as a National Historic Trail, with strong limits on land acquisition, buffer zones, new permits, and any interference with energy projects.
summary:
This bill would officially name Route 66 a National Historic Trail. The trail would include every path U.S. Highway 66 followed between 1926 and 1985. It runs about 2,400 miles from Chicago, Illinois, to Santa Monica, California. The Secretary of the Interior would run the trail in a way that keeps its quirky, one-of-a-kind character. Before taking actions that would strongly affect Indian Tribes, the Secretary would have to consult with them.

The bill also sets many limits. The federal government could not take land by eminent domain, which is the power to force a sale. Outside federal areas, it could only get land from owners who agree. It could not acquire land more than an average of a quarter mile on either side of the trail. The bill says the trail creates no "buffer zone." Activities that can be seen or heard from the trail could not be limited because of it. Nothing about the trail could block, hinder, or disrupt energy development or transport, such as pipelines and power lines. The designation would not add new permit requirements and would not change who can grant easements or rights-of-way (permission to cross land). It would also keep the trail from being treated as National Park System land under a pipeline law.

The text does not list any money amounts. It passed the Senate on November 12, 2026, and now goes to the House. The text does not say whether Congress would set aside money, and a CRS summary was not available.

summary: This bill changes the Higher Education Act, the main federal law covering colleges that receive federal student aid. First, colleges would have to accept several kinds of existing paperwork as enough proof that a student has a disability. These include a high school IEP (a special education plan) or a Section 504 plan used at any point in high school, a record from another college, a record from a licensed professional, a service record under the Americans with Disabilities Act, or documentation of a disability from military service. Colleges could still choose rules that are easier than these. Second, colleges would have to clearly explain how they decide who gets accommodations. They would need to share this with students, parents, and faculty, including at orientation and on a public website. Third, colleges would report yearly numbers to the federal data system (IPEDS): how many students are registered with disability services, how many get accommodations, what share of students that is, and how many degrees or certificates they earn. This bill would set up a new national historical park in New York State at Fort Ontario. During World War II, 982 refugees, mostly Jewish people who had fled the Holocaust, were housed there from August 1944 to February 1946. The park would not start right away. The Secretary of the Interior must first decide that enough land, or interests in land, has been acquired inside the "Proposed Boundary" on a September 2024 map to make a manageable park. Within 30 days after that decision, the Secretary must announce the park in the Federal Register, the government's daily public notice.

The National Park Service could get land by donation, by purchase with donated or taxpayer-appropriated money, or by exchange. Land owned by the State or a local government could be obtained only by donation. The Secretary could sign agreements with the State and with public or private groups to provide education and interpretation. The Secretary could also make agreements to restore important historic resources on non-federal land in or near the park. Any such agreement that helps non-federal land must allow reasonable public access. Within 3 fiscal years after funding becomes available, the Secretary must finish a general management plan in consultation with the State. The bill text does not give a dollar amount or say how much land is involved.

label: H.R. 1013
title: Retirement Fairness for Charities and Educational Institutions Act of 2025
short_title: Retirement Fairness for Charities and Educational Institutions Act
one: The bill changes federal securities laws so 403(b) retirement plans, used by public school staff, charity workers, and church employees, can invest in pooled bank trust funds and insurance company separate accounts, as 401(k) plans already can.
summary:
Many teachers, nurses at nonprofit hospitals, charity workers, and church employees save for retirement in 403(b) plans. Today, federal securities rules mostly limit these plans to mutual funds and annuities. Larger 401(k) plans can also use other pooled investment options, such as collective investment trusts (CITs). A CIT is a pooled fund run by a bank or trust company. 401(k) plans can also use insurance company "separate accounts," which are investment accounts an insurer keeps apart from its other money. These options often have lower fees.

This bill would update three securities laws: the Investment Company Act of 1940, the Securities Act of 1933, and the Securities Exchange Act of 1934. After that, 403(b) plans could invest in CITs and insurance company separate accounts without those products having to follow the full registration and disclosure rules that apply to mutual funds.

The bill sets conditions. A plan must be covered by ERISA (the main federal private-pension law), or the employer must agree to act as a fiduciary for choosing the plan's investment options. A fiduciary has a legal duty to act in participants' best interest. Government plans would need the employer or another responsible person to review and approve each investment option before it is offered. The bill does not say when it would take effect. It passed the House and is now in the Senate Banking Committee.

label: H.R. 10238
title: Cybersecurity for Small Businesses Act of 2026
short_title: Cybersecurity for Small Businesses Act of 2026
one: Requires the Small Business Administration to create and share cybersecurity guidance with small businesses, including information on Defense Department cybersecurity certification for federal contractors, and to report yearly to Congress.
summary:
This bill tells the Small Business Administration (SBA) to help small businesses protect themselves from hackers and online threats. The SBA would work with two other federal agencies that focus on cybersecurity, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). Together they would develop and share guides and resources on good cybersecurity habits.

The bill also covers small businesses that want to work as contractors or subcontractors for the federal government. The SBA, working with the Department of Defense and other agencies, would give them information about the Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification (CMMC). This is a set of cybersecurity standards for Defense Department contractors. The SBA would draw on existing Defense Department resources, including a small business office, a program created in the 2026 defense bill, and the APEX Accelerator program. The SBA would post this information on its website and in its outreach.

Each year the SBA would also consult its Office of Advocacy on the best ways to share other cybersecurity information. Within 90 days of the bill becoming law, and every year after that, the SBA would send Congress a report. The report would give the number and a description of small businesses that contacted the SBA about cybersecurity. The bill does not set aside new money, and it does not create new penalties or requirements for businesses.

This bill would change the law that governs Small Business Investment Companies (SBICs). SBICs are privately owned investment firms licensed by the Small Business Administration (SBA). They invest in small businesses and can borrow money that the federal government guarantees. The bill would not change who can get that money or how much. It only adds a reporting duty.

Starting 90 days after the bill becomes law, the SBA would have to post a report on its website every three months. The report would include the same information the SBA already puts in its yearly report on this program, such as how many SBICs are licensed and how much government-backed financing each has received. It would also list how many applicants were approved to move to the final licensing stage. It would list how many of those applicants went on to meet the legal requirements for a license. It would give the dollar value of debentures issued, which are loans the government backs. Finally, it would give the number of jobs created or sustained because of SBIC investments.

The bill passed the House on November 11, 2026. It is now in the Senate Small Business and Entrepreneurship Committee. The text does not say how the SBA would count jobs.

SBIC Reporting Modernization Act of 2026

label: H.R. 10355
title: Disaster Loan Outreach Consistency Act
one: Requires the Small Business Administration to set up standard procedures so its disaster loan outreach materials (press releases, fact sheets) are accurate, current, and consistent across all its disaster field offices.
summary: This bill tells the Small Business Administration (SBA) to clean up how it talks to the public about disaster loans. The SBA's disaster loan program offers low-interest loans to homeowners, renters, businesses, and nonprofits recovering from declared disasters. Today, each disaster field operations center prepares its own outreach materials, such as press releases and fact sheets. The bill would require the SBA head to create procedures within 180 days of the bill becoming law so those materials always include accurate, up-to-date information on loan terms and on any changes to federal disaster assistance eligibility steps. The procedures must include standard templates, a check before anything is released to confirm it uses the current template and current rules, and a review every year (and right after any major change to the procedures) to make sure all field centers are consistent. The Administrator may add other information or procedures. Within 30 days of creating or significantly changing the procedures, the SBA must notify the House and Senate small business committees. The bill does not create new loans, change who qualifies, or provide new money. The text does not include a cost estimate. The bill passed the House on November 11, 2026, and is now in a Senate committee.

one: Gives the SBA's veterans business office 60 days after enactment to set up policies that make sure it files its required reports on veteran-owned small businesses.
summary: This bill is a short, government-accountability measure. Under a 1999 law, the Small Business Administration (SBA) must report on the needs of small businesses owned and controlled by veterans, including veterans with service-connected disabilities. Those reports must also include proposals for improving these businesses' access to government help. The bill tells the head of the SBA's Office of Veterans Business Development (the Associate Administrator) to write and put in place policies and procedures that make sure those reporting rules are followed. The deadline is 60 days after the bill becomes law. The bill does not create new reporting rules, new programs, or new grants. It only requires the SBA to build internal processes to follow a rule that already exists. The bill's title refers to GAO (Government Accountability Office, Congress's watchdog agency) recommendations. The bill text itself does not mention a GAO report or list its findings, so I can't say from the material provided exactly which GAO recommendations prompted it. The House passed it on November 11, 2026, and the Senate Committee on Small Business and Entrepreneurship now has it.
does: Requires the SBA's Associate Administrator for Veterans Business Development to develop and implement policies and procedures within 60 days of enactment.
Aims to ensure compliance with section 603 of the Veterans Entrepreneurship and Small Business Development Act of 1999.

Creates no new programs, money, or penalties in the text provided.

label: H.R. 10375
title: 504 Modernization and Small Manufacturer Enhancement Act of 2026
short_title: 504 Modernization and Small Manufacturer Enhancement Act
one: This bill loosens and updates rules for the SBA 504 loan program, which helps small businesses finance buildings and equipment, with changes aimed at small manufacturers, workforce training, disaster recovery, and faster loan closings.
summary:
The SBA 504 loan program helps small businesses buy or build property and equipment. A nonprofit-style lender called a certified development company (CDC) works with a bank and the SBA to make these loans. This bill changes the program in several ways, mostly for loans made on or after October 1, 2027.

First, it adds new goals that can qualify a project for help: job training programs of at least 12 weeks, helping areas recover after a declared disaster (generally for five years, with one-year extensions), and expanding businesses with 10 or fewer employees.

Second, it lets certain top-rated CDCs fix typos, move up to 10% of project costs between categories, and add or change guarantors and co-borrowers at closing. It also shifts some file-review duties from SBA district lawyers to the SBA's Office of Credit Risk Management, and sets requirements for approved closing attorneys.

Third, it changes leasing rules. Borrowers may lease out part of a building to other tenants. Small manufacturers building new facilities may occupy as little as 50% instead of 60%. For existing buildings, a business that has been in place 12 months may lease up to 66%, with yearly checks and "anti-investor" certifications to keep out real estate developers.

Fourth, it requires an SBA marketing plan and a report to Congress within five years. It also removes the "credit elsewhere" test, which asks whether a borrower could not get credit elsewhere, for CDC-related financings.

Lets accredited lender CDCs fix typos, shift up to 10% of project costs, and add or swap guarantors and co-borrowers at closing.
Moves file-review duties for loans closed by designated attorneys from SBA district counsels to the Office of Credit Risk Management.
Sets requirements for designated closing attorneys: licensed, malpractice insurance, and SBA-approved training.
Requires SBA to create a marketing and outreach plan, possibly with resource partners.

Changes leasing limits: new facilities may lease up to 20% (small manufacturers need to occupy only 50%); existing buildings may lease up to 50%, or up to 66% with conditions, annual or biennial checks, and an anti-investor certification.
Caps residential leases at 1 year and commercial leases at 5 years under these rules.
Requires an SBA report to Congress within 5 years on how the leasing changes affect access to capital.
Exempts CDC loans and financings under the Small Business Investment Act from the 'credit elsewhere' test.
Applies to loans made or guaranteed on or after October 1, 2027.

Certified development companies and participating banks
SBA staff, including district counsels and the Office of Credit Risk Management
Attorneys who close 504 loans
Workers in employer training programs
Communities recovering from declared disasters
Commercial and residential tenants in 504-financed buildings
Taxpayers, who back the SBA guarantee

crs:
504 Modernization and Small Manufacturer Enhancement Act of 2026
This bill generally expands the Small Business Administration (SBA) 504 Loan Program to include additional objectives and flexibilities (e.g., new economic development objectives that may be used to qualify for assistance under the program). The program provides a small business with SBA financing—through a certified development company intermediary—for expansion or modernization.
Specifically, the bill expands the public policy goals that allow an intermediary to qualify for assistance to include additional objectives. These include (1) workforce development through work-based or work-integrated training, and (2) aiding the revitalization of an area for which a disaster has been declared or determined.
The bill also authorizes an intermediary to take specified actions to facilitate the closing of 504 loans, such as correcting borrower or lender information on loan documents or reallocating up to 10% of the cost of a project.
Further, the bill allows small businesses to lease a larger portion of renovated buildings that are financed with 504 loans to other tenants in certain circumstances. In the case of a project to renovate or reconstruct an existing building, a small business may lease a maximum of 66% of the building to commercial or residential tenants if certain conditions are met. For example, the small business must have occupied the building for 12 consecutive months prior to the project.
Additionally, the bill exempts intermediaries from the requirement to demonstrate they are unable to obtain credit elsewhere to receive 504 loans.

label: H.R. 1047
title: GRID Power Act
one: Requires FERC to write a rule letting grid operators move "dispatchable" power plants (like gas, coal, and other on-demand generators) ahead of other projects in the line to connect to the electric grid.
summary: Before a new power plant can send electricity into the high-voltage grid, it has to wait in a line called the interconnection queue. This bill tells the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC), the agency that oversees the interstate power grid, to change the rules for that line. Within 90 days of the bill becoming law, FERC must start a rulemaking. Within 180 days, it must finish a final rule. The rule must let grid operators (called transmission providers) ask FERC for permission to move "dispatchable" projects higher in the line. Dispatchable means a power source that can be turned up or down on demand and provides predictable supply. The bill does not name specific fuels. The official summary gives fossil fuel plants as examples. Grid operators who make such a request must show why it is needed and explain how it will improve grid reliability or resilience. They must also hold public comment and stakeholder engagement before sending the request to FERC. They must report regularly to FERC on grid reliability and resilience. FERC then has 60 days to approve or deny each request. FERC must review the rule at least every five years. The bill does not say what happens to projects that get bumped down the line. It also does not mention clean energy, cost limits, or environmental review.
does: Orders FERC to start a rulemaking within 90 days of enactment and finish a final rule within 180 days.
Directs FERC to address delays and inefficiency in processing grid connection requests so new dispatchable projects can connect quickly, cost-effectively, and reliably.
Changes the standard large-generator connection procedures and agreement so grid operators may propose moving dispatchable projects higher in the queue.
Requires each proposal to show a need and explain how it improves grid reliability or resilience.
Requires public comment and stakeholder engagement before a proposal goes to FERC.
Requires grid operators to report regularly to FERC on grid reliability and resilience and on actions taken under the Act.
Requires FERC to approve or deny each proposal within 60 days.
Requires FERC to review and update the rule at least every five years.
who: Developers of dispatchable plants (such as gas, coal, nuclear, hydro, or storage, depending on how FERC defines the term)
Developers of wind, solar, and other variable generation waiting in connection queues
Grid operators, regional transmission organizations, and utilities
FERC staff and commissioners
Electricity customers and ratepayers
Communities near new power plants

stage.last_action: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.

crs:
Guaranteeing Reliability through the Interconnection of Dispatchable Power Act or the GRID Power Act

This bill requires the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) to issue and periodically review a rule that revises the approval process for interconnection requests of generating units that produce electricity to prioritize dispatchable power projects (e.g., certain fossil fuel projects). 
Under the bill, 
dispatchable power
 generally refers to an electric energy generation resource, such as a generating unit that produces electricity from fossil fuels, capable of providing known and forecastable electric supply in time intervals necessary to ensure grid reliability. Currently, FERC receives interconnection requests from those projects and other generating units, such as units that produce electricity from renewable energy. Interconnection requests are requests from generating units to connect to the high voltage transmission lines of the electric grid.
First, the rule must address the efficiency and effectiveness of the existing procedures for processing interconnection requests to ensure that new dispatchable power projects that improve grid reliability and resource adequacy can interconnect to the electric grid quickly, cost-effectively, and reliably. 
Second, the rule must revise the pro forma Large Generator Interconnection Procedures, and the pro forma Large Generator Interconnection Agreement as appropriate, to authorize transmission providers to submit proposals to FERC to prioritize new dispatchable power projects that will improve grid reliability and resource adequacy by assigning those projects higher positions in the interconnection queue of the provider. FERC must review and approve or deny such proposals within 60 days after the proposal is submitted.

life.reason: Prioritizing fossil fuel plants in the queue could speed fossil generation and its pollution-related health and ecological harms, with no environmental review required.

water.reason: Fast-tracking fossil plants may increase cooling-water withdrawals and discharges from thermal plants, and the bill has no water protections.

air.reason: Moving fossil fuel plants ahead of clean generators in the queue would likely increase emissions of air pollutants and greenhouse gases, and the bill has no environmental review.

transparency.reason: Grid operators must hold public comment and stakeholder engagement and file regular public-facing reliability reports with FERC before proposals are sent.

people_over_profit.reason: The bill speeds access to the grid for favored dispatchable projects, which mainly benefits developers' schedules and returns, while wind and solar developers would be pushed back without cost or ratepayer protections.

local_say.reason: The bill includes a public comment step but does not give communities a real veto or say over siting, so the effect is unclear.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill does not provide direct subsidies or tax breaks, though it does not address who bears costs of reprioritizing the queue.

honesty_kindness.reason: The bill is neither clearly honest nor dishonest and does not touch on kindness in a clear way.

news.overall: Lean Left coverage is numerous (seven pieces across two outlets) and centers on internal environmental division, clean energy prospects, and affordability concerns, with the bill treated as one part of a wider energy story. The Center perspective has only one Christian Science Monitor article, so its evidence is limited; it frames the bill neutrally as a tradeoff between benefits and risks. No right-leaning coverage was included, so this comparison cannot show how conservative outlets frame the bill.

label: H.R. 1453
title: Clean Energy Demonstration Transparency Act of 2025
one: Requires the Department of Energy to publish, at least twice a year, contracts, milestone status, and major changes for clean energy demonstration projects it funds or manages.
summary: This bill adds a reporting rule to the 2021 Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act. It covers clean energy demonstration projects, which are pilot-scale projects the Department of Energy (DOE) funds to test new energy technology. Starting six months after the bill becomes law, and at least every six months after that, the Energy Secretary must send a report to key House and Senate committees. The report must also be posted online for the public. For each project, the report must include a copy of the first contracts or financial assistance agreements between DOE and the award recipient, along with related documents the Secretary thinks are appropriate. It must list technical, material, or financial milestones that were met or missed. It must also describe major changes to the project's scope, schedule, funding (including cost-share requirements, meaning the share the recipient pays), partners, or budget. DOE may combine these reports with other required reports, where practical, to avoid duplicating work. The bill does not add money, change which projects get funded, or set penalties for missing the deadlines. The bill passed the House on May 19, 2025, and is now in the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee.
does: Requires DOE reports on clean energy demonstration projects starting six months after enactment, then at least every six months.
who: Department of Energy and its Office of Clean Energy Demonstrations (new reporting work)
