transparency.reason: Declining reviews and narrowing the committee's focus, with the decision made internally, means fewer public expert reviews of license applications are likely to occur.

people_over_profit.reason: Faster licensing with fewer independent reviews mainly benefits applicants seeking to move projects forward, which can favor industry timelines over public safety scrutiny.

label: H.R. 1318
title: United States Research Protection Act
one: Narrows and clarifies the federal ban on researchers joining "malign foreign talent recruitment programs" so it covers programs run by foreign countries of concern (such as China, Iran, North Korea and Russia), whether they pay or reward researchers directly or indirectly.
summary: A 2022 law (part of the CHIPS and Science Act) bars researchers who get federal research money from joining "malign foreign talent recruitment programs." These are programs where a foreign government offers pay or other rewards in ways that create conflicts of interest or involve unauthorized activity, like sharing protected information without permission. This bill makes a small wording fix to that definition. First, it says the programs covered are those tied to a "foreign country of concern," a term already defined in federal law, and the CRS summary says this includes China, Iran, North Korea and Russia. Second, it removes the older two-part structure of the definition and folds the list of covered activities into one list. The bill text does not show what the removed subparagraph (B) said, so I can't describe it. Third, it says the pay or rewards can come "directly or indirectly," which could catch money routed through middlemen. The bill adds no new money, no new agency, and no new penalties. Its effect is to define which foreign programs researchers who get federal funds must avoid. It passed the House on March 24, 2025, and is now with the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee.

United States Research Protection Act
This bill clarifies the definition of a 
malign foreign talent recruitment program
 under the Research and Development, Competition, and Innovation Act.

The Research and Development, Competition, and Innovation Act, which was included in the CHIPS and Science Act, prohibits researchers who receive federal funds from participating in malign foreign talent recruitment programs, in which foreign countries incentivize or compensate researchers for activities that present a conflict of interest for the researcher or that are otherwise unauthorized (e.g., sharing proprietary information without proper authorization).
The bill clarifies that these restrictions apply to programs that are sponsored by a foreign country of concern, including China, Iran, North Korea, and Russia. The bill also clarifies that malign foreign talent recruitment programs may involve direct or indirect compensation or incentives from such countries.

label: H.R. 2102
title: Major Richard Star Act
one: The bill would let certain medically retired veterans with combat-related disabilities and fewer than 20 years of service keep their full military retired pay while also receiving their VA disability compensation, instead of having one reduced by the other.
summary:
Today, many veterans who retire from the military and also get VA disability pay see their military retired pay cut by the amount of the disability pay. This is called an "offset." Some veterans who served 20 or more years have had that offset removed over time. But veterans who were medically retired because of injury or illness (under "chapter 61" of the law) with fewer than 20 years of service are still hit by the offset, even when their disability came from combat.

This bill would end the offset for that group. If a veteran was medically retired with fewer than 20 years of service and is eligible for combat-related special compensation (a separate payment for combat-related disabilities), their retired pay could no longer be reduced because of their VA disability pay. They would receive both in full.

The bill also cleans up the law. It changes a section title and deletes old language about a phase-in period that has already ended. The changes would start on the first day of the first month after the bill becomes law. They would apply to payments for months from that date on. The bill does not say it pays back money withheld in the past. It also does not state a cost. The House has passed it, and it now goes to the Senate Armed Services Committee.
does: Stops the reduction of military retired pay for combat-related disabled veterans who retired for medical reasons (chapter 61) with fewer than 20 years of service.
Applies to those veterans who are eligible for combat-related special compensation.
Changes the title of section 1414 of title 10 to refer to "concurrent receipt" of retired pay and VA disability compensation.
Removes outdated phase-in language that no longer applies.
Takes effect the first day of the first month after enactment, covering payments from then on.
who: Veterans medically retired with fewer than 20 years of service who have combat-related disabilities
Families and survivors who depend on those veterans' income
The Department of Defense and the Department of Veterans Affairs, which administer the payments
Federal taxpayers, because the government would pay out more

stage.last_action: Motion to reconsider laid on the table Agreed to without objection.

crs:
Major Richard Star Act
This bill allows a veteran with a combat-related disability to receive retirement pay, without reduction, concurrently with their disability compensation. This includes veterans with a combat-related disability and fewer than 20 years of creditable service. (Currently, veterans who receive combat-related special compensation and retirement pay are subject to an offset in retirement pay for concurrent receipt of such benefits.)

people_over_profit.reason: Veterans with combat-related disabilities keep their full retired pay instead of having it reduced by VA disability pay, which favors individual people's income over government payment limits, though it is not a corporate profit issue.

no_bailouts.reason: It increases federal payouts to a specific group without offsetting funding, and the bill states no cost, so it adds to federal spending that taxpayers fund.

honesty_kindness.reason: Ending the offset for combat-disabled veterans who were medically retired treats them more fairly and compassionately, and the bill also cleans up outdated language.

news.overall: Lean Left coverage centers on the real-world effects of VA staffing cuts and a federal move toward psychedelic therapy for veterans, with a critical tone toward the administration's VA changes. Center coverage is more procedural, focusing on House votes on competing veterans' benefits bills and on the general principle of keeping promises to veterans. Neither group's headlines describe the Major Richard Star Act's specific provisions, and the evidence is limited to two articles per group, so these observations reflect headline and description-level framing only.

label: H.R. 10136
title: Crossett Experimental Forest Act of 2026
one: Requires the Forest Service to hand over the Crossett Experimental Forest in Arkansas, including a research natural area and facilities, to the State of Arkansas for free if the state asks, with the land kept for forest research and education.
summary: This bill would move ownership of the Crossett Experimental Forest in Arkansas from the federal government to the State of Arkansas. The transfer covers the forest, the R.R. Reynolds Research Natural Area, and the buildings and facilities that go with them. It happens only if Arkansas asks in writing within 180 days after the bill becomes law. The state pays nothing for the land but must cover the costs of the transfer, such as surveys and paperwork. Once it owns the land, Arkansas must name it the Crossett Experimental State Forest and manage it under the rules that apply to Arkansas state forests. The state must use it for forest research, education, and demonstration, in line with its long research history. It must also work with the University of Arkansas at Monticello and the University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture and give them reasonable access. If the state breaks these rules and doesn't fix the problem within 180 days after written notice, the Secretary of Agriculture may take back all or part of the land. The Forest Service must also give the state copies of its research records and data for the site, while federal records laws still apply. The bill does not give acreage, and it does not say what the land is worth. It passed the House.

title: Don Young Doug LaMalfa Indian Buffalo Management Act
one: Directs the Interior Department to help Tribes and Tribal organizations restore and manage buffalo herds and habitat on Indian land through contracts, grants, technical help, consultation, and transfers of surplus federal buffalo, for seven years.

label: H.R. 8195
title: Responsible Cormorant Management and Control Act of 2026
short_title: Responsible Cormorant Management and Control Act of 2026
one: Requires the Fish and Wildlife Service to write rules for regional plans that set how, when, and by whom double-crested cormorants may be killed or otherwise controlled, with population limits, public reporting, and non-lethal measures, ending in 2034.
summary: This bill tells the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to create regional plans for managing double-crested cormorants, a native waterbird that eats fish and sometimes clashes with fisheries, fish farms, and private ponds. Within one year, the agency must issue rules, working with the four regional Flyway Councils (groups of state and federal wildlife officials). Each plan must keep every breeding population healthy and make sure the total number of birds killed or otherwise "taken" stays at a level science says is sustainable. Plans must spell out allowed methods and times for taking birds, who may do it (state and tribal wildlife agencies, plus trained or authorized lake and pond managers), steps to avoid harming other birds and species, and non-lethal tools that must be used. Plans must also require yearly public reports of how many birds, including non-target birds, were taken. The agency must weigh the birds' effects on fish, plants, other birds, human health, water quality, and endangered species. It must also recommend actions on National Wildlife Refuges. Population surveys and plan updates happen every five years. Within 90 days, the agency must report to Congress on whether hunting licenses for cormorants are feasible. The whole law stops having effect on January 1, 2034. The bill does not state a dollar amount.
does: Orders the Interior Secretary (through FWS) to issue rules within 1 year for regional cormorant management frameworks, working with the four Flyway Councils.
who: Double-crested cormorants and other birds near them

stage.last_action: Motion to reconsider laid on the table Agreed to without objection.

crs:
Responsible Cormorant Management and Control Act of 2026
This bill requires the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) to develop frameworks to manage regional populations of double-crested cormorants (a type of waterbird native to North America).
Specifically, FWS must coordinate with the four Regional Flyway Councils to develop regional management frameworks for double-crested cormorants. Among other elements, each framework must (1) ensure the breeding population is managed at a sufficient level to ensure conservation, (2) include parameters regarding the taking (e.g., capturing or hunting) of double-crested cormorants, and (3) consider any documented effects of double-crested cormorants in the region (e.g., impacts on fisheries). 
In developing each framework, FWS must also work with state and tribal game and fish agencies and the applicable Regional Flyway Council to make recommendations for managing double-crested cormorants within the National Wildlife Refuge System. 
FWS must coordinate with the Regional Flyway Councils every five years to survey the population of double-crested cormorants. Additionally, each framework must be reviewed and updated every five years, incorporating results of the most recent population survey. FWS must also report to Congress on the feasibility of issuing hunting licenses to manage double-crested cormorants in accordance with the frameworks.
The requirements of this bill terminate on January 1, 2034.

label: H.R. 8483
title: Barona Group of Capitan Grande Band of Mission Indians Land Transfer Act of 2026
one: Moves about 847 acres of federal land in San Diego County into trust for the Barona Group of Capitan Grande Band of Mission Indians, keeps public access and fire-response access, and bans gambling on the land.
summary:
This bill would give about 847 acres of federal land in San Diego County, California, to the Barona Group of Capitan Grande Band of Mission Indians. The land would be held "in trust" by the United States for the Tribe. That means the federal government keeps legal title, and the Tribe uses and manages the land. The land would become part of the Tribe's reservation. One parcel of 164 acres now belongs to the Bureau of Land Management. Two parcels totaling 683 acres now belong to the Forest Service. Control of the Forest Service land would move to the Interior Department.

The bill puts conditions on the transfer. Existing rights-of-way, leases, permits, and easements stay in place. The public keeps its current access for recreation, scenery, science, and conservation, including roads and trails. Federal employees keep access for search and rescue, wildfire fighting, evacuations, and other management work. The Tribe must maintain the fuel break (a cleared strip that slows wildfire) on the two Forest Service parcels, following Forest Service standards. Federal agencies can still carry out fuel reduction work in consultation with the Tribe. Gambling is banned on the land. Existing water rights and service agreements are not changed. The bill says nothing about its cost. The House has passed it.
does: Takes three federal parcels (about 847 acres) in San Diego County into trust for the Barona Tribe and makes them part of its reservation.
Moves control of the two Forest Service parcels (683 acres) to the Interior Department.

label: S. 4784
title: National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027
short_title: National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027 (NDAA)
one: The yearly Senate defense policy bill sets spending limits, troop levels, weapons buying rules, military pay and benefits, and nuclear-weapons programs for fiscal year 2027, and it bundles in hundreds of smaller policy changes.
summary:
This is the annual "must-pass" defense policy bill. It does not hand out money itself. It sets the maximum amounts that Congress may later spend (a separate spending bill does that) on the Pentagon, military construction, and the Energy Department's nuclear weapons work. It also sets troop numbers and policy.

Big pieces include: multiyear contracts for weapons such as F-35 and F-15EX jets, E-2D aircraft, and Army vehicles; a push for cheaper missiles and air-defense interceptors; a military pay raise and more hostile-fire pay; and many health care, child care, housing, and family changes. It would let the Pentagon's Office of Strategic Capital buy ownership stakes in private companies working on batteries and critical minerals. It has many AI and cyber rules, including a requirement for human oversight of use of force. It also covers aid and cooperation with Israel, Ukraine, Taiwan, and others, and Guantanamo detainee limits.

Some sections deal with PFAS ("forever chemical") cleanup, military housing health and safety, and limits on contractor stock payouts. Others deal with social policy, such as restrictions on diversity programs and on males in women's academy sports. It would also rename the Department of Defense the Department of War. I could only read part of the text. The funding tables and many later sections were cut off, so details on those are not confirmed here.

Authorizes Department of Energy national security programs, including National Nuclear Security Administration weapons work (about $32.3 billion in the visible table) and defense environmental cleanup (about $7.0 billion), plus the Defense Nuclear Facilities Safety Board.
Allows multiyear contracts for F-35 and F-15EX aircraft, Infantry Squad Vehicles, E-2D aircraft, and certain munitions.
Directs development of low-cost alternative missiles and interceptors, with production planning by FY2030.
Sets minimum aircraft inventories, such as at least 1,800 Air Force fighters through 2035, 180 MQ-9 drones, and 16 E-3 AWACS planes (with an exception).

Authorizes the Office of Strategic Capital to make equity investments (ownership stakes) in non-federal companies for batteries and critical minerals, materials, and chemicals; adds ownership reviews and notification rules.
Includes PFAS provisions: dashboard update notices, a contracting study, starting cleanup actions, and public-participation technical assistance in cleanup.
Adds military housing health and safety standards, protection from retaliation for tenants who report problems, and rules on nondisclosure agreements.
Sets policy on AI and cyber, including human oversight of use of force, security standards for AI agents, and bans on certain China-linked equipment.
Limits contractor capital distributions, requires reporting of price increases, and adds post-government employment limits for senior officials.
Repeals the GAO review of missile defense programs and gives financial-audit reporting relief, and repeals certain other reporting requirements.
Redesignates the Department of Defense as the Department of War and restructures combatant commands.
Includes social policy provisions on DEI, merit-only personnel actions, women's athletics and privacy spaces at service academies, and sex-neutral performance standards.
Extends Guantanamo transfer bans, aid to Ukraine and Taiwan programs, and Israel cooperation programs.

label: H.R. 3495
title: Direct Seller and Real Estate Agent Harmonization Act
short_title: Direct Seller and Real Estate Agent Harmonization Act
one: Says that direct sellers (like people who sell products through home-party or network sales companies) and qualified real estate agents are not "employees" under the federal wage-and-hour law, so minimum wage and overtime rules would not apply to them.
summary:
This bill changes the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA), the main federal law that sets the minimum wage and overtime pay. It adds one sentence to the law's definition of "employee." Under that sentence, anyone who counts as a "direct seller" or a "qualified real estate agent" would not be an employee under the FLSA. Those two terms are not defined in the bill itself. Instead, it points to section 3508(b) of the tax code, which already treats these groups as independent contractors for federal tax purposes. That tax rule generally covers people paid based on sales or output, not hours worked, who work under a written contract saying they are not employees for tax purposes.

In practice, a company that works with these sellers or agents would not have to pay them the federal minimum wage or overtime under the FLSA. The bill supporters call it "harmonizing" labor law with tax law so the two match. The bill does not say what happens under state wage laws, and it does not change any other federal worker protection laws, as far as the text shows. It does not include any spending. The House Rules Committee has set it for floor debate under a closed rule, meaning no floor amendments, with one hour of debate.
does: placeholder

Real estate agents who meet the tax code definition of a qualified real estate agent

benefits: Aligns federal labor-law and tax-law treatment, which could reduce confusion and legal disputes over classification.
Could keep the flexible, commission-based work arrangements many sellers and agents say they prefer.
Could lower legal and compliance risk for direct selling companies and brokerages, which may help small independent sellers keep access to the work.
concerns: Takes away federal minimum wage and overtime coverage from these workers, even if a particular worker is in practice controlled like an employee.
Could make it harder for workers to challenge misclassification under the FLSA, and might encourage companies to push more control over workers without paying wage protections.
Could shift risk and costs onto individual workers, and the exclusion is written to be broad rather than tied to actual independence.
imp.cost: The bill has no spending or funding provisions. Any cost would fall indirectly on workers (lost wage protections) or benefit businesses (lower labor costs). I could not see a Congressional Budget Office estimate in the material provided.
unknowns: How many workers would actually lose FLSA coverage today versus those already treated as contractors.
Whether state minimum wage and overtime laws would still apply to these workers.
How the tax-code definitions, which depend on written contracts and pay based on sales, would interact with real working conditions.
The text of the amendment is short, but the committee report and any floor changes were not available to me.

label: H.R. 9640
title: Earth MRI Reauthorization Act of 2026
one: Extends the U.S. Geological Survey's Earth Mapping Resources Initiative through fiscal 2031 with $84 million, adds new data sources and technologies, and requires contractor ownership disclosure with a preference for U.S.-owned firms.
summary:
This bill keeps alive a U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) program called the Earth Mapping Resources Initiative, often called Earth MRI. The program maps what is under U.S. ground, especially critical minerals such as lithium and titanium, and the bill's text also names geothermal and geologic hydrogen resources. The bill would authorize $84 million for fiscal years 2027 through 2031. "Authorize" means Congress says the money may be spent. A separate spending law must actually provide it.

The bill also updates how the mapping is done. It says the program may use newer tools such as airborne gravity gradiometry (measuring tiny changes in gravity from aircraft), digital chemical analysis, real-time data collection, and data-driven analysis. It adds the USGS 3D Hydrography Program, which maps U.S. water features, to the data sources the program must combine.

Finally, the bill sets new rules for contracts. Any company that wants a contract under the program must disclose who owns the main contractor and each subcontractor. The USGS must also, when practical, prefer companies that are owned and controlled in the United States, while still considering specialized expertise it needs.

crs:
Earth MRI Reauthorization Act of 2026
This bill reauthorizes through FY2031 the Earth Mapping Resources Initiative, a U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) program charged with integrating and modernizing the mapping of U.S. natural resources, with a focus on critical mineral resources such as lithium and titanium. The bill also expands the initiative’s data integration functions and requires the USGS to give preference to U.S. contractors under the initiative.
Specifically, the bill requires entities contracting with the USGS pursuant to the initiative to disclose the ownership of the primary contractor and each subcontractor carrying out a part of the contract. To the extent practicable, the USGS must give preference to entities owned and controlled in the United States when entering contracts under the initiative, while giving appropriate consideration to specialized expertise essential to the objectives of the initiative.
Further, under current law, the initiative is required to provide certain types of integrated mapping, including geologic, geophysical, and topographical mapping. Under the bill, the initiative must include data from the USGS 3D Hydrography Program, which maps U.S. water resources. The bill also explicitly allows the initiative’s integrated mapping to include data from modern sensing technologies, including real-time data acquisition systems and data-driven analytical methods.

label: H.R. 2116
title: Law Enforcement Support and Counter Transnational Repression Act
short_title: Law Enforcement Support and Counter Transnational Repression Act
one: Requires the Department of Homeland Security to run a public awareness campaign about foreign governments harassing or threatening people in the U.S., and to research tools to help law enforcement counter it.
summary: This bill adds a new section to the Homeland Security Act. It tells the Secretary of Homeland Security to have the department's Office of Partnership and Engagement run a public service announcement campaign. The campaign would teach the public and U.S. international allies about "transnational repression." That term means a foreign government, or someone acting under its control, trying to scare, harass, coerce, or hurt people in the U.S. or U.S. persons abroad. It includes threats against family members, efforts to silence people's First Amendment rights, and extrajudicial killings (killings outside any legal process). The campaign must also explain what help is available to victims and how to anonymously report suspected cases to the FBI. It should be run in languages the Secretary finds relevant. Within one year, and "to the extent practicable," DHS must also research and test technologies and methods to better support federal, state, local, tribal, and territorial officials in countering this kind of repression and related terrorism threats. That work must follow constitutional, privacy, civil rights, and civil liberties protections. The bill sets no dollar amount and does not create new crimes or new police powers. It does not say where the money comes from. The bill is out of committee and on the House calendar.

Law Enforcement Support and Counter Transnational Repression Act
This bill requires the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to take actions to combat transnational repression against individuals inside the United States. The term 
transnational repression
 generally refers to actions of a foreign government or agent to harm, intimidate, threaten, harass, or coerce individuals in the United States.
Specifically, the bill requires DHS to direct the Office of Partnership and Engagement to conduct a public service announcement campaign to educate the public and international allies on the issue of transnational repression and related terrorism threats.
The bill also requires DHS to conduct research and development into technologies and techniques for enhancing its support to federal, state, local, tribal, and territorial officials in combating transnational repression and related terrorism threats.

label: H.R. 143
title: Unauthorized Spending Accountability Act
one: Starting in fiscal year 2026, the bill automatically cuts the spending limits for federal programs whose congressional authorization has expired, by 10% and then 15% a year, and ends those programs after three years unless Congress reauthorizes them.
summary:
Congress usually works in two steps. First, it passes a law that "authorizes" a program, which means it permits the program to get money. Second, it passes yearly spending bills that actually fund it. Many programs keep getting money after their authorization runs out. This bill targets those programs.

Each year, the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) publishes a list of programs whose authorizations have expired or will expire that year. Under the bill, every program on that list would face automatic cuts to its share of the spending ceiling set for the House and Senate Appropriations Committees. The first year after expiration, the ceiling drops by 10% of what the program got in its last authorized year. In the second and third years, it drops by 15% each year, if the program is still unauthorized.

If a program is still unauthorized after the third year of cuts, it ends on October 1 of the following year. Only already-made commitments could still be paid off. No new money could be committed unless Congress reauthorizes it for no more than three years.

If Congress reauthorizes a program in time, with a sunset of three years or less, the cuts are cancelled and any lost funding is restored. Programs that expired before 2026 and are funded in 2026 are treated as if they expire in 2026. The cycle repeats every three years.
does: Creates a repeating three-year cut cycle for unauthorized programs, starting in fiscal year 2026.
Defines an unauthorized program as one listed in CBO's 'Expired and Expiring Authorizations of Appropriations' report.
Treats programs that expired before fiscal 2026 and are funded in 2026 as expiring in 2026.
Cuts the spending ceiling by 10% of the program's last-authorized-year funding in the first year after expiration.
Cuts it by 15% in each of the second and third years if the program is still unauthorized.
Requires the House and Senate Budget Committee chairs to send the revised levels to the Appropriations chairs.
Terminates programs after the third reduction year, with funds left only to close out valid earlier obligations.
Bars new spending on a terminated program unless Congress reauthorizes it for three years or less.
Cancels and restores cuts if a program is reauthorized in time with a sunset of three years or less.
who: Recipients and workers of federal programs with expired authorizations
Federal agencies running those programs
House and Senate Appropriations and Budget Committees
State and local governments and nonprofits that depend on federal grants
Congressional authorizing committees, which would face deadlines
Taxpayers and the public served by affected programs

label: H.R. 1640
title: HEIRS Act of 2025
one: Lets HUD give grants to help families who inherited land or homes without a will (heirs' property) pay for the legal and title work needed to keep their property and protect it from forced sale.
summary:
When someone dies without a will, their home or land often passes to several relatives who all own it together, as "tenants in common." In many places, any one of those relatives, or an outsider who buys that person's share, can ask a court to force a sale of the whole property. This has caused many families, especially low-income and Black rural families, to lose land and homes that were passed down for generations.

This bill would let the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) run two grant programs. The first would give money to states, local governments, territories, and tribal governments that have adopted (or will adopt) the Uniform Partition of Heirs Property Act, a model law with protections against forced sales. They would use the money to help residents pay for things like title reports, land surveys, heirs searches, estate planning, filing fees, and legal fees. The second would give grants to HUD-approved housing counseling agencies, college legal clinics, and qualifying nonprofits to give counseling, legal help, and financial help to clear titles and keep homes. Housing counselors that already get HUD money would also have to explain heirs' property risks and point people to help. Both grant programs end seven years after the bill becomes law. The bill says HUD "may" create the programs and does not set a dollar amount.
does: Lets HUD create a grant program for states, localities, territories, and tribes that have adopted or later adopt the Uniform Partition of Heirs Property Act (or something HUD finds substantially equivalent).
who: Families who own inherited land or homes without clear title, especially low- and moderate-income and rural families

crs:
Heirs Estate Inheritance Resolution and Succession Act of 2025 or the HEIRS Act of 2025
This bill authorizes the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) to provide grants to assist individuals with the legal processes associated with inheriting certain real property.
Under the first program, HUD may provide grants to states that have enacted the Uniform Partition of Heirs Property Act (UPHPA) (or similar state law). The UPHPA provides due process protections against forced property sales for individuals who inherit real property from a landowner without a will. Historically, state property laws have provided that recipients of such property become tenants-in-common, which permits a single tenant to exercise their right to partition and sell the property.
A state, tribe, or local government must use grant funds to assist residents in the jurisdiction with expenses related to establishing and documenting property ownership rights or settling a decedent's estate, including costs related to
obtaining title reports, title abstracts, copies of public records, and land surveys;
estate planning;
heirs searches or tracing services; and
recording and filing fees, notary fees, and legal fees and expenses.
Under the second program, HUD may provide grants to housing counseling agencies, legal services clinics at institutions of higher education, and qualified nonprofits. Such organizations must use grant funds to provide housing counseling, legal assistance, and financial assistance related to title clearing and home retention efforts for individuals who inherit property as tenants-in-common.
Both grant programs terminate seven years after the enactment of this bill.

life.reason: Helping families keep inherited homes and land protects housing stability and the wellbeing that comes with it, though the effect on life broadly is indirect.

transparency.reason: Requires HUD-funded housing counselors to explain heirs' property risks and points residents to help, and the grant programs are publicly administered, which modestly improves public understanding of their rights.

people_over_profit.reason: It shields families from forced sales that can be triggered by outside investors buying a single heir's share, putting household land retention ahead of investor gains from partition sales.

local_say.reason: It encourages states and localities to adopt the UPHPA, a local legal protection that limits forced sales and keeps decisions about family property with the owners and heirs.

no_bailouts.reason: It is a grant program for individuals and governments, not a corporate bailout or ratepayer-funded tax break, and the bill sets no dollar amount.

honesty_kindness.reason: It provides compassionate help to grieving families navigating complicated estate and title processes, and it is not contrary to honesty.

label: H.R. 2613
title: Next Generation Pipelines Research and Development Act
short_title: Next Generation Pipelines Research and Development Act
one: Sets up Department of Energy research, demonstration, and standards programs to develop better pipeline materials, leak sensors, and safety technology, funded by shifting money already authorized for other energy research.
summary: This bill would create several federal programs to research and test new pipeline technology. Pipelines covered include natural gas, liquid fuel, hydrogen, carbon dioxide, and water lines, plus liquefied natural gas (LNG) and fuel storage sites. First, the Department of Energy (DOE) would run a demonstration program giving competitive grants to colleges, labs, nonprofits, and private companies. Projects could cover leak detection, stronger materials and coatings, sensors, robots, self-repairing pipe, cybersecurity, and tools to judge whether old pipelines can carry hydrogen or carbon dioxide. Projects that measurably reduce pipeline harm to air, water, or soil, especially in rural and underserved areas, get priority, as do projects with matching non-federal money. Second, DOE, the Department of Transportation, and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) would run a joint early-stage research program. Third, DOE would set up a National Pipeline Modernization Center with a university or similar partner, and it would help train federal and state pipeline safety inspectors. Fourth, NIST would run pipeline measurement and standards research. The bill authorizes (allows Congress to spend, but does not itself pay) $45–50 million a year for demonstrations, $20–30 million for the joint program, $10–15 million for the center, and up to $2.5 million a year for NIST. Most programs end after five years. The money would come from existing authorizations for other DOE energy research, which would be reduced.
does: Creates a DOE competitive grant program for pipeline technology demonstration projects, running five years.
who: Pipeline, LNG, and fuel storage operators, who could use the new technologies and join the projects

label: H.R. 5089
title: Weather Act Reauthorization Act of 2025
one: Renews and updates federal weather research, forecasting, warning, and data programs at NOAA through fiscal year 2030, including tornado, hurricane, tsunami, drought, flood, landslide and harmful algal bloom work, and expands use of commercial weather data.
summary: This bill renews and updates the laws that guide how the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) and the National Weather Service study and predict weather. It sets funding ceilings (called "authorizations," which are limits on what Congress may later pay for, not actual money) through fiscal year 2030. It keeps and updates programs for tornado and hurricane forecasting, adds a program for rain and atmospheric river forecasts, and renews tsunami warning, landslide preparedness, and harmful algal bloom programs. It tells NOAA to make a plan to replace its national weather radar network by 2040 and to find ways to work around radar interference, such as from wind turbines. It pushes NOAA to buy more weather data from private companies, including through radar-as-a-service contracts and a pilot program. It calls for upgrades to NOAA Weather Radio and to how warnings reach people, including in rural areas. It supports farm and water planning through drought information, a nationwide network of weather stations (the National Mesonet), and a soil moisture network. It also directs more use of artificial intelligence and cloud computing. The bill says no additional funds are authorized beyond the amounts listed for the first title. Note: part of the bill text (the middle sections on Titles II to V) was cut off, so some provisions, such as commercial data and communication sections, are known only from the table of contents and the CRS summary.

Rewrites the tornado (VORTEX) and hurricane forecast programs to focus on longer warning lead times, probabilistic forecasts, and better public risk communication, and tells NOAA to review the tornado rating system.
Renews the tsunami warning program at $30 million per year through 2030, with updates to alert levels, warning centers, inundation maps, and backup systems.
Creates a precipitation forecast program, including atmospheric rivers, and a coastal flooding and storm surge program.
Directs a plan to replace the NEXRAD weather radar network by Sept. 30, 2040, and lets NOAA contract with third parties to fill radar gaps (radar-as-a-service).
Sets up a radar research program to reduce interference from wind turbines, buildings, and other structures.
Pushes NOAA to buy and test commercial weather data, and to compare federal and private options for satellites and observations.
Expands use of AI, machine learning, cloud and quantum computing, with a Department of Energy partnership and multi-year contracts.
Renews the landslide preparedness law through 2030, adding atmospheric river risks and more inclusion of Tribal and Native Hawaiian organizations.

Rewrites harmful algal bloom and hypoxia (low-oxygen water) programs for marine and freshwater, authorizes $27.5 million per year, adds an incubator program for control technologies, and treats related forecasting work as an emergency service during government shutdowns.
Authorizes drought information ($15M–$17M per year), National Mesonet (up to $50M–$70M per year), soil moisture network, and National Water Center ($46M per year).
Requires many reports and briefings to Congress, and consolidates some older reports.
Modernizes NOAA Weather Radio and weather communications (from the bill's table of contents and CRS summary; text not fully visible).

Weather Research and Forecasting Innovation Reauthorization Act of 2025 or the Weather Act Reauthorization Act of 2025
This bill reauthorizes, revises, and establishes several programs related to weather forecasting, monitoring, and research. 
For example, the bill reauthorizes through FY2030 programs that are administered by the Office of Oceanic and Atmospheric Research in the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), including the U.S. Weather Research Program. It also provides statutory authority for NOAA's Verification of the Origins of Rotation in Tornadoes Experiment (known as VORTEX-USA).
The bill also requires NOAA to establish programs that support weather forecasting technology, including improvements to radar accuracy, weather forecasting in underserved areas, and coastal flooding forecasting. NOAA must also acquire weather-related data from the private sector and establish a pilot program to test the compatibility of this data with NOAA infrastructure. 
In addition, NOAA must improve weather-related communication systems, including those related to hazardous weather events, through system upgrades that use more modern technology (e.g., cloud-based services) and that allow for expanded coverage (e.g., in rural areas).
Finally, NOAA must administer programs that support weather forecasting for agricultural and water management, including pilot programs to improve precipitation forecasts in the western and central states and a soil moisture monitoring network.

label: H.R. 5276
title: Community Bank LIFT Act
one: Lowers the capital cushion required for simplified-rule community banks, raises the size cap for those banks from $10 billion to $15 billion in assets, and orders regulators to review and rewrite the rules.
summary: Banks must hold a certain amount of their own money, called capital, as a cushion against losses. Smaller "community banks" can use a simple version of this rule called the community bank leverage ratio (CBLR). Under current law, a bank can use it if it has under $10 billion in assets, and regulators must set the required ratio between 8% and 10%. This bill makes two changes. It raises the asset limit to $15 billion, so larger banks can use the simple rule. It also lowers the allowed range for the ratio to 6% to 8%, which would let regulators require less capital. The bill also tells the Federal Reserve, the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), and the FDIC to review the CBLR and report to Congress within 150 days. The report must suggest ways to get more community banks to join, especially smaller ones, and to cut paperwork. It can cover how the ratio is calculated, how certain assets are treated, who qualifies, how banks opt in or out, and any needed law changes. Within 180 days regulators must propose rules, and within one year they must finalize rules carrying out the bill and the report's recommendations. The bill does not set a specific ratio. Regulators would pick one within the new range.
does: Raises the asset cap for CBLR-eligible community banks from $10 billion to $15 billion.
Lowers the legal range for the CBLR from 8%-10% to 6%-8%.
Requires the Fed, OCC, and FDIC to review the CBLR and report to Congress within 150 days of enactment.
Requires the report to consider how to get more banks, especially smaller ones, to opt in and how to reduce compliance burdens.
Lets the report recommend changes to ratio calculation, asset risk treatment, qualifying criteria, opt-in/out procedures, and grace periods.
Requires proposed rules within 180 days and final rules within one year, implementing the bill and the report's recommendations.
who: Community banks with $10-15 billion in assets, which could newly use the simplified rule
Community banks already using the CBLR, which could face lower capital requirements
Federal bank regulators (Fed, OCC, FDIC), who must do the review and rulemaking
Bank customers, depositors, and communities served by these banks
Taxpayers and the federal deposit insurance fund, which backstops bank failures
Congress committees that will receive the report

crs:
Community Bank Leverage Improvement and Flexibility for Transparency Act or the Community Bank LIFT Act
This bill relaxes requirements related to the community bank leverage ratio, which is a simplified capital standard applicable to qualified community banks. Community banks qualify by having less than $10 billion in assets, along with meeting other criteria.
Specifically, the bill increases this asset limit to $15 billion. Additionally, it reduces the statutory range of the leverage ratio from 8%-10% to 6%-8%. (The specific rate is set by regulation. A reduction in the leverage ratio eases capital requirements.)
The Federal Reserve Board, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation must review and report on the leverage ratio and the rules issued to carry out its implementation. The report must include a consideration of how to modify the leverage ratio to encourage more participation in the community bank leverage ratio framework, with a focus on community banks with fewer assets and providing relief from regulatory compliance burdens.
After this report is issued, the participating agencies must propose and finalize rules to implement this bill and the recommendations contained in the report.

transparency.reason: The bill requires the Fed, OCC, and FDIC to review the CBLR and report to Congress, which gives lawmakers and the public a documented review of the rule's workings.

people_over_profit.reason: Lower capital requirements and a higher asset cap let banks hold less of a cushion and expand their use of a simplified rule, which mainly benefits bank shareholders and margins at the expense of added safety for depositors and the public.

no_bailouts.reason: Thinner capital cushions raise the chance that banks fail and need taxpayer-backed deposit insurance or emergency support, which is a form of implicit bailout exposure.

label: H.R. 7086
title: Equitable Access to School Facilities Act
short_title: Equitable Access to School Facilities Act
one: The bill reworks federal Charter Schools Program grants so states can get money to buy, lease, renovate and maintain charter school buildings. It also removes federal property-tracking rules for these funds and gives priority to states with certain local land-use limits.
summary: This bill changes parts of the federal Charter Schools Program, which gives money to help charter schools (publicly funded schools run independently of the regular district) open and grow. First, it replaces an existing facilities grant with a new competitive grant for state agencies and similar groups. The money would help pay up to 60 percent of the cost of buying, leasing, renovating, and maintaining charter school buildings. The rest must come from non-federal sources, including outside organizations. States get priority if they offer charter schools tax-exempt financing, treat charters like other public schools in land use rules, or stop local governments from putting deed restrictions on property (for example, limits on charters buying surplus public property). Second, it lets another existing grant pay for help finding buildings and one-time fixes to meet building codes. States could put up to 10 percent of those grants into a revolving loan fund. It also appears to lower the minimum share that must go out as subgrants from 90 to 80 percent. Third, it says federal money in this program does not create a "federal interest" in property. That means the usual federal recording and reporting rules for property would not apply. Fourth, groups that got credit enhancement grants would have to file annual reports for 10 years. The bill does not list a dollar amount. I could not see the text of the existing law it edits.
does: Replaces the State Charter School Facilities Incentive Grant with a new competitive grant for state entities, lasting up to 5 years.
Caps the federal share at 60 percent of project costs and lets outside partner organizations cover any part of the non-federal share.

Gives priority to states with tax-exempt financing for charters, equal land-use treatment for charters, or bans on local deed restrictions that limit charter access (including buying surplus public property).
Allows grant money to fund charter building purchases, leases, renovations, ongoing facility costs, and "alternative ownership models."
Lets state entities keep up to 5 percent of the new grants for evaluation, technical help, and sharing information.
Requires applications to describe how the state will help charters in low-income and rural areas and narrow funding gaps with other public schools.
Allows State Entity grants to pay for help finding facilities and one-time help meeting building codes.
Lets states put up to 10 percent of State Entity grant funds into a revolving loan fund, and appears to lower the required subgrant share from 90 to 80 percent.
Declares that no funds under this part create a "federal interest" in property, so federal property recording and reporting rules would not apply.
Requires credit enhancement grant recipients to file annual reports for 10 years after the grant, including recipients from before the law.
Applies the changes only to grants awarded after the bill becomes law.
who: Charter school operators and the students and families in them
State education agencies and other state entities that apply for the grants
Local governments and school districts, especially their land use, permitting and surplus property rules
Nonprofit and private lenders, developers and partner organizations that help finance charter buildings
Taxpayers, whose federal money would help pay for the buildings
Students in low-income and rural communities, who the bill names as a focus

crs:
Equitable Access to School Facilities Act
This bill expands and revises certain grant programs under the Charter Schools Program (CSP).
Currently, the CSP's State Charter School Facilities Incentive Grant (SFIG) program provides competitive grants to help states establish and enhance or administer per-pupil facilities aid for charter schools.
The bill replaces the SFIG program with a new grant program, which requires the Department of Education to (1) award competitive grants to state entities with the highest-quality applications for paying the federal share of acquiring and maintaining charter school facilities; and (2) give priority to certain state entities, such as those located in a state that has tax-exempt financing for charter schools. Further, the bill outlines program requirements (e.g., cost-sharing) and allowable uses of grants.
Currently, the CSP's State Entities (SE) program authorizes competitive grants to state entities and, through them, subgrants to eligible applicants to enable them to open and prepare for the operation of a new charter school or replicate or expand a charter school. 
The bill revises the SE program by allowing grants to be used for (1) providing assistance to charter schools with locating and accessing a facility, and (2) providing one-time assistance to ensure the facility complies with building codes. Further, state entities may reserve up to 10% of grant funds for a revolving loan fund.
The bill (1) specifies that no funds made available under the CSP create a federal interest in associated property, and (2) revises reporting requirements for the CSP's Credit Enhancement grants.

transparency.reason: Declaring that federal money creates no federal interest in property and exempts it from federal recording and reporting rules reduces public visibility into how federally funded charter buildings are held and used, though credit enhancement recipients must file annual reports for 10 years, which partly offsets this.

local_say.reason: Priority for states that ban local deed restrictions and require equal land-use treatment for charters limits local control over zoning and surplus public property decisions.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill uses federal money to subsidize charter building purchases, leases, and maintenance, including tax-exempt financing support, and lets outside partners cover non-federal shares, which is a federally funded facilities subsidy for private-operated schools.

label: H.R. 8437
title: Geo POWER Act
one: The bill would create a Department of Energy program that gives milestone-based financing to next-generation geothermal power demonstration projects in new regions, with a focus on places with little or no geothermal power today.
summary: This bill would set up a new Department of Energy program, called the Milestone-Based Geothermal Demonstration Program. The program would help pay for next-generation geothermal power projects. These projects drill into hard, low-permeability rock (rock that water doesn't flow through easily), which older geothermal plants couldn't use. The Energy Department would have 180 days after the bill becomes law to start the program. Developers would compete for the money. They would get it in stages, only after they hit technical and financial goals. The department must give priority to projects in regions with little or no geothermal power now, including on or near Indian (tribal) land. It must also favor projects that share data publicly, projects aiming for at least 30 megawatts of power, and projects likely to attract private investment. The department must fund at least 3 proposals, in at least 3 states, from at least 3 different sponsors. The bill removes one existing paragraph in current law, and the text doesn't say what that paragraph covers. It also authorizes "such sums as are necessary" in appropriations, so Congress would still have to decide the actual amount. The text does not set a dollar cap or spell out environmental, water, or community-input rules.
does: Creates the Milestone-Based Geothermal Demonstration Program within the Department of Energy, to start within 180 days of enactment.
Awards "innovative financing" (financial tools, which can include transactions under existing Energy Department authority) to geothermal projects in low-permeability and impermeable reservoirs.
Ties awards to hitting technical and financial milestones through a competitive process.
Prioritizes regions with little or no geothermal power, including on or near Indian land.
Prioritizes projects that collect and share data on new geothermal resources.
Prioritizes facilities or drilling advances aimed at 30 megawatts or more, and projects likely to draw private investment.
Requires awards to at least 3 proposals, in at least 3 states, from at least 3 sponsors.
Requires the Secretary to keep enough staff to run the program.
Strikes paragraph (3) of section 615(d) of the 2007 energy law, and authorizes "such sums as are necessary" for subsections (d) and (e).
who: Geothermal developers and drilling companies
Department of Energy staff
Tribal nations and communities in regions with little geothermal power
Residents and landowners near possible project sites
Taxpayers who fund the program
Electricity customers in areas that might get new geothermal power

air.reason: Geothermal power produces little or no air pollution, so funding projects that could displace fossil fuel generation somewhat advances clean air, though the bill's direct air effect is modest.

transparency.reason: The bill favors projects that share data publicly on new geothermal resources, which somewhat increases public access to information.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill uses taxpayer-funded financing for private developers, and the text sets no dollar cap, so it is a public subsidy to particular companies, though it is milestone-based and not a rescue of failing firms.

news.overall: Lean Left coverage (seven headlines across Politico and the New York Times) centers on intra-environmental-movement tension, whether the bill serves clean energy, and grid constraints, and it links permitting to wider Iran-war and Trump energy-policy themes. The Center group has only one article from the Christian Science Monitor, so its evidence is thin. It presents the bill as a balanced trade-off of benefits and risks without much detail on the bill's mechanics.

label: H.R. 9468
title: STAR Act
short_title: STAR Act (Saving Today's Acute-Care Resources Act)
one: The bill would let more very sick Medicare patients in long-term care hospitals qualify for the higher Medicare payment rate, while extending a payment cut on other long-term care hospital stays through fiscal year 2032.
summary:
Long-term care hospitals (LTCHs) treat patients who are very sick and need hospital care for a long time. Medicare pays them one of two ways. Stays that meet certain rules get a higher, specialized rate. Stays that don't meet the rules get a lower "site-neutral" rate. That lower rate is based on what Medicare would pay a regular acute-care hospital, or the stay's cost if that is lower.

This bill would change who gets the higher rate. For stays ending on or after October 1, 2026, it adds a new "high acuity" test. A stay would qualify if the patient came straight from a regular hospital or a critical access hospital (a small rural hospital). The patient must also have a diagnosis group with a "relative weight" of 0.8 or more, a measure of how costly the case is. The diagnosis group must not be one assigned because of 96 or more hours on a ventilator. The LTCH must also have been enrolled, been in its qualifying period, been under construction, or had state approval before the bill became law. That limit blocks new LTCHs from using the exemption.

The bill would also count ICU and ventilator care given at a critical access hospital, or at an LTCH, toward the existing ICU and ventilator tests. Finally, it extends a payment reduction that applies to the site-neutral rate. The extension runs through fiscal year 2032 instead of ending in 2026. The text doesn't give cost estimates.
does: Adds a new 'high acuity' exemption from the lower site-neutral Medicare rate for LTCH stays that follow a hospital or critical access hospital stay and meet a diagnosis-weight test (0.8 or higher, not ventilator-based).

Limits the new exemption to LTCHs that were enrolled, in their qualifying period, mid-construction (with a binding contract and spending of at least 10% or $2.5 million), or had state certificate-of-need approval before enactment.
Requires mid-build hospitals to send a written certification from their CEO or COO to the Secretary within 60 days of enactment.
Lets ICU and ventilator care at a critical access hospital, or at an LTCH, count toward the existing ICU and ventilator exemptions for discharges on or after October 1, 2026.
Extends an adjustment that reduces the site-neutral payment rate by changing the end date from 2026 to 2032.
Applies the new exemptions to discharges on or after October 1, 2026.

label: S. 1254
title: A bill to amend the Aquifer Recharge Flexibility Act to clarify a provision relating to conveyances for aquifer recharge purposes.
one: The bill would let holders of existing federal land water-conveyance permits (like ditches and canals) use them to refill underground aquifers, for themselves or for public bodies, without new federal approval, after giving 30 days' notice to the Bureau of Land Management.
summary: Many ditches, canals, and pipelines cross federal land under permits, easements, or rights-of-way. A earlier law, the Aquifer Recharge Flexibility Act, said holders could move water to refill underground water supplies (aquifers) without extra federal approval, as long as the use did not expand or change the operation. This bill would clarify and widen that rule. The holder could use the existing authorization for aquifer recharge, acting for itself or for a state, local government, Indian Tribe, or other public entity. It would not need new approval from the Interior Secretary, and this use would not count as an expansion, modification, or substantial deviation from the original permit. The holder would have to tell the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) at least 30 days ahead. The notice must name who will use it, identify the permit, describe the planned use, and include a copy of the agreement between the parties. The bill also says the law does not excuse anyone from following all other applicable federal laws and BLM policies, and it does not allow building, changing, or expanding infrastructure. The Senate committee's amended version replaced the first draft. The first draft would have had a rent exemption and named specific laws, and it would have said these uses are not "major Federal action." The amended text drops those parts. CRS has not yet published a summary, so this is based on the bill text alone.

label: S. 1262
title: A bill to require the Secretary of Agriculture to release a reversionary interest in certain land in the Black River State Forest in Millston, Wisconsin, and for other purposes.
short_title: Black River State Forest Land Swap (Deli, Inc.) Release Bill
one: The bill would have the federal government give up its legal claim requiring about 31.83 acres of Black River State Forest in Wisconsin to stay in public use, so Wisconsin can trade that land to a moss-producing company, Deli, Inc., for about 37.27 acres that would be added to the forest.
summary: Some of the land in Wisconsin's Black River State Forest, near Millston, came with a federal strings-attached rule. Under an older farm law, the United States keeps a "reversionary interest." This means the land must always be used for public purposes. If it isn't, the federal government could claim it back. This bill would remove that rule from about 31.83 acres. The release would happen only if the State of Wisconsin offers, in a written agreement, to trade that land to Deli, Inc. Deli is a sphagnum moss (a bog plant used in gardening) business in Millston. In return, Deli would give the state about 37.27 acres in two separate parcels, and those acres would be added to the state forest. After the release, the Secretary of Agriculture (through the Forest Service) must provide a quitclaim deed. A quitclaim deed is a paper that passes along whatever federal interest exists, at no charge. It must be recorded before the swap deeds. The Secretary may fix mistakes in the land descriptions, working with the state. The bill's land definition says the swap is subject to approval by the Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources, the Natural Resources Board, and the Governor. The bill text does not mention appraisals, environmental review, or public comment.

Triggers the release only if Wisconsin makes a written offer to trade that land to Deli, Inc. for about 37.27 acres of Deli land.
Says the Deli land would be added to Black River State Forest after the swap.
Requires the Agriculture Secretary to provide a free quitclaim deed 'as expeditiously as practicable', to be recorded before the swap deeds.
Lets the Secretary, working with the state, correct the legal descriptions of the state land.
Describes the Deli land as subject to existing public water use or easements on Lee Lake, plus existing roads, zoning rules, and the railroad right-of-way.

Visitors and nearby residents of Jackson County and the Town of Millston who use or live near the forest

Wisconsin taxpayers and the public, who own the state forest

This bill directs the Forest Service to release its reversionary interest in approximately 31.83 acres in the Black River State Forest if the State of Wisconsin offers to exchange those acres for approximately 37.27 acres of land owned by Deli, Inc., a sphagnum moss production business located in Millston, Wisconsin. one: The bill would expand the official boundary of Alabama's Talladega National Forest to include land shown on a 2024 Forest Service map and let the Agriculture Department acquire land inside that area only from willing sellers.
summary: This bill would change the official boundary of the Talladega National Forest in Alabama so it includes additional land shown on a map dated September 6, 2024, titled "Talladega National Forest Proposed Proclamation Boundary Addition." The map must be kept on file at the appropriate Forest Service office, where the public can look at it. Once land is inside the boundary, the Secretary of Agriculture (who oversees the Forest Service) may acquire land, water, and related interests there using the usual National Forest tools, including the 1911 Weeks Law. label: S. 140
title: Wildfire Prevention Act of 2026
one: Sets rising targets for forest thinning and prescribed burns on federal land, speeds up environmental review for some projects, adds data reporting, and also wipes out the 2001 Roadless Rule that protects about 58 million acres of national forest from road building.
summary:
This bill aims to cut wildfire risk on National Forest and Bureau of Land Management (BLM) land. It tells the agencies to work out how many acres they thinned and burned on purpose (prescribed fire) from 2021 to 2025. Starting in 2027 they must set yearly goals at least equal to that average. Goals rise to 20% above it in 2029 and 30 and 40% above it from 2031 on. The bill requires standard ways of tracking this work, public yearly reports, and budget reports that include cost per acre and whether the work reduced fire risk or helped land health.

It also makes several changes that speed up or ease logging and land use. Utility companies could cut trees up to 150 feet from power lines on federal land, up from 10 feet. The size limit for timber sales that can skip some formal bidding steps rises from $10,000 to $55,000. Removing dangerous trees near roads, trails and campgrounds, on up to 6,000 acres, would skip full environmental review. Agencies must use existing fast-track review tools. Local governments and tribes could step into lawsuits over nearby wildfire or timber projects. The agencies must study using livestock grazing to cut fuels. A seven-year pilot program would test wildfire technology from private firms, nonprofits and universities. A required report on wildfire costs (FLAME report) is repealed.

Finally, Title IV cancels the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule and bars the Forest Service from making a similar one. Idaho and Colorado state rules stay in place.

Requires state-by-state acreage allotments within 90 days of enactment, and exempts setting these goals from NEPA environmental review.
Requires standardized data tracking, public annual reports, and budget-linked reports covering cost per acre, wildfire risk, effectiveness and land-health benefits.

Raises the distance for hazard tree removal near power lines on federal land from 10 to 150 feet and lets utilities cut vegetation in rights-of-way without a separate timber sale; any sale proceeds go to the agency.
Changes the definition of 'owner or operator' of power facilities so it no longer includes contractors or agents.
Raises a National Forest timber sale threshold from $10,000 to $55,000.

Creates a categorical exclusion (skips full environmental review) for removing high-priority hazard trees near roads, trails and developed recreation sites, up to 6,000 acres, excluding wilderness and some other areas.
Gives local governments and tribes the right to intervene in lawsuits over nearby approved wildfire-risk or timber-revenue projects and join settlement talks.
Directs a strategy on using livestock grazing to cut wildfire fuels, including use of vacant allotments in drought or disaster.
Requires use of existing streamlined environmental review authorities on units with land at risk from insects, disease or high wildfire hazard.
Sets up a 7-year public-private wildfire technology testbed pilot program run by the Interior Department's Wildland Fire Service.
Repeals a FLAME Act reporting requirement.
Nullifies the 2001 Roadless Rule and bars similar future rules, while keeping the Idaho and Colorado state rules.

crs:
This bill establishes forest management requirements for federal lands, particularly with respect to reducing wildfires. 
For example, the bill establishes annual goals to increase (1) the number of acres of Forest Service and Bureau of Land Management (BLM) land that are mechanically thinned (i.e., a management process related to the removal of trees and vegetation); and (2) the number of acres of Forest Service and BLM land treated by prescribed fire. By FY2029, the goals must be to increase the number of acres of each by at least 40% compared to the average number of acres of each in FY2019-FY2023.
The bill also directs the Forest Service and the BLM to (1) implement standardized procedures for tracking data relating to hazardous fuels reduction activities they carry out, and (2) develop a strategy to identify opportunities to use livestock grazing as a wildfire risk reduction tool on federal land. Additionally, the Forest Service and the Department of the Interior must establish a deployment and test bed pilot program for wildfire prevention, detection, communication, and mitigation technologies.
The bill mandates use of existing authorities for expedited environmental review for certain forest land at high risk from wildfire, insects, or disease.
Finally, the bill provides local governments and Indian tribes the right to intervene in lawsuits concerning certain projects on federal land that (1) reduce risks posed by wildfire, insects, or disease; or (2) generate revenue from harvesting timber.

label: S. 1680
title: Virginia Wilderness Additions Act of 2025
one: The bill would add about 1,000 acres to the Rough Mountain Wilderness and about 4,600 acres to the Rich Hole Wilderness in Virginia's George Washington National Forest, allowing temporary use of motorized equipment on the Rich Hole land for water quality work before it becomes full wilderness.
summary:
This bill would protect more public forest land in western Virginia as wilderness. Wilderness is the strongest level of federal land protection. It generally bans roads, permanent buildings, and motor vehicles or machines.

About 1,000 acres would be added to the Rough Mountain Wilderness right away. The land is in the George Washington National Forest and is shown on a 2014 Forest Service map.

About 4,600 acres would be added to the Rich Hole Wilderness in two steps. First, the land becomes "potential wilderness," and the Forest Service must manage it under the Wilderness Act. The one exception is that the Forest Service may use motorized equipment and mechanized transport (such as machines or wheeled carts) to carry out water quality and fish passage projects. Those projects are described in a 2015 Forest Service decision called the Lower Cowpasture Restoration and Management Project. While doing this work, the agency must use the least intrusive tools it practically can.

The land becomes full wilderness on the earlier of two dates. One is when the Secretary of Agriculture publishes notice in the Federal Register that the work is done. The other is five years after the bill becomes law.

The bill does not say how much money it would cost, and it does not set aside new funding.

label: S. 1682
title: Alex Gate Safety Act of 2025
one: Requires the Consumer Product Safety Commission to make existing industry gate safety standards mandatory for large and vehicle gates within one year, and to run a national public education campaign about gate dangers.
summary: This bill would make gate safety rules mandatory. Right now, many gate safety standards are voluntary guidelines written by industry groups. The bill tells the Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC), the federal agency that handles dangerous consumer products, to issue a final safety rule within one year of the bill becoming law. The rule would require "covered gates" to meet certain existing standards from ASTM (a standards group) and, for gates with motors or similar operators, a standard called UL 325. Covered gates include automatic and manual vehicle gates and any other gate wider than 48 inches or 84 inches or taller. The CPSC would decide exactly which types of gates fall under the rule. If those standards groups update their standards, the update would automatically become part of the rule after 180 days unless the CPSC says within 90 days that the change does not improve safety. The CPSC could also change the rule later to reduce injury risk. Within two years, the CPSC must also launch a national campaign to teach manufacturers, contractors, owners, consumers, building officials, and school agencies about the dangers of falling or detached gates and about low-cost ways to prevent injuries. Within three years, it must report to Congress on what it did. The bill text does not state a dollar amount or any new money.
