label: S. 81
title: Guidance Clarity Act of 2025
one: Requires federal agencies to put a standard notice on the first page of their guidance documents saying the document is not law and doesn't bind the public or the agency.
summary: Federal agencies often publish "guidance" documents. These explain how an agency reads a law or how it plans to handle something. They aren't formal rules, and they skip the public comment process that formal rules go through. This bill would make agencies put a set statement on the first page of that kind of guidance. The statement says the document does not have the force and effect of law, does not by itself bind the public or the agency, and is meant only to give the public clarity about existing legal requirements or agency policies. The Office of Management and Budget (OMB, the White House office that oversees agency management) would have 90 days after enactment to write instructions for carrying out the law. Agencies would have to start using the statement 30 days after OMB issues those instructions. The Senate committee rewrote the bill and changed which part of the Administrative Procedure Act (the main law on how agencies make rules) it points to. The text does not describe any penalty for agencies that skip the statement. It also doesn't say how the statement would be enforced or how it would be handled in court. The bill doesn't change what guidance can legally do. It only requires the label.
does: Requires every federal agency to put a "guidance clarity statement" on guidance documents covered by the bill.
Requires the statement to appear prominently on the first page.
Sets exact wording: the document lacks the force and effect of law, does not by itself bind the public or the agency, and is only meant to clarify existing legal requirements or agency policies.
Directs OMB to issue implementing guidance within 90 days of enactment.
Starts the requirement 30 days after OMB issues that guidance.

Applies to guidance under a specific part of the Administrative Procedure Act, apparently the section that exempts certain documents from public notice and comment. The committee amendment changed the cross-reference from 553(b)(3)(A) to 553(b)(4)(A).

label: S. 90
title: Historic Roadways Protection Act
one: The bill would bar the Bureau of Land Management from spending money to carry out or finish certain Utah road and trail (travel management) plans until Utah's long-running "historic road" lawsuits are resolved, and in six areas it would put older pre-2017 plans back in force.
summary:
This bill deals with which roads and trails are open on federal land managed by the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) in Utah. Utah and many of its counties have sued the federal government for years. They say they own old rights-of-way (legal claims to use old roads across federal land) under a law from 1866 called R.S. 2477. Congress repealed that law in 1976 but kept rights that already existed.

While those lawsuits are pending, the bill would stop BLM from spending federal money on certain travel management plans. These are plans that decide which routes stay open to vehicles. The bill covers 11 named areas, including the San Rafael Swell, Nine Mile Canyon, Dolores River, Book Cliffs and Henry Mountains. In all 11 areas, BLM could not carry out plans finished after a January 2017 legal settlement with conservation groups. In six of them, BLM could not finish new plans. Those six areas would go back to the plans in effect before the settlement.

The ban would last until the Interior Secretary tells Congress that every listed lawsuit has been decided or otherwise resolved. It applies "notwithstanding any other law," meaning it overrides other laws that might conflict. The Senate committee rewrote the bill. The summary from the Congressional Research Service (CRS, Congress's neutral research office) describes the earlier version, so some details here differ from it.

Hikers, campers, and visitors to the named areas

Congress would be overriding a negotiated legal settlement and a public planning process, which may reduce public input and transparency.

crs:
Historic Roadways Protection Act
This bill prohibits the Bureau for Land Management (BLM) from closing historical roads on public lands in certain areas of Utah until the Federal District Court for Utah makes a decision on each of the R.S. 2477 cases, which are cases brought by Utah and counties to keep historical roads on BLM land in Utah open for public use.
By way of background, a provision of the Mining Law of 1866, commonly known as R.S. 2477, granted rights-of-way to states and counties across public lands for the construction of roads for public use in order to promote settlement of the American West. In 1976, Congress repealed R.S. 2477 when it enacted the Federal Land Policy and Management Act (FLPMA), but FLPMA preserved rights-of-way that had been established under R.S. 2477. After the BLM released travel management plans that closed some historical roads, Utah and 22 counties filed lawsuits about their rights-of-way across public lands for historical roads.
Until the BLM certifies that those cases have been decided, the bill prohibits the BLM from obligating or expending federal funds to (1) finalize or implement a new travel management plan for certain travel management areas in Utah; or (2) implement, with respect to land within the boundary of Utah, the Indian Creek (Canyon Rims) Travel Management Plan, the San Rafael Desert Travel Management Plan, the San Rafael Swell Travel Management Plan, or the Labyrinth/Gemini Bridges Travel Management Plan.

life.reason: Blocking travel plans written to limit vehicle damage could expose wildlife, plants, and cultural sites in the named areas to more disturbance, though the effect is indirect.

water.reason: Freezing plans that restrict routes near water sources could allow more vehicle impacts on streams and springs in the affected areas.

transparency.reason: The bill overrides a negotiated settlement and public planning process and applies 'notwithstanding any other law,' which reduces public visibility into and input on land decisions.

people_over_profit.reason: The bill favors state and county claims and some user groups over the broader public interest in land protection, though it does not directly involve corporate profits.

local_say.reason: It advances the wishes of Utah and its counties, who are seeking to keep routes they consider historic and locally important open.

label: H.R. 2385
title: CREATE AI Act of 2025
short_title: CREATE AI Act (National AI Research Resource)
one: Sets up a national program, run through the National Science Foundation and a outside operator, to give U.S. researchers and students access to AI computing power, data, training, and testing tools.
summary:
This bill would create the National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource (NAIRR), a shared national toolbox for AI research. Today, the computing power and large datasets needed for advanced AI work are mostly held by very large tech companies. The bill aims to open access to university researchers, students, educators, nonprofits, some small businesses that have federal funding, and federal employees with a job need.

The National Science Foundation (NSF) would have one year after enactment to set up the program, with a program office of at least three full-time staff. A White House–led steering group of federal agencies would oversee the plan and budget. NSF would pick a nongovernmental organization through a competitive, transparent process to run day-to-day operations, and could replace it if it performs poorly.

NAIRR would offer computing, data, an open data commons, training, and AI testing tools. A significant share of computing time must go to projects on AI privacy, ethics, safety, security, and trustworthiness. Users would face minimum security rules, and people tied to certain foreign adversary governments would be barred. The operator could charge fees, but must offer a free tier. The program could also accept donations of cash, services, and property from private companies. Many resources depend on Congress providing money; the bill text itself does not set a dollar amount.

crs:
Creating Resources for Every American To Experiment with Artificial Intelligence Act of 2025 or the CREATE AI Act of 2025
This bill establishes a national program to provide U.S. researchers, educators, and students with access to artificial intelligence (AI) data, computational resources, educational tools and services, and testbeds.
The program, to be known as the National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource (NAIRR), must be established by the National Science Foundation (NSF) to improve U.S. AI research capacity and spur the strategic development of AI capabilities. NAIRR may accept and use donated resources from the private sector and federal agencies.
Those eligible to use NAIRR resources are (1) researchers, educators, and students based in the United States and affiliated with a U.S. institution of higher education, nonprofit, executive agency, or other specified entity; and (2) employees of U.S. executive agencies or federally funded research and development centers with a demonstrable mission need.
NSF must select a nongovernmental organization to operate NAIRR (i.e., an 
operating entity
) through a competitive and transparent process. The operating entity must ensure that a significant percentage of the annual allotment of computational resources is provided to projects primarily focused on AI privacy, ethics, safety, security, risk mitigation, or trustworthiness. The operating entity must also establish minimum security requirements for all individuals interacting with NAIRR.
The operating entity may establish a fee schedule for access to NAIRR, which must include a free tier of access and must ensure that the primary purpose of NAIRR is to support research.

label: H.R. 3087
title: Civil Rights Cold Case Records Collection Reauthorization Act
short_title: Civil Rights Cold Case Records Collection Reauthorization Act
one: The bill extends the Civil Rights Cold Case Records Review Board's life from 7 to 11 years, helps state and local governments pay to send old civil rights case records to the National Archives, and limits a privacy exemption for records created in 1990 or earlier.
summary: A 2018 law created a Review Board and a collection at the National Archives for records about unsolved civil rights–era crimes, called "cold cases." This bill would make that system stronger and keep it going longer. First, it says Congress believes federal, state, and local records on these cases should be presumed open to the public right away and eventually released. This is only a statement of opinion, not a binding rule. Second, it lets the Board repay state and local governments in full for the cost of scanning, copying, or mailing records to the National Archives. Third, it removes the wording that excused state and local governments from the requirement to send their records to the Archives. Fourth, it changes the privacy exemption in the law so that personal information in records created on or before January 1, 1990 can no longer be withheld under the Freedom of Information Act privacy exemption (section 552(b)(6)). Finally, it extends the Board's lifespan from 7 years to 11 years. The bill does not give a dollar amount. The text does not say how reimbursements would be funded, and I could not see the committee's amendments. The House committee voted 36–4 to report an amended version.

label: H.R. 3108
title: RPM Access Act
short_title: RPM Access Act (Rural Patient Monitoring Access Act)
one: Sets a minimum geographic payment level for Medicare remote patient monitoring, requires providers to meet care-quality and data-reporting conditions to be paid, and orders a report on savings and costs.
summary:
This bill changes how Medicare pays for remote patient monitoring (RPM). RPM means using devices, like blood pressure cuffs or glucose monitors, that send a patient's health readings to a care team while the patient is at home.

First, Medicare adjusts what it pays doctors by location using "geographic indices," which are numbers that reflect local costs. Right now, some areas, often rural, have indices below 1.00, so they get paid less. Starting January 1, 2026, the bill would raise any practice expense or malpractice index to 1.00 for RPM payments. It would not offset this with cuts elsewhere, so total Medicare spending on RPM could go up.

Second, starting in 2026, Medicare would only pay for RPM if three things are true. A physician, nurse practitioner, clinical nurse specialist, or physician assistant must be available in real time to respond to any unusual reading. The system must be able to send data in a form that works with electronic health records. And the provider must report data that the Health Secretary requires so savings can be measured. The Secretary can excuse a provider if reporting would cause unreasonable hardship.

Third, within five years, the Health Department must report to Congress on savings from earlier care and fewer hospital days, savings from patients taking medicines as prescribed, and the practice costs of RPM, over 2026 to 2029.

The bill's findings say RPM pays least in states with high rates of heart failure, high blood pressure, and diabetes. The committee advanced it 39-0.

Requires a report to Congress within 5 years covering 2026-2029 on savings from fewer hospital days, better medication adherence, and RPM practice costs.

This bill conditions Medicare payment for remote patient monitoring services on certain requirements.

label: H.R. 3514
title: Improving Seniors’ Timely Access to Care Act of 2025
short_title: Improving Seniors' Timely Access to Care Act of 2025
one: Requires Medicare Advantage insurance plans to use secure electronic systems for prior authorization, publicly report how often they approve, deny, and delay requests (including when AI is used), and lets the government set faster response deadlines.
summary: Prior authorization is when an insurance plan must approve a treatment, test, or service before it will pay for it. This bill would add rules for private Medicare Advantage plans, which are the private-insurer versions of Medicare. Starting in 2027, plans that use prior authorization would have to report data each year to the government, which would post it publicly for each individual plan. The data includes how many requests were approved or denied, how many denials were appealed and overturned, how long decisions took, and how often computer tools such as artificial intelligence (AI) were used to decide. Plans must also share their approval criteria with doctors and, on request, with patients. Starting in 2028, plans must set up secure electronic systems to send and answer prior authorization requests, instead of using fax or certain private portals. They must also build their programs with input from patients and providers, review which services need approval each year, and may ease the rules for providers with good track records. The bill lets the Health and Human Services Secretary set response deadlines, such as 24 hours, including for "real-time" decisions on routine items. It also orders reports: one from CMS (the Medicare agency) on real-time decisions and AI's effect on access, including for rural and low-income people, plus reports from MedPAC (an advisory commission) and the GAO (a congressional watchdog agency).

label: H.R. 4464
title: Preventive Health Savings Act
one: Lets key congressional leaders ask the Congressional Budget Office to estimate long-term (10–30 years out) spending savings from preventive health care in a bill, shown as an extra estimate that cannot be used for budget enforcement.
summary: Right now, the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) mostly estimates what bills cost over 10 years. That can make prevention look like a bad deal, because the savings from preventing disease often show up many years later. This bill changes the rules for one narrow situation. If the top Republican and Democrat on the Budget Committee and on the main committee handling a bill (in either the House or Senate) ask for it, CBO must decide whether the bill would cut government spending in later years by using preventive health care. "Later years" means the two 10-year periods that start 10 years from now, so roughly years 11 through 30. If CBO finds net savings, it must include in its estimate a description and number for those savings and explain how it got them. CBO may then produce projections covering those longer periods. These longer-term numbers are only extra information. They cannot be used to decide whether a bill follows the Congressional Budget Act or other budget rules, such as spending limits or pay-for requirements. Preventive health care is defined as actions that protect and promote health and prevent disease, disability, and early death. The definition includes approaches backed by public, credible evidence such as clinical trials and long-term studies. The bill spends no money and does not create any new health programs.
does: Lets the budget and main committee chairs and ranking members (of the House or Senate) jointly ask CBO to check if a bill would cut spending in later years through preventive health care.

Allows CBO to project beyond the usual time periods.
Says the estimate is supplementary only and cannot be used for budget enforcement or compliance under the Budget Act.
Defines preventive health care as actions that protect health and prevent disease, disability, and early death, including interventions backed by credible, public evidence.

preventive health care
 generally refers to an action that focuses on the health of the public, individuals, and defined populations in order to protect, promote, and maintain health and wellness and prevent disease, disability, and premature death.
If CBO determines that the proposed legislation would result in net reductions in budget outlays from the use of preventive health care, any CBO projection regarding the legislation must include (1) a description and estimate of the reductions in outlays, and (2) a description of the basis for these conclusions. 
Any estimate provided by CBO pursuant to this bill must be used as a supplementary estimate and may not be used to determine compliance with the Congressional Budget Act of 1974 or any other budgetary enforcement controls.

life.reason: It could make disease-prevention policies easier to justify, which may save lives, though the effect is indirect.

transparency.reason: CBO must describe and explain the basis for long-term savings estimates, giving Congress and the public more information.

The evidence is limited: none of the headlines names the Preventive Health Savings Act, so any link to the bill is inferred from broader health-policy themes rather than stated in the coverage.

label: H.R. 5490
title: Dismantle Foreign Scam Syndicates Act
one: Creates a White House–led task force to shut down foreign online scam compounds (mainly in Southeast Asia) that use trafficked workers to steal from Americans, requires sanctions review of named people and companies, and funds help for trafficking victims.
summary:
This bill targets large criminal "scam compounds" in places like Burma, Cambodia, and Laos. Many of these use trafficked people, forced to run online scams such as "pig butchering" (fake romance or crypto investment cons). The bill says Americans lost at least $10 billion to these scams in 2024.

Within 30 days of becoming law, the President must set up a task force led by the Secretary of State. It would include State, Justice, Homeland Security, and Treasury, and could include the SEC, FTC, FCC, and others. Within 180 days it must write a strategy to close scam centers, go after the criminals and corrupt officials, build up foreign police partners, recover stolen money, and work with banks, social media, crypto exchanges, and phone companies. The strategy also lists "offensive cyber" tools and pushing for international financial watchlisting of countries such as Cambodia.

The President must decide, within 180 days, whether about 50 named people and companies should be sanctioned (frozen assets, visa bans). If someone isn't sanctioned, the President must explain why. The President can waive sanctions for national security reasons after notifying Congress. Trafficking victims are exempt from sanctions.

The State Department may fund care, shelter, and reintegration help for trafficking victims. The bill authorizes $30 million per year for 2026 and 2027. The task force ends after seven years and must report to Congress yearly.
does: Requires the President to create a task force, chaired by the Secretary of State, within 30 days of enactment.
Requires a government-wide strategy within 180 days to shut down scam centers, stop trafficking into them, and hold corrupt officials accountable.
Requires the President to decide whether about 50 named individuals and companies (e.g., Prince Group, Huione Group) meet sanctions criteria, and to impose sanctions if so.
Requires a written justification to Congress for any named person who is not sanctioned; allows a national-security waiver with 15 days' notice.
Exempts people the President finds to be trafficking victims from sanctions.

Directs agencies to fully share data and plans with the task force, and to consult state and local police, anti-trafficking groups, and private companies like banks, social media, and crypto exchanges.

Lists strategy goals including investigating Chinese and Burmese military involvement, building foreign law enforcement capacity, using offensive cyber tools, recovering stolen assets, and urging Financial Action Task Force listing of countries like Cambodia.
Authorizes State Department programs for trauma-informed care, shelter, and reintegration of trafficking victims in scam centers.
Requires annual unclassified reports to Congress (with possible classified annex) for five years on sanctions, losses, recovered funds, victims, and known scam centers.
Authorizes $30 million for each of fiscal years 2026 and 2027, and ends the task force after seven years.

The following analysis is based on draft 
bill text
 that was made available by the House of Representatives and may differ from the bill text as introduced.
Dismantle Foreign Scam Syndicates Act
This bill establishes an interagency task force to shut down criminal syndicates perpetuating mass online scams. This bill also explicitly authorizes sanctions against foreign individuals or entities operating or providing support to scam compounds. (Scam compounds target individuals for financial fraud and are concentrated in Southeast Asia.)  
The President must establish an interagency task force to shut down transnational criminal syndicates that use large scam centers and forced labor of trafficked persons to perpetuate mass online scams against Americans. The task force must submit to Congress and oversee implementation of a strategy to combat scam centers, dismantle the criminal elements involved with them, and hold corrupt officials accountable. The task force must periodically report to Congress, including a list of foreign persons sanctioned by the United States for their involvement with online financial scams from Southeast Asia against U.S. nationals.
The President is explicitly authorized to impose visa- and property-blocking sanctions on (1) any foreign individual or entity that owns, controls, directs, or provides significant support to a significant scam compound operation or an enabling service; and (2) foreign government officials who knowingly enable or benefit from scam compound operations within their jurisdiction.
The Department of State is authorized to provide (1) trauma-informed care and other support services for trafficked persons within online scam centers, and (2) high-resolution satellite imagery to nongovernmental organizations and research institutions for the purposes of monitoring and documenting human rights abuses related to online scam centers in Southeast Asia.

label: H.R. 5525
title: Stop DC CAMERA Act
one: Congress would repeal Washington, D.C.'s legal authority to use traffic cameras (speed, red-light and other automated enforcement) and to post "no right turn on red" signs.
summary:
This bill would overrule local law in Washington, D.C. by removing the city's power to run automated traffic enforcement. That means the cameras that catch speeding, red-light running and similar violations would lose their legal basis. The bill does this by repealing Title IX of a 1996 D.C. budget law, which is the part that set up the automated enforcement program. It also repeals a section of a 2012 D.C. law that required a plan to expand the camera program. Separately, it repeals a section of the 1925 D.C. Traffic Act that lets the city put up signs banning right turns on red lights.

The bill's full name, "Stop DC Capital Authoritarian Motorvehicle Enforcement and Restoration of Autonomy Act," shows the sponsors' view that the cameras are an overreach by the D.C. government. The bill text does not say what happens to existing cameras, pending tickets, fines already issued, or the money the program brings in. It also does not say what would replace the cameras. The Congressional Research Service has not yet published a summary. The House Oversight Committee reported the bill with an amendment that replaced the original text, and it is now on the House calendar. It has not passed the House.

label: H.R. 5688
title: Non-Domiciled CDL Integrity Act
one: Sets federal rules for when states may issue commercial driver's licenses (CDLs) to people who live outside the state or in a foreign country, requiring proof of lawful status, a work-related visa, short license terms, and records kept for federal review.
summary:
This bill changes the federal law that tells states who they can give a commercial driver's license (CDL) to. A CDL is the license needed to drive big trucks and buses. Under the bill, a state could issue a CDL only to someone who lives in that state, or in a state that does not issue CDLs. There is one narrow exception for people who live in a foreign country.

For a foreign resident to get a CDL, they must be lawfully in the United States and hold a visa the Secretary of Transportation decides is directly tied to a real job that needs a CDL. The state must check their lawful status each time it issues, transfers, renews, or upgrades the license. The license can last at most one year, or until the person's authorized stay ends, whichever is sooner. The state must keep its records for at least two years, and hand them to the federal government within 48 hours if asked.

People who live in U.S. territories (Puerto Rico, the U.S. Virgin Islands, Guam, American Samoa, and the Northern Mariana Islands) have a separate path. They must show proof of U.S. citizenship or lawful permanent residence (a green card). The state must confirm it and keep the same records.

The text does not say when the rules start or what happens to states that do not follow them. It also does not say which visas the Secretary would approve.
who: Foreign-born truck and bus drivers with temporary work visas
Immigrants who currently hold non-domiciled CDLs
Trucking and bus companies that hire foreign-born drivers
State driver licensing agencies (DMVs)
U.S. Department of Transportation
Residents of U.S. territories seeking CDLs in a state
Other road users and the general public

benefits: Could make license checks more consistent and tighter across states.
Short license terms and status checks could help ensure licenses match authorized stays.
The 48-hour records rule could make federal oversight easier and more transparent.
Supporters say it could improve road safety and trust in the licensing system.
concerns: Could shrink the pool of eligible drivers and worsen trucking labor shortages, which may raise costs.
One-year terms and repeated status checks could burden drivers and state DMVs with more paperwork and fees.
Lawfully present immigrant drivers could lose work or face disruption, which may fall hardest on them and their families.
Residents of territories face a different, stricter test (citizen or permanent resident), which some could see as unequal treatment.
Giving the Secretary wide power to pick qualifying visas could lead to sudden shifts in who is eligible.
imp.cost: No cost estimate or funding is in the bill text. States would likely bear administrative costs for status verification and record keeping. The federal government would bear oversight costs.
unknowns: Which visas the Secretary would approve.
The effective date and any transition period for current license holders.
Penalties or enforcement for states that do not comply.
How states would verify status (what systems they could access).
Whether there is a link between non-domiciled CDLs and crash data; the bill text includes no findings or safety data.
No CRS summary was available, and the committee amended the bill (35-26 vote), so the final text may differ from this introduced version.

life.reason: Stricter licensing checks and records could improve road safety, though the bill text offers no safety data.

transparency.reason: States must keep records and give them to federal regulators within 48 hours of a request.

local_say.reason: It narrows what states may decide on who gets a CDL and sets federal terms like one-year licenses.

honesty_kindness.reason: It could disrupt the livelihoods of lawfully present immigrant drivers and treats territory residents under a stricter test than foreign visa holders in some respects.

news.overall: Across the provided headlines, none directly covers the Non-Domiciled CDL Integrity Act, so this comparison rests on thin and indirect evidence. Lean Left coverage (four pieces) centers on Democratic immigration strategy and political dynamics, plus a human-impact story on immigration enforcement, while Center coverage (two pieces) is a single leadership-priority item and an unrelated federal hiring story. Neither group's headlines show how outlets would characterize the bill's licensing provisions, so any claim about partisan framing of this specific bill would require articles that address it directly.

label: H.R. 6213
title: Heat Workforce Standards Act of 2025
one: Bars the Labor Department from finalizing, implementing, or enforcing OSHA's proposed workplace heat safety rule, or any similar rule.
summary: This bill would stop the U.S. Department of Labor from finishing or enforcing a workplace heat safety rule that the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) proposed in August 2024. That proposal, called "Heat Injury and Illness Prevention in Outdoor and Indoor Work Settings," would require many employers to write a plan to find and reduce heat dangers. It would apply to outdoor and indoor work in general industry, construction, maritime, and agriculture. According to the Congressional Research Service, the proposal would kick in when the heat index reaches 80°F (an initial trigger) or 90°F (a high-heat trigger). The bill also blocks any "substantially similar standard," so OSHA could not simply write a close copy later. The bill does not set up any new heat protections of its own. Right now, OSHA has no specific heat rule. It can still cite employers for dangerous heat under the general duty to provide a workplace free of recognized hazards. It also runs a National Emphasis Program on heat. This bill does not mention either of those, so they appear to be left as they are. The text does not say how much "substantially similar" would cover, and a court or agency would have to decide that.

Does not create any replacement heat protections.
Does not mention OSHA's general duty authority or its heat National Emphasis Program, so those appear unchanged.

crs:
Heat Workforce Standards Act of 2025
This bill prohibits the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) from finalizing, implementing, or enforcing a safety standard requiring certain employers to create a heat injury and illness prevention plan to evaluate and control heat hazards in their workplaces.
Specifically, OSHA is prohibited from finalizing the proposed rule titled 
Heat Injury and Illness Prevention in Outdoor and Indoor Work Settings,
 which was published on August 30, 2024, or any substantially similar standard. The proposed standard generally applies to employers conducting outdoor and indoor work in all general industry, construction, maritime, and agriculture sectors where OSHA has jurisdiction. Employers must develop plans in accordance with the specified standards to address employee exposures to heat indexes at or above 80 degrees (initial heat trigger) or 90 degrees (high heat trigger) Fahrenheit.
As background, the Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970 generally requires employers to provide their employees with a place of employment that is free from recognized hazards that are causing or likely to cause death or serious harm to employees. OSHA conducts workplace inspections and cites employers that fail to satisfy these requirements. Currently, OSHA does not have specific heat exposure standards; however, OSHA has historically used its general authority to cite employers for violations involving excessive heat, including through a National Emphasis Program that focuses on indoor and outdoor heat exposure in industries that have the highest risks.

news.overall: The Lean Left group provides only eight headlines, and none mention the Heat Workforce Standards Act by name, so the evidence for how this outlet group frames the bill is very limited. The coverage instead frames climate change as urgent and largely international or environmental, with some attention to cost-of-living effects. Descriptions are empty for all items, so no article bodies were available to confirm any connection to the bill.

label: H.R. 8801
title: DC ROADS Act
short_title: DC ROADS Act (Ban on DC Congestion Tolls)
one: Bars the District of Columbia's Council and Mayor from creating or enforcing any congestion toll, meaning a charge to enter or drive through roads in DC.
summary: This bill would stop the District of Columbia's local government from charging drivers a "congestion toll." The bill defines that as any charge for entering or passing through roads, bridges, tunnels, approaches, or ramps located in or leading into DC. The DC Council would not be allowed to pass a law, resolution, or rule that sets up such a toll. The Mayor would not be allowed to enforce one. The bill also changes the DC Home Rule Act, which is the federal law that gives DC its local government. It adds a new item to the list of things the Council is not allowed to do. That item is passing any toll requirement of this kind. The bill's short name is the "DC Rejecting Oppressive Automotive Driving Surcharges Act." The text does not say that DC has a toll in place now or is about to adopt one. The text has no exceptions, no start date, and no cost estimate. Because the definition covers any charge for entering or passing through DC roadways, it may be read broadly. The bill text alone doesn't say how far that reading would go. The House committee reported it with an amendment that replaced the original text. It is now on the House calendar. It has not passed the House, and nothing here shows it has passed the Senate.

label: H.R. 9250
title: Great American Outdoors Act 250
one: Renews and renames a fund that pays to fix the repair backlog on national parks, forests, wildlife refuges, other public lands and Indian schools, paid for by energy revenue and new fees on foreign visitors, while speeding up environmental review and contracting.
summary: This bill continues a program that pays for long-delayed repairs on federal lands. It renames the existing fund the "America's Legacy Restoration Fund." Money goes in from three sources: new fees on foreign visitors, donations, and half of the federal government's oil, gas, coal, and renewable energy revenue from federal land. Deposits from fees and energy revenue are capped at $1.9 billion a year for fiscal years 2026 through 2030. The money can be spent without a yearly vote in Congress. Of that money, 70% goes to the National Park Service, 15% to the Forest Service, and 5% each to Fish and Wildlife, Bureau of Land Management, and Bureau of Indian Education schools. It can't be used to buy land, tear out roads, or pay bonuses. Up to 15% can go to outdoor recreation and hunting and fishing access projects. Agencies must publish project-picking criteria, run a public online project tracker, ask governors for ideas, and report to Congress. The bill pushes private donations and matching, and nonprofit partners. It also tells agencies to build a shortcut environmental review (a "categorical exclusion"), allows emergency-style contracting rules, caps architect fees, and requires disposing of unneeded buildings and other assets. Foreign visitors would pay at least $100 per person to enter fee-charged federal sites, or at least $250 for an annual pass.

one: Moves the federal office that runs career, technical, and adult education programs from the Department of Education to the Department of Labor, with its staff and money, within six months of enactment.
summary:
This bill would move the programs run by the Education Department's Office of Career, Technical, and Adult Education over to the Department of Labor. These programs include career and technical education (job-focused classes in high schools and colleges) under the Perkins Act. They also include adult education and family literacy programs, such as help for adults to learn to read, earn a high school diploma, or move on to more training, under Title II of the Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act. Two sections of the Perkins Act (sections 116 and 117) would stay out of the transfer.

The staff, property, records, and unspent money tied to these programs would move to Labor, and the money could only be used for the purposes it was first approved for. The White House budget office (OMB) would settle any questions about which functions move. It must also make sure the move does not add to the total number of federal employees at the agencies involved. It must tell the House and Senate education committees that the bill is being followed. Existing rules, grants, contracts, lawsuits, and pending applications would continue as before. The change would start six months after enactment, though the transfer could begin earlier. The bill does not say how much it would cost or save, and it does not change what the programs are required to do. The CRS summary notes that Education and Labor already signed an agreement in July 2025 for Labor to help run these programs.

The transfer of these functions does not affect any suits, proceedings, or applications for benefits, services, licenses, permits, certificates, or financial assistance that are pending on the date of this bill's enactment.

label: H.R. 9641
title: Essential Caregivers Act of 2026
one: Requires nursing homes and certain other long-term care facilities that take Medicare or Medicaid to let each resident name two essential caregivers who can still visit in person when regular visits are suspended.
summary:
During emergencies like disease outbreaks, nursing homes have sometimes shut their doors to visitors. This bill would stop families from being fully cut off from loved ones in those times. Facilities covered by Medicare or Medicaid would have to let each resident pick two "essential caregivers." Residents could change their picks at any time. If a resident can't decide because of dementia or a mental disability, their legal representative can choose for them. Caregivers must agree to follow the facility's written safety and infection rules. Those rules can't be stricter than the ones for the facility's staff.

There are limits. Federal guidance could let a facility bar in-person visits for the first 7 days of a visitation shutdown, but only if it offers video calls in that time. Only one caregiver can be in the room at a time. A facility could turn away a caregiver who has symptoms of a serious contagious disease until a negative test, or who breaks safety rules. Roommates' rights must be reasonably protected. For residents in hospice-style end-of-life care, access can't be denied or time-limited. State inspectors must put caregiver-access complaints first and tell the person who complained the outcome within 3 days. Emergency waivers couldn't set these rules aside. The rules would start one year after enactment, and federal regulations are due within 18 months.

Bars any denial or time limit on caregiver access for residents who have elected Medicare hospice care.
Requires caregiver safety rules to be written down and no stricter than those for staff.
Requires state inspectors to prioritize caregiver-access complaints and notify the complainant within 3 days.
Stops emergency waivers from setting aside these requirements.
Requires HHS to write regulations within 18 months; the law applies 1 year after enactment.

Family members and friends who act as caregivers
Resident representatives for people with dementia or cognitive disabilities
Facility owners, administrators, and staff
State survey and certification agencies
HHS/CMS, which writes the rules and guidance

Essential Caregivers Act of 2026
This bill requires certain nursing and long-term care facilities to ensure residents have access to their designated essential caregivers during periods of restricted visitation.
Specifically, the bill requires Medicare skilled nursing facilities, long-term care hospitals, and inpatient rehabilitation facilities, as well as Medicaid nursing facilities and intermediate care facilities for individuals with intellectual disabilities, to allow residents to designate two essential caregivers and to allow these caregivers in-person access to residents even when visitation is otherwise restricted. 
Facilities may limit access of essential caregivers only in accordance with guidance from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, as specified. Essential caregivers must agree to follow all safety protocols established by the facility, which may be no more restrictive than the protocols for staff.

label: S. 1321

one: After the federal government finishes cleaning up the Moab uranium mill tailings site in Utah, it would give the land, and a Green River water pipeline and water right, to local Grand County entities for free, with limits on reselling and with some federal water rights and cleanup duties kept.
summary: For decades the Department of Energy (DOE) has been cleaning up a big pile of radioactive waste, called uranium mill tailings, left by an old uranium mill near Moab, Utah. This bill says that once DOE decides the cleanup is far enough along for the land to be handed over, DOE must give the Moab site to Grand County, Utah, at no cost. DOE or the Nuclear Regulatory Commission can still put rules or use limits on the land if they are needed to protect human health and safety. DOE keeps whatever water rights it needs to finish its cleanup duties, including access to the wells and the ground they sit on if groundwater cleanup is still going on. Grand County would not be allowed to pass any of the land on to a private company or nonprofit. DOE can also add other conditions to protect U.S. interests. The bill also requires DOE to give the Grand County Water Conservancy District the water pipeline from the Green River to the Crescent Junction disposal site, along with pumps, easements, a holding pond, and the Crescent Junction water right. That district must use these to ease water shortages in the communities it serves and cannot give them to private or nonprofit groups. DOE may keep water rights strictly needed to finish groundwater cleanup. The bill does not say what the transfer will cost or who pays for long-term care.

label: S. 1885
title: Stop the Scroll Act
one: Requires social media and anonymous content-sharing platforms to show a mental health warning label, with a link to resources like the 988 Lifeline, each time a U.S. user accesses them, and again after each hour of continuous use.
summary:
This bill would make social media companies show a mental health warning to people in the United States every time they open the platform. The label would warn that using the platform could harm mental health. It would also point users to federal help, including the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. A user could not turn the label off. It would go away only if the person leaves the platform or clicks to say they understand the risk and want to continue. If they continue, the label would appear again after every hour of nonstop use. The label could not be hidden only in a link or in the fine print, and it could not be crowded out by extra information.

The Federal Trade Commission (FTC), with approval from the Health and Human Services Secretary acting through the Surgeon General, would write detailed rules within 180 days of the bill becoming law. The rules would be reviewed at least every five years. The requirements would start one year after enactment. The FTC could enforce the law, treating violations like unfair or deceptive business practices, and it could also reach nonprofits and common carriers. State attorneys general and other state consumer protection officers could also sue for civil penalties. The law would cover violations that involve people in the U.S., even if the company is based elsewhere. The bill covers "social media platforms" as defined in an existing law, plus websites or apps that let people share content without registering.

who: Social media users in the U.S., including teens and parents

benefits: Could raise public awareness of possible mental health risks from heavy social media use.

concerns: Evidence on how much warning labels change behavior with social media is still developing; the bill's own findings lean on tobacco and alcohol studies.
A pop-up at every access and every hour could become an annoyance that users click through without reading (warning fatigue).
Platforms may argue the mandatory message is compelled speech under the First Amendment, which could lead to court challenges and delays.
Covering anonymous platforms and extending to nonprofits and common carriers could raise compliance costs for smaller services.
Forcing a label on every access might raise questions about how platforms determine a user's location, with possible privacy implications.
imp.cost: No funding amount is stated and no cost estimate was provided. Costs would fall on platform companies to build the labels, and on the FTC and HHS to write and enforce the rules. Civil penalties could bring in some money from violators.
unknowns: The exact wording and design of the label, which will be set later by FTC regulation.
How 'clearly and conspicuously' and 'hour of continuous use' will be defined and measured.
How platforms would detect that a user is physically in the U.S.
Whether courts would uphold the label requirement.
No CRS summary or cost estimate was available.

label: S. 371
title: SBA Disaster Transparency Act
one: Requires the Small Business Administration to post on its public website the disaster assistance reports it already must send to Congress.
summary:
When a disaster hits, the Small Business Administration (SBA) offers loans to small businesses, homeowners, and renters to help them recover. A 2008 law already requires the SBA to send several kinds of reports about this work to Congress. Those reports cover things like how the disaster loan program is performing. Right now, the law only requires them to go to congressional committees, so the public may have a hard time finding them.

This bill makes a small change. It adds the words "and publish on the website of the Administration" to four reporting requirements in the 2008 law. It also says the information in those reports must be "submitted and published." That means the SBA would have to put the same reports on its own website where anyone can read them.

The bill does not create new reports, change who can get disaster loans, or add money to any program. It does not set a deadline for posting or say how easy the reports must be to find. The text does not list what each report covers. I could only see the amendments, not the full 2008 law. Because of that, I can't describe the content of each report in detail. No Congressional Research Service summary is available yet.

label: S. 68
title: Complete COVID Collections Act
one: Pushes the government to keep collecting on COVID-era small business loans, extends the pandemic fraud watchdog to 2030, sets a 10-year deadline for fraud charges on some programs, and requires regular public reporting on fraud and recoveries.
summary:
This bill is about money the government gave to businesses during the COVID-19 pandemic through the Small Business Administration (SBA). That includes Paycheck Protection Program loans, COVID disaster loans, and grants for restaurants and live-event venues.

The bill requires the SBA to send any unpaid COVID loan claim under $100,000 to the Treasury Department. Treasury then decides whether to keep collecting, suspend collection, or end it. The SBA must brief Congress every 30 days on its collection progress, and the SBA head must testify every year.

The bill extends the Special Inspector General for Pandemic Recovery, a watchdog office, through September 30, 2030. It also makes the SBA share data with that office. It sets a 10-year deadline for filing fraud charges or civil cases tied to certain COVID programs. Those are the CARES Act section 4003 loans, restaurant grants, and shuttered venue grants.

The Justice Department must send Congress monthly reports on COVID fraud cases, including prosecutions, money recovered, and cases it declined. The Pandemic Response Accountability Committee must put real-time data on recovered funds on its website. Money recovered through fraud must go only toward reducing the federal debt.

The bill's title says it prohibits suspending collections, but the text itself leaves the final decision to Treasury.

label: H.R. 10956
title: IHS Workforce Parity Act of 2026
one: The bill lets health workers who got Indian Health Service scholarships or loan repayment help pay back their service commitment by working half-time instead of full-time, for a longer period.
summary:
The Indian Health Service (IHS) helps pay for health training and student loans. In return, the health worker agrees to work for a set time in Native American health care. Right now, the scholarship rules require full-time work to meet that promise. This bill would add a half-time option.

For scholarship recipients, half-time work would be allowed at the same kinds of sites as full-time work: the IHS, tribal programs, urban Indian programs funded under title V, or certain private practices in shortage areas that serve many Native Americans. The catch is that the person must agree in writing to serve twice as long. If they fail to start or finish, the damages for breaking the contract would be figured by converting their half-time service into its full-time equivalent.

For the loan repayment program, a person could choose full-time service for 2 years, half-time service for 4 years, or half-time service for 2 years with a loan payment of 50 percent of the full-time amount. The same full-time conversion would be used if someone breaks the contract.

The bill does not add money by itself. It changes service rules. It was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and the Energy and Commerce Committee, and then to a subcommittee. The text does not give a start date.

label: H.R. 1390
title: Ocean Pollution Reduction Act II
one: Lets the EPA issue a permit that allows San Diego's Point Loma sewage plant to keep using a reduced level of treatment, instead of full "secondary" treatment, if it meets set pollution limits and builds enough recycled drinking water capacity by 2039.
summary:
The Point Loma Wastewater Treatment Plant in San Diego sends treated sewage through a long pipe into the Pacific Ocean. Under the Clean Water Act, most plants must give sewage "secondary treatment," a more thorough cleaning. Point Loma has long run on a temporary waiver (a "variance") from those standards. The city has applied for a new waiver. If it doesn't get one, it would have to build a full secondary treatment plant.

This bill creates a third path. It lets the EPA give the plant a regular discharge permit with special conditions, without the city having to ask for another waiver. The plant would have to keep its deep ocean pipe (at least 300 feet deep and 4 miles out). It would also have to cut the yearly amount of solid waste it releases in steps: 12,000 metric tons now, 11,500 from the end of 2029, and 9,942 from the end of 2031. It would have to remove at least 80% of suspended solids each month and 58% of a measure of oxygen-depleting waste each year. It would have to meet the other secondary treatment limits, run a pretreatment program and an ocean monitoring program, give the EPA 10 years of ocean data, and get California's sign-off. Finally, if state and federal rules allow it, the city would have to show it will make 83 million gallons a day of water clean enough to recycle into drinking water by the end of 2039. The city can still choose to apply for full secondary treatment instead.
does: Allows the EPA Administrator to issue a Clean Water Act discharge permit for Point Loma "notwithstanding" other provisions of the Act.
Requires keeping the deep ocean outfall at least 300 feet deep and at least 4 miles from shore.
Caps solids discharged at 12,000 metric tons per year, falling to 11,500 (from Dec. 31, 2029) and 9,942 (from Dec. 31, 2031).
Limits suspended solids to 60 mg/L on a 30-day average.
Requires at least 80% removal of suspended solids (monthly average) and 58% removal of biochemical oxygen demand (annual average), counting treatment upstream of the plant too.
Requires meeting all other secondary treatment limits.
Keeps California's concurrence (state sign-off) and the ocean discharge criteria review in place.
Requires pretreatment program rules and an ocean monitoring program, plus 10 consecutive years of ocean monitoring data with each application.
Requires showing at least 83 million gallons per day (annual average) of water suitable for potable reuse by Dec. 31, 2039, to the extent regulators permit potable reuse.
Directs the EPA to set development milestones as permit conditions.
Lets the city still apply for a full secondary treatment permit instead.
City of San Diego and the ratepayers who fund its sewer and water system
Residents, swimmers, surfers and fishers along the San Diego coast
Marine life and ocean ecosystems off Point Loma
The EPA and the State of California, which share permit review
Communities that would use the recycled drinking water
Puts firm, written limits in law on solids discharged, including cuts in 2029 and 2031, instead of relying on repeated waivers.
Ties the permit to producing 83 million gallons per day of recycled drinking water, which could reduce ocean discharge and add local water supply.
Keeps California's sign-off, ocean discharge review, monitoring and pretreatment requirements.
Could avoid the cost of building a full secondary treatment plant, which could protect ratepayers from a large bill.
The city can still choose full secondary treatment.

It uses the phrase "notwithstanding any provision" of the Clean Water Act to create a special rule for one plant. This could set a precedent for other utilities to seek exceptions to federal standards.
The 80% solids and 58% oxygen-demand removal levels are offered as an alternative to full secondary treatment. Ocean discharge of partly treated sewage could still harm marine life or water quality.
The recycled water requirement applies only "to the extent potable reuse is permitted" by regulators, and the deadline is far off (2039), so the promise could slip.
Replacing the periodic waiver process with a permit could change how often and how openly the public gets to weigh in. The bill text does not spell out public comment steps.
The EPA, not the bill, sets the milestones, which gives agency discretion over how strict they are.
How much the recycled water buildout will cost and how it will be paid for.
How the proposed limits compare with current actual discharges and with full secondary treatment in effect on ocean health.
What public comment and review steps the permit would go through, and whether California would approve it.
Whether other cities might seek similar exceptions.
What happens if the city misses the 2039 recycled water target or a milestone.

life.reason: Allowing partly treated sewage (80% solids, 58% oxygen-demand removal) to continue into the ocean instead of full secondary treatment could still harm marine life, though deep outfall and solids caps limit the harm.

water.reason: Ocean discharge of partly treated sewage continues under a permit that falls short of full secondary treatment, though the solids caps and recycled-water goal partly offset this.

air.reason: The bill does not meaningfully address air quality.

transparency.reason: Replacing the periodic waiver process with a permit may reduce or leave unclear the public comment steps, and the bill does not spell out public review requirements.

people_over_profit.reason: The bill mainly concerns a public city utility, so it does not clearly favor corporate profit over people or the reverse.

local_say.reason: A special federal permit path for one city, with EPA discretion over milestones and an unspecified public comment process, reduces the local and public role compared with the existing waiver process.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill avoids a full secondary plant, which may lower ratepayer costs, but it creates no tax break or bailout and the cost and funding of the recycled water buildout are unspecified.

honesty_kindness.reason: The bill does not bear on honesty or kindness in a clear way.

label: H.R. 2518
title: Fishing Industry Credit Enhancement Act of 2025
one: Lets Farm Credit System lenders make loans and offer financial services to businesses that provide services to commercial fishermen and other harvesters or producers of aquatic products.
summary: The Farm Credit System is a network of lending institutions that make loans to farmers, ranchers, and some related businesses. Under current law, the Farm Credit Act already covers certain fishing and aquatic producers. This bill would widen who can borrow. It would let Farm Credit Banks and Production Credit Associations lend to "persons furnishing" services directly related to the operating needs of producers or harvesters of aquatic products. In practice, that could mean businesses that serve fishing operations, though the bill does not list examples or define the term. The bill changes three spots in the Farm Credit Act: the section on who is eligible for credit at Farm Credit Banks, the section on the purposes of those loans, and the section on who can borrow from Production Credit Associations. It does not give out any new money, grants, or tax breaks. It does not create a new program or change environmental or fishing rules. Loans would still be made by Farm Credit lenders under their normal business practices. The bill is short and technical. It was introduced March 31, 2025, with bipartisan cosponsors, and sent to a House Agriculture subcommittee. No hearing or vote has been reported.

label: H.R. 2626
title: PIGS Act of 2025
short_title: PIGS Act of 2025 (Pigs In Gestation Stalls Act)
one: The bill would make it illegal under federal law to keep breeding pigs in gestation crates or other spaces where they can't move freely, with limited exceptions, and would set up grant money for pig farmers to comply.
summary: This bill would change the Animal Welfare Act to ban the use of gestation crates (small cages where mother pigs are kept during pregnancy). It would be illegal to confine a breeding pig in a way that stops her from lying down, standing up, or turning around in a full circle without touching the sides of the enclosure or another animal. Starting December 31, 2025, each pig would also need at least 24 square feet of usable floor space. Space is figured by dividing an enclosure's total floor space by the number of animals in it. There are exceptions for transport, veterinary care done by or under a licensed vet, slaughter under the Humane Methods of Slaughter Act, and the five days before a sow is due to give birth. Violators would face the penalties used in the Animal Health Protection Act, enforced by the Agriculture Department. States and cities could still pass identical or stricter rules. The bill also directs USDA to create a financial help program for pig farmers, with priority for independent farmers who own their own pigs. It would be paid for by requiring the National Pork Board to set aside at least $10 million of its industry-collected fees in each of two fiscal years. The ban would apply one year after the bill becomes law. (The bill text lists a December 31, 2025 date for the space rule, which may conflict with that one-year delay.)

benefits: Could reduce physical and psychological suffering for breeding pigs.

Aid is aimed first at independent producers rather than large corporations.
Funding comes from industry fees rather than general taxpayer money.
Matches changes that many retailers and states have reportedly already made.
concerns: Farms may face costs to rebuild barns, and some smaller farms could struggle or leave the business despite the aid.
$10 million over two years may not cover conversion costs across the industry.
Pork prices could rise if costs are passed to consumers.
Pork producers who pay the fees may object to having them redirected, and the Pork Board's purpose is promotion and research.
Exceptions, such as the five days before farrowing, and the way space is averaged across a pen, could leave some confinement in place.
imp.cost: No federal appropriation is specified. At least $10 million per year for two fiscal years would come from National Pork Board assessments (industry fees). No cost estimate is given in the material provided. USDA enforcement costs are not addressed.
unknowns: Total cost to farms of converting housing.
How USDA would inspect and enforce the rules on farms.
Whether the December 31, 2025 date for the space rule conflicts with the one-year delay after enactment.
The exact penalty amounts, which come from the Animal Health Protection Act and are not in this text.
Whether the bill will receive a hearing; it is in subcommittee only.
No CRS summary was available.

stage.last_action: Referred to the Subcommittee on Livestock, Dairy, and Poultry.

life.reason: Bans confining breeding pigs in gestation crates that prevent lying down, standing, or turning around, reducing physical and psychological suffering for sows.

transparency.reason: The bill does not meaningfully change public access to government information or decision-making.

people_over_profit.reason: Imposes new confinement standards that raise producer costs and may affect pork prices, but directs aid toward independent farmers and gives priority to individual ownership over large corporations.

local_say.reason: Expressly preserves states and cities' ability to pass identical or stricter rules, so local communities keep their power to go further.

no_bailouts.reason: The aid program is funded by industry fees rather than taxpayer money or tax breaks, but it is still a financial aid program for farmers; the effects on bailout principles are unclear.

honesty_kindness.reason: Requiring humane conditions for breeding pigs reflects greater kindness toward animals, though exceptions such as the five days before farrowing leave some confinement in place.

label: H.R. 264
title: Train EATS Act
one: Requires Amtrak to offer sit-down dining (when practicable) and a cheaper alternative food service on overnight routes, with open seats offered to coach passengers and healthy and dietary-restriction meal options.
summary:
This bill would add a new rule for Amtrak's overnight routes, meaning trains that leave and arrive on different dates. On those routes, Amtrak would have to offer traditional dining "to the extent practicable." Traditional dining means sitting at a table in a dining car and being served by wait staff. Amtrak would also have to offer all passengers a second food and beverage option that costs less than the sit-down meal.

If a train has a dining car, any seats not used by first-class or business-class passengers would have to be offered to coach passengers for a fee, first come, first served. Sit-down dining would also have to include at least one healthy meal that fits the federal Dietary Guidelines for Americans. Passengers could pre-order meals that meet their dietary restrictions. The bill does not say what counts as a dietary restriction.

The Secretary of Transportation would write any rules needed to carry this out. The bill gives no start date and no dollar amount. It does not say how Amtrak would pay for the requirements or how they would be enforced. It was introduced in January 2025 and sent to a House subcommittee. It has not moved beyond that.
does: Requires Amtrak to offer traditional table service with wait staff on overnight routes, to the extent practicable.
who: Amtrak overnight and long-distance passengers, especially coach passengers

stage.last_action: Referred to the Subcommittee on Railroads, Pipelines, and Hazardous Materials.

crs:
Train Establishment of Appetizing Table Service Act or the Train EATS Act 
This bill requires Amtrak to provide a range of dining services to passengers on overnight routes.
Specifically, Amtrak must make available (1) traditional dining (i.e., table service), to the extent practicable; and (2) an alternative food and beverage service that is more affordable than traditional dining.
On each overnight route, Amtrak must offer any traditional dining capacity not otherwise used by first-class or business-class passengers to passengers in coach class for a fee. 
In addition, Amtrak must ensure that traditional dining on overnight routes includes (1) a healthy meal option, and (2) the option for passengers to preorder meals that satisfy their dietary restrictions.
The Department of Transportation must issue any necessary regulations.

life.reason: Requiring a healthy meal option that fits the Dietary Guidelines and accommodating dietary restrictions could modestly support passenger health.

people_over_profit.reason: The bill mainly changes dining service and fees; it does not clearly shift benefits between passengers and corporate profit, and the cost impact is unspecified.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill gives no dollar amount and does not state a funding source, so it neither provides a subsidy nor a tax break.

label: H.R. 2674
title: Department of Homeland Security Climate Change Research Act
one: Directs the Department of Homeland Security's science chief to review existing research on how climate change threatens homeland security and, if funded, to research ways to reduce those threats, with yearly reports to Congress.
summary: This bill adds a new section to the Homeland Security Act of 2002. It requires the Under Secretary for Science and Technology at the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to review existing federal research on ways to reduce the harm climate change could do to homeland security. The review must look at how climate change affects emergency planning and disaster preparedness, response and recovery. It must also look at whether the way the federal government pays for major disaster and emergency declarations fits those effects. After that review, the Under Secretary may do new research and development on ways to reduce these effects, but only if Congress provides the money. Any such work must put first the problems that hurt DHS's ability to carry out its own operations. While doing this work, the Under Secretary must consult with other federal agencies, state, local, Tribal and territorial governments, and owners and operators of critical infrastructure (like power, water and transport systems). The Under Secretary may also coordinate with them. The bill defines climate change as detectable changes in the climate system that are directly or indirectly caused by human activity and that change the makeup of the global atmosphere. One year after enactment, and then every year for three more years, DHS must send Congress a report on any research it carries out.
does: Requires the DHS Under Secretary for Science and Technology to evaluate existing federal research on reducing climate change's negative effects on homeland security.
Requires that evaluation to consider effects on disaster preparedness, response and recovery, and whether federal disaster-declaration funding is set up to handle those effects.
Lets the Under Secretary conduct new research and development, only if Congress appropriates money.
Tells DHS to prioritize research on effects that impair DHS's own operations.
Requires consultation with federal agencies, state, local, Tribal and territorial governments, and critical infrastructure owners and operators.
Defines climate change as human-caused changes to the climate system and atmosphere.
Requires a report to Congress one year after enactment and annually for three more years.
who: Department of Homeland Security Science and Technology Directorate
Federal, state, local, Tribal and territorial emergency management agencies
Owners and operators of critical infrastructure such as utilities
Communities exposed to climate-driven disasters like floods, storms, heat and wildfires
Congressional committees receiving reports
Federal taxpayers

stage.last_action: Introduced in House

life.reason: Research on reducing climate-driven disaster harms to communities could eventually help protect lives, though the bill only authorizes review and conditional research.

transparency.reason: It requires an annual public report to Congress on research carried out and consultation with governments and infrastructure operators.

local_say.reason: It requires consultation with state, local, Tribal and territorial governments during the research work.

no_bailouts.reason: It asks whether disaster-declaration funding fits climate effects but does not itself change funding, bailouts, or tax breaks.

news.overall: The Lean Left headlines are about climate science, international climate negotiations, and environmental effects, and none of them address the DHS bill. The Center headlines are about DHS Secretary Mullin's travel and the FAA ground stop, and they also do not address the bill. Neither group's provided coverage discusses the Department of Homeland Security Climate Change Research Act, so the evidence on how outlets frame this specific bill is absent; the coverage shown is limited to headlines without descriptions.

label: H.R. 4892
title: Seedlings for Sustainable Habitat Restoration Act of 2025
short_title: Seedlings for Sustainable Habitat Restoration Act
one: The bill lets the Forest Service sign contracts, grants, and agreements with states, tribes, nonprofits, colleges, and others to collect native seeds and grow seedlings for restoring damaged forests and habitats.
summary:
This bill changes two existing laws to make it clearer that the U.S. Forest Service can pay partners to collect native seeds and grow seedlings. These seedlings would be used to replant damaged land, such as areas hurt by wildfire or other disturbances.

The first change adds to a section of the 2021 Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act on ecosystem restoration. It says the Forest Service may enter into contracts, grants, or agreements with state forestry agencies, local private or nonprofit groups, colleges and universities, Indian Tribes, and groups of several states. The work covered is collecting and maintaining native seeds, including from managed seed orchards, and producing seedlings for revegetation (replanting).

The second change updates the Collaborative Forest Landscape Restoration Program, an existing program from a 2009 law. It adds seed collection and seedling production to the work that can be done through contracts and agreements under that program. It also adds colleges and universities to the list of groups the Forest Service can work with.

The bill does not set a dollar amount or create new money. It only widens what the Forest Service is allowed to do and who it can work with. The text does not say how much would be spent, so that would depend on separate funding decisions.
does: Allows the Forest Service to enter contracts, grants, or agreements for native seed collection and maintenance, including managed seed orchards.
Allows the same kinds of agreements for producing seedlings for revegetation.
Names eligible partners: state forestry agencies, local private or nonprofit entities, colleges and universities, Indian Tribes, and multistate coalitions.
Adds seed collection and seedling production to the Collaborative Forest Landscape Restoration Program's allowed activities.
Adds institutions of higher education to the list of eligible partners in that program.
who: Forest Service and the national forests it manages
State forestry agencies and multistate coalitions
Indian Tribes
Local nonprofits and private nurseries or seed businesses
Colleges and universities
Communities near forests hurt by wildfire or other damage
Wildlife and plant species that depend on native habitat

stage.last_action: Referred to the Subcommittee on Forestry and Horticulture.

life.reason: Native seed collection and seedling production for replanting burned or damaged land supports recovery of plant and wildlife habitat, though effects are indirect and depend on implementation.

water.reason: Revegetating disturbed land with native plants can help stabilize soils and protect watersheds, a modest indirect benefit to water quality.

news.overall: Only one outlet group was provided, with five headlines from the New York Times and Politico, and the descriptions are blank, so the evidence is limited. The coverage centers on the permitting and energy-approval aspects of the legislation rather than on the seedling or habitat restoration aspects named in the bill's title. Without the article text or any other perspective groups, no comparison across viewpoints is possible.
