label: H.R. 11002
title: Protecting Our Public Lands from Data Centers Act of 2026
short_title: Protecting Our Public Lands from Data Centers Act of 2026
one: The bill would ban building data centers on National Forest and Interior Department-managed federal land, and require that any federal land sold or transferred in the future return to the government if it is used for a data center.
summary: This bill would stop anyone from building a data center on certain federal public lands. Data centers are large buildings full of computers that store and process online information, and they often use a lot of electricity and water. The ban would cover National Forest System land and land managed by the Secretary of the Interior (which includes agencies like the Bureau of Land Management and National Park Service). The ban applies "notwithstanding any other provision of law," so it would override other laws that might allow such projects. Tribal lands are left out of the ban. That includes reservations, pueblos, rancherias, and land held in trust or with restrictions for Tribes or individual Indians. The bill also deals with land the government sells or gives away. Any transfer of federal land after the bill becomes law would need a "reversionary clause." That is a legal term meaning the land goes back to the United States if it is used for a data center. The only exception is when Congress passes a specific law allowing a data center on that land. The bill does not create new spending or programs, and it does not set penalties or name an agency to enforce the rules. It has been introduced and sent to the House Natural Resources and Agriculture Committees. It has not yet been voted on. Land managed by other agencies, such as the Defense or Energy Departments, does not appear to be covered by the definition.

one: Creates a voluntary national "Green Alert" network, run through the Department of Justice, to help states and tribes issue alerts and organize searches for missing veterans, with $3 million authorized.
summary: This bill would have the U.S. Attorney General set up a national "Green Alert" network, similar in spirit to AMBER Alerts for missing children, but for missing veterans. It covers people who are currently serving or who served in the armed forces, including the National Guard and Reserves. The Justice Department would name a national coordinator. That person would work with states, tribes, local police, broadcasters, and the Department of Veterans Affairs to encourage states to set up their own Green Alert plans. The coordinator would write voluntary guidelines. These would cover when an alert is warranted (including a veteran's mental or physical condition and whether the person reporting is credible), how to avoid overusing alerts, and how to protect missing veterans' privacy and medical information. Alerts would be aimed at the areas a missing veteran could reasonably reach. The coordinator would also offer training and materials. They could fund a full-time state coordinator and help states connect Green Alerts to their existing alert systems. An advisory board would be created, and the coordinator would send Congress yearly reports on how states are doing, including costs and results. Participation by states is voluntary, and the coordinator may not interfere with existing voluntary arrangements between local broadcasters and law enforcement. The bill authorizes $3 million, but the money would still need to be approved separately.

title: CURD Act
one: Creates a federal legal definition of "natural cheese" and makes it illegal to sell a food labeled "natural cheese" if it does not meet that definition, while setting a single national standard for this label term.
summary:
This bill would add a legal definition of "natural cheese" to the federal food safety law. Natural cheese would mean cheese made by curdling the protein in milk, cream, buttermilk, or similar dairy ingredients (using rennet or other suitable agents) and draining off some of the whey. It can be soft, semi-soft, or hard, ripened or not, and may have a coating. It can also include safe, suitable non-milk ingredients of the kind already allowed in existing federal cheese standards. Milk from animals other than cows counts. Cheese made under most existing federal cheese standards also qualifies.

The definition leaves out process cheeses, process cheese foods, cheese spreads, blended cheeses, cold pack cheeses, grated American cheese food, similar products, and anything else the FDA Secretary designates as process cheese.

If a product's label uses "natural cheese" to describe a kind of cheese but it doesn't meet the definition, it would be "misbranded" (illegally labeled) and could not be sold. The bill says companies can still use "natural" or "all-natural" in ways that follow current FDA rules. Finally, the bill would add this new rule to the list of labeling rules where states cannot set different requirements. Congress's stated goal is to help shoppers tell natural cheese from process cheese. The bill was just introduced and sent to committee.
does: Adds a federal definition of 'natural cheese' to the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.
Defines it as cheese made by coagulating milk-based ingredients and draining some whey, or made under most existing FDA cheese standards.
Allows safe and suitable non-milk ingredients of the type already permitted in those standards.
Counts milk from animals other than cows.
Excludes pasteurized process cheeses, cheese foods, spreads, blended cheeses, cold pack cheeses, grated American cheese food, and comparable products.
Lets the FDA Secretary designate other products as process cheese, which would also be excluded.
Makes a food misbranded if its label uses 'natural cheese' as a category descriptor but it doesn't meet the definition.
Says companies may still use 'natural' or 'all-natural' claims consistent with FDA rules and guidance.
Adds the new labeling rule to the list of rules where states cannot impose different (non-identical) requirements.
who: Shoppers who buy cheese and want to know what they are getting
Cheese makers and dairy processors, especially those making process cheese or cheese products
Food manufacturers that use cheese in prepared foods
Dairy farmers who supply milk for cheese
Retailers and grocers selling cheese
FDA, which would enforce the new definition
State governments, whose own labeling rules on this term would be limited

crs:
Codifying Useful Regulatory Definitions Act or the

CURD Act
This bill establishes a statutory definition for 
natural cheese

natural cheese

A food that does not meet this definition is deemed misbranded and may not be sold if its label includes the term
 natural cheese
 as a factual descriptor of a category of cheese.

transparency.reason: Labeling rules that define 'natural cheese' and make mislabeled products illegal give shoppers clearer information about what they are buying.

honesty_kindness.reason: Making it illegal to label non-qualifying process cheese as 'natural cheese' discourages misleading marketing and promotes honest labeling.

label: H.R. 1924
title: Securing Access to Care for Seniors in Critical Condition Act of 2025
short_title: Securing Access to Care for Seniors in Critical Condition Act
one: The bill would let long-term care hospitals get Medicare's higher, specialized payment rate for very sick patients whose diagnosis group has a relative weight of 0.8 or more, for discharges starting October 1, 2026.
summary: Long-term care hospitals (LTCHs) treat patients with serious, long-lasting illnesses, often after an intensive care stay. Medicare pays LTCHs a higher, specialized rate only for stays that meet certain rules. Stays that don't meet those rules are paid a lower "site-neutral" rate. That rate is the lower of two amounts: what a regular acute care hospital would be paid, or 100% of the cost of the stay. Today, a stay can avoid the lower rate if it follows an ICU or hospital stay of a certain type, or if the patient needed a ventilator for a long time. This bill adds a third way to qualify. A discharge would get the higher LTCH rate if the patient's case falls into a Medicare diagnosis group (a billing category for an illness and its severity) with a "relative weight" of 0.8 or higher. The relative weight is a number that reflects how costly a case usually is. The change would apply to discharges on or after October 1, 2026. The bill does not name specific diseases, and it does not say how much it would cost. The text does not include a cost estimate. Whether more LTCH stays would be paid at the higher rate depends on how many cases fall in those diagnosis groups.
does: Adds a third "high acuity criterion" to the existing ways an LTCH discharge can avoid Medicare's lower site-neutral payment.
who: Long-term care hospitals, which could be paid more for qualifying stays

stage.last_action: Introduced in House

crs:
Securing Access to Care for Seniors in Critical Condition Act of 2025
This bill exempts discharges from long-term care hospitals (LTCHs) from the Medicare site-neutral payment rate if the discharge meets specified high acuity criteria and occurs on or after October 1, 2026.  (The site-neutral rate is the lower of Medicare’s acute care hospital payment rate under the inpatient prospective payment system or 100% of the cost of the stay. LTCH stays that do not qualify for the specialized LTCH payment rate under Medicare are instead paid at the lower, site-neutral rate.)

life.reason: It would keep higher-acuity seniors with serious illnesses in specialized LTCH care by paying more for those stays, which may support access to needed treatment.

people_over_profit.reason: It raises Medicare payments to LTCH operators for qualifying stays, tilting payment toward provider revenue rather than lower costs for patients and taxpayers.

no_bailouts.reason: It exempts qualifying LTCH discharges from the lower site-neutral payment, effectively a federal payment boost to a specific provider category with no cost offset and no cost estimate given.

label: H.R. 2203
title: Innovative FEED Act of 2025
one: Creates a new legal category for animal feed additives that act only in the gut (such as ones that change digestion byproducts, cut human-pathogen germs, or alter gut bacteria) and regulates them through the FDA's food additive process instead of the animal drug process.
summary:
Right now, if a feed ingredient is meant to change how an animal's body works, such as by shifting gut bacteria or lowering methane from digestion, the FDA may treat it as an animal drug. Drug review can be slower and more costly. This bill creates a new category called "zootechnical animal food substances." These are things added to animal feed or water that work only inside the digestive tract. They may be meant to change the byproducts of digestion, reduce germs in food animals that could make people sick, or change the animal's gut microbiome (the community of microbes in the gut).

Under the bill, these substances would be reviewed as food additives. The company would file a petition with the FDA. It would have to include data showing the substance works as intended and full reports of its studies. The FDA would set the conditions of use, and could deny the petition if the company fails to show the substance achieves its intended effect. The bill keeps the usual food additive process, which centers on safety.

Labels would have to say the product is not for diagnosing, curing, treating, or preventing disease in animals. They could also state the intended effect on the animal's body. Disease treatments, hormones, ionophores (a type of antimicrobial feed additive), and certain ingredients already in approved or studied animal drugs are excluded. The FDA could exclude other substances by rule. The bill does not let the government force anyone to use these substances.
does: see items
who: see items

stage.last_action: Introduced in House

crs:
Innovative Feed Enhancement and Economic Development Act of 2025 or the Innovative FEED Act of 2025
This bill provides for the regulation of zootechnical animal food substances as food additives.
The bill defines 
zootechnical animal food substance 
as a substance that is added to the food or drinking water of animals and that affects only the animal's gastrointestinal tract, with the intended purpose of affecting the byproducts of the animal's digestion, reducing foodborne pathogens, or altering the animal's gastrointestinal biome.
The definition does not include substances that are used to treat or prevent diseases in animals, hormones, or active ingredients of animal drugs. Labels for zootechnical animal food substances must include a disclaimer that the substance may not be used to treat or prevent diseases in animals.

air.reason: Substances meant to change the byproducts of animal digestion, such as methane, could reduce air emissions from livestock, though the bill does not require any emissions reduction and effects are speculative.

transparency.reason: The bill moves these substances into the food additive pathway and requires studies to be filed with FDA, but the full study reports may be kept from public view and the review is less rigorous than drug approval, which reduces public visibility.

people_over_profit.reason: The bill speeds up and lowers the cost of approval for companies by replacing drug review with a food additive petition, which mainly benefits manufacturers' commercial interests.

honesty_kindness.reason: Labels must carry a disclaimer that the product is not for treating or preventing disease, and the bill does not force use, which is neutral to mildly positive on honesty, but the overall effect on honesty is unclear.

label: H.R. 2731
title: Great Lakes Mapping Act of 2025
one: Directs NOAA to create a high-resolution public map of the floors of all five Great Lakes by the end of 2030, working with Great Lakes states and regional groups, and authorizes $50 million per year for five years.
summary: This bill tells the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) to survey and map the bottoms of the Great Lakes in high detail by December 31, 2030. Right now, much of the lakebed is not mapped at high resolution. The work would include collecting depth data (called bathymetric data), building a full map, and storing the data and related background information (metadata). NOAA would have to work with the governors and relevant agencies of the states that border the lakes, a national ocean mapping council, the Great Lakes Observing System's Lakebed 2030 initiative, other regional observing groups, and anyone else NOAA thinks is relevant. NOAA must release finished pieces of the map to the public within a "reasonable time" it decides, and release the full map and any legally required data, where practical, within 180 days after finishing. The data would also be added to products like nautical charts and tools for resource mapping and habitat studies. The bill does not change how NOAA runs two existing mapping laws. It authorizes up to $50 million each year for fiscal years 2025 through 2029, available through fiscal year 2030. "Authorizes" means Congress allows the spending, but a separate spending bill must actually provide the money. The bill is at the start of the process and has been sent to the House Natural Resources Committee.
does: placeholder
who: People who live near or rely on the Great Lakes, including drinking water users (tens of millions)
Great Lakes states and their agencies
Commercial and recreational boaters and shipping
Scientists, researchers, and habitat managers
NOAA and regional groups such as the Great Lakes Observing System
Taxpayers, who would fund the work

stage.last_action: Introduced in House

life.reason: High-resolution lakebed maps support habitat studies and science that help protect fish and aquatic species, though the benefit is indirect.

water.reason: Better bathymetric data supports understanding of the lakes that supply drinking water to tens of millions, though the bill does not directly regulate water quality.

transparency.reason: NOAA must publicly release finished map pieces and the full map and legally required data within set timeframes, making government-held data more accessible.

local_say.reason: NOAA must consult with governors and state agencies of the Great Lakes states, giving those states a formal role in the mapping work.

news.overall: Lean Left coverage (four headlines, mostly NPR) centers on ecological restoration and pollution, while Center coverage (two Christian Science Monitor headlines) centers on Western water supply and scarcity. Neither group's headlines mention the Great Lakes Mapping Act, and the descriptions provided are blank, so the evidence is thin: these are topical water and environment stories that appear to be loosely related to the bill rather than direct coverage of it. No Right-leaning coverage was provided, so no comparison with that perspective is possible.

label: H.R. 2740
title: To modify the boundaries of the Talladega National Forest, and for other purposes.
one: The bill expands the official boundary of Alabama's Talladega National Forest to include land on a specific map, and lets the Forest Service acquire land inside that area only from willing sellers.
summary:
This bill would change the official boundary of the Talladega National Forest in Alabama. The new boundary would include land shown on a Forest Service map titled "Talladega National Forest Proposed Proclamation Boundary Addition," dated September 6, 2024. The map must be kept on file where the public can look at it.

Inside the new boundary area, the Secretary of Agriculture (who oversees the Forest Service) could use existing national forest land-buying powers, including the 1911 Weeks Law, to acquire land, water, and related interests. Any private land or water would have to come from a willing seller. The land could be donated, swapped for other land, or bought with donated or appropriated money (money Congress sets aside). The government is asked to do this without undue delay when practical.

Land acquired this way would be managed under the same rules as other national forest land bought under the Weeks Law. Drawing the boundary does not by itself make anyone sell, and the bill does not say that land already in private hands becomes federal. The bill text does not give the size of the area, name the landowners, or set a dollar amount. I could not see the map itself.
does: Expands the Talladega National Forest boundary to cover land on a map dated September 6, 2024.
Requires the map to be on file and open to public inspection at the Forest Service.
Lets the Agriculture Secretary use existing national forest land acquisition powers, including the Weeks Law, inside the mapped area.
Limits acquisition of private land and water to willing sellers, by donation, exchange, or purchase.
Allows purchases only with donated or appropriated funds.
Requires acquired land to be managed under the Weeks Law and all national forest laws and regulations.
who: Landowners inside the new boundary area, who may be approached to sell, swap, or donate but cannot be forced
Residents and communities near the Talladega National Forest in Alabama
Forest Service and the Department of Agriculture
Hunters, hikers, and other recreation users of the forest
Wildlife, plants, and watersheds on and near the added land
Federal taxpayers, if land is bought with appropriated funds

stage.last_action: Introduced in House

life.reason: Expanding the national forest boundary and allowing acquisition of land in the mapped area could protect habitat for wildlife, plants, and watersheds over time.

water.reason: Acquiring land and water interests inside the forest boundary could help protect watersheds, though no specific water protections are written into the bill.

transparency.reason: The bill requires the boundary map to be kept on file where the public can inspect it.

local_say.reason: Acquisition is limited to willing sellers, so landowners keep their say, but local communities get no new formal role in the decision.

label: H.R. 3212
title: LAST ACRE Act of 2025
short_title: LAST ACRE Act of 2025 (Farm Broadband Grants)
one: Creates a USDA grant-and-loan program, funded at $20 million a year for 2026–2030, to bring high-speed internet and wireless connections to farmland that lacks it. It also adds broadband questions to USDA farm surveys and repeals two existing USDA broadband programs.
summary:
This bill would set up a new "Last Acre Program" at the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA). The program would help internet and wireless companies connect farms and ranches that have little or no high-speed internet. The money could pay for service to tractors, irrigation systems, drones, soil sensors, barns, and farm offices. It could also pay for towers and poles, or for adding equipment to existing structures such as water towers and grain elevators.

Companies would bid for money. Once one company bids on a piece of land, nearby registered companies get a chance to submit competing bids. Other companies can also challenge a bid if they already serve the land or are already committed to serving it. USDA must pick the bid with the lowest cost to the government that can also reliably meet the farm's needs. The federal government could pay up to 80% of a project's cost, or 90% for low-income, small-sales farmers. Remote, unserved land gets priority. Companies must meet basic cybersecurity rules and finish building within 4 years, or face penalties.

The bill would authorize $20 million a year for fiscal years 2026 through 2030, which is $100 million in total. Authorizing money does not guarantee it, because Congress must still appropriate it. The bill also requires farm surveys to ask about broadband use. It repeals two existing USDA broadband programs: the innovative broadband program and the middle-mile program. USDA must report on outcomes each year, and the reports would be public.
does: placeholder
who: Farmers and ranchers on land without fast internet
Low-income, small-sales farmers (eligible for a higher federal share)
Internet and wireless providers, including rural and small companies
USDA, which would run the program, and the FCC, which would get data for its broadband maps
Taxpayers, who would fund the grants and loans
Rural communities near funded projects and USDA Agricultural Research Service research centers

stage.last_action: Introduced in House

crs:
Linking Access to Spur Technology for Agriculture Connectivity in Rural Environments Act of 2025 or the LAST ACRE Act of 2025
This bill requires the Department of Agriculture (USDA) to make grants and loans to facilitate broadband and wireless connectivity projects on active agricultural land.
To be eligible for support, projects must involve (1) the provision of broadband service to structures and devices, including tractors, irrigation systems, and drones; (2) the provision of wireless connectivity to facilitate data transmission between structures and devices; or (3) activities that support the construction of wireless infrastructure. Projects must involve agricultural land that is used for the active production of agricultural commodities or livestock and that lacks broadband service at specified minimum speeds.
To apply for funding, a broadband or wireless connectivity provider must submit an initial bid to USDA relating to a project on eligible agricultural land. The application must include information on the provider’s engagement with the relevant farmer or rancher and a description of how the grant or loan assistance would be used to establish connectivity on the land. Once an initial bid is received, USDA must allow other providers that operate on or near the relevant land to submit competing bids.
Separately, the bill requires USDA to include in certain surveys of U.S. farmers questions related to whether and how respondents use broadband service at farm sites.
Finally, the bill repeals two USDA loan and grant programs that support innovative broadband projects and middle mile broadband infrastructure, respectively.

transparency.reason: USDA must publish annual outcome reports and the bill requires farm surveys to collect broadband-use data, which somewhat increases public visibility into the program.

local_say.reason: Farmers and rural communities gain better connectivity on their own land, and the bid process lets nearby providers compete and lets the farm's needs drive which bid wins, which somewhat strengthens farmers' voice in what gets built.

label: H.R. 3584
title: Stratton Ridge Air Force Memorial Act
short_title: Stratton Ridge Air Force Memorial Act
one: Lets the Secretary of Agriculture allow a memorial for 9 Air Force crew members killed in a 1982 crash to be moved from private land onto a rest area in Nantahala National Forest, with no federal money used.
summary: This bill deals with a memorial for the nine Air Force crew members who died when their C-141B transport plane crashed over the Cherokee and Nantahala National Forests in North Carolina on August 31, 1982. The memorial now sits on private land next to the Cherohala Skyway, a scenic road. If the private landowner agrees, the bill lets the Secretary of Agriculture (whose department oversees the U.S. Forest Service) approve moving it to the Stratton Ridge rest area at mile marker 2 of the Skyway in Graham County, inside the Nantahala National Forest. The move would be done through a "special use authorization," which is a permit the Forest Service gives to use national forest land for a specific purpose. The exact spot must be approved by the Secretary along with the North Carolina Department of Transportation. If the site is next to a federal-aid highway, the Federal Highway Administration must also agree. No federal money may be used to move, install, or maintain the memorial. Whoever asks for the move must pay all costs, including processing the application, any environmental review, and the move and upkeep. The Secretary can set conditions on the permit, including a ban on making the memorial bigger.
does: Allows the Agriculture Secretary to approve, by special use permit, moving the memorial to the Stratton Ridge rest area in Nantahala National Forest.
Requires the consent of the private landowner where the memorial now sits.
Requires the site to be approved by the Secretary with the North Carolina DOT, and the Federal Highway Administration if next to a federal-aid highway.
Bars any federal funds from being used to relocate, install, or maintain the memorial.
Makes the requester pay all costs, including application processing and related environmental analysis.
Lets the Secretary add permit conditions, including no enlargement or expansion of the memorial.
who: Families, friends, and fellow service members of the nine airmen who died
The private landowner who currently hosts the memorial
The U.S. Forest Service and Nantahala National Forest managers
Visitors and drivers on the Cherohala Skyway
The person or group that requests and pays for the move
Residents of Graham County, NC

stage.last_action: Introduced in House

transparency.reason: The bill requires a public-facing process with approvals from the Secretary, NCDOT, and possibly FHWA, and a documented environmental review, which makes the decision more traceable.

local_say.reason: The move requires the consent of the private landowner and approval involving state and local-facing agencies, giving the affected landowner a real say over the outcome.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill bars federal funds for moving, installing, or maintaining the memorial and requires the requester to pay all costs, so no taxpayer money or subsidy flows to the project.

honesty_kindness.reason: The bill honors the nine airmen who died by providing a fitting memorial site in a rest area that visitors can access.

news.overall: Coverage is thin and only loosely connected to the bill. The Lean Left group has one NPR headline on a national forest policy with no visible link to the Stratton Ridge Air Force Memorial Act. The Center group has three Government Executive headlines on veterans' hiring, House veterans' benefits votes, and keeping promises to veterans, which suggests a veterans-focused frame, but none names the bill and the descriptions are empty. Conclusions about how these outlets view the bill itself are limited.

label: H.R. 382
title: Exported Carbon Emissions Report Act of 2025
short_title: Exported Carbon Emissions Report Act of 2025
one: Requires the EPA to publish a yearly public report on carbon dioxide and methane emissions from U.S. fossil fuel use at home and from U.S. fossil fuels that are exported and burned or leaked abroad.
summary: This bill would make the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) track and publish how much carbon dioxide and methane comes from fossil fuels (coal, oil, and natural gas) tied to the United States. The first report would be due within 180 days after the bill becomes law, and new ones would come out every year. Each report would cover the previous ten calendar years. It would include two numbers. The first is emissions released inside the U.S. and its territories from digging up, processing, moving, burning, and otherwise using fossil fuels. The second is emissions released outside the U.S. from leaks and burning of fossil fuels that were produced or refined in the U.S. and then exported. The EPA would have to use the best available science, such as direct measurements and data that other governments publish about their own emissions. It would also be guided by international accounting standards, including the Greenhouse Gas Protocol. The EPA would have to consult the Energy Information Administration and the International Energy Agency. The results would be posted on the EPA's website for anyone to see. The bill does not limit emissions, create fees or taxes, or change any rules for energy companies. It only requires measuring and publishing information. It does not state a dollar amount for the work.
does: Requires the EPA to publish a report within 180 days of enactment, then every year.
Covers the previous ten calendar years of data in each report.
Counts CO2 and methane released in the U.S. and territories from fossil fuel extraction, processing, transport, burning, and other use.
Counts CO2 and methane released abroad from leaks and burning of U.S.-produced or U.S.-refined fossil fuels that were exported.
Directs the EPA to use the best available science, including direct monitoring and other governments' disclosures, and to be informed by international standards like the Greenhouse Gas Protocol.
Requires consultation with the Energy Information Administration and the International Energy Agency.
Requires the data to be made widely public, including on the EPA website.
Defines fossil fuel as coal, oil, natural gas and other carbon material formed from prehistoric organisms.
who: The EPA, which would take on new data collection and reporting work
Fossil fuel producers, refiners, and exporters, who may face more public scrutiny, though no new duties are placed on them directly in the text
The general public, researchers, journalists, and policymakers who would gain access to the data
Communities near extraction, processing, and export sites
The Energy Information Administration and International Energy Agency, which would be consulted

stage.last_action: Introduced in House

crs:
Exported Carbon Emissions Report Act of 2025
This bill directs the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to annually collect, calculate, and publish information on certain emissions of carbon dioxide and methane from fossil fuels. Specifically, the EPA must publish information, for each of the previous 10 years, on the total emissions of carbon dioxide and methane that are released (1) within the boundaries of the United States that are the result of the extraction, processing, transportation, combustion, and other use of fossil fuels; and (2) outside the boundaries of the United States that are the result of leakage and combustion of fossil fuels produced or refined in the United States and subsequently exported.

life.reason: The bill only requires measurement and publication of emissions data and does not directly reduce or regulate pollution affecting human, animal, or plant life.

water.reason: The bill does not address water quality or water pollution.

air.reason: Publishing emissions data does not itself reduce emissions or change air quality; the bill imposes no limits.

transparency.reason: It requires EPA to publish ten years of fossil fuel carbon emissions data, including exported-fuel emissions, on a public website every year.

people_over_profit.reason: The bill imposes no new duties, fees, or rules on energy companies, so it neither favors nor burdens corporate margins directly.

local_say.reason: Publicly available emissions data for extraction, processing, and export areas gives nearby communities information they can use in advocacy, though it grants no new decision-making power.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill involves no subsidies, tax breaks, bailouts, or ratepayer-funded financial support.

honesty_kindness.reason: Requiring official, science-based public reporting of emissions tied to U.S. fossil fuels promotes honest accounting of their climate impact.

news.overall: Only one outlet grouping is provided, and none of the headlines names the Exported Carbon Emissions Report Act directly, so this analysis reflects only the broader climate subject matter. The headlines cover international diplomacy, emissions data, and industry accountability, with the bill itself absent from view. The evidence is limited to eight headlines with no descriptions, so the framing is inferred from titles alone and no comparison across perspectives is possible.

label: H.R. 4400
title: Farmers First Act of 2025
one: The bill renews and raises funding for a USDA program that gives grants for mental health counseling, helplines, and crisis lines for farmers, ranchers, and agricultural workers, and lets grantees set up referral ties with health providers.
summary:
This bill renews the Farm and Ranch Stress Assistance Network, a U.S. Department of Agriculture program. The program gives competitive grants (money groups must apply for and win) to states, Indian tribes, and qualified nonprofit groups. They use the money to offer stress and behavioral health help to people who farm, ranch, or work in farm-related jobs. That help includes counseling, helplines, websites, and other resources.

The bill makes three changes. First, it says money for farm helplines and websites can also be used for crisis lines. Second, it raises yearly funding authorized for the program from $10 million to $15 million for each of fiscal years 2026 through 2030. "Authorized" means Congress allows that spending, but a separate spending bill must actually provide the money. Third, it replaces the current referral section. Grant recipients may now set up referral relationships with certain health providers to help people get mental health and substance use care. Those providers are certified community behavioral health clinics, health centers, rural health clinics, federally qualified health centers, and critical access hospitals. The word "may" means referrals are optional, not required. The bill was introduced July 15, 2025, and sent to the House Agriculture Committee. It has not advanced further.
does: Extends the Farm and Ranch Stress Assistance Network through fiscal year 2030.
Raises authorized funding from $10 million to $15 million per year for fiscal years 2026–2030.
Allows helpline and website grant money to also fund crisis lines.
Lets grant recipients set up referral relationships with community behavioral health clinics, health centers, rural health clinics, federally qualified health centers, and critical access hospitals.
Replaces the existing referral subsection (e) with the new referral language.
who: Farmers, ranchers, and agricultural workers and their families
States, Indian tribes, and nonprofits that apply for the grants
Rural clinics, health centers, and critical access hospitals that may receive referrals
Taxpayers, who fund the program

stage.last_action: Introduced in House

crs:
Farmers First Act of 2025
This bill extends through FY2030 and revises the Farm and Ranch Stress Assistance Network (FRSAN). This Department of Agriculture program provides competitive grants to states, Indian tribes, and qualified nonprofit organizations to provide stress assistance programs (i.e., professional agricultural behavioral health counseling, helplines, and resources) to individuals engaged in farming, ranching, and agriculture-related occupations.
The bill specifies that the grant funding for farm telephone helplines and websites may also be used for crisis lines.
Further, FRSAN grant recipients may establish referral relationships with providers, including Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinics, health centers, rural health clinics, and critical access hospitals.

life.reason: Expanding stress, crisis-line, and behavioral health help for farmers and ranchers may help prevent suicide and other harms in a group with elevated distress.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill authorizes grants for a public health service program; it does not create corporate bailouts or ratepayer-funded tax breaks, and the funding is authorized rather than appropriated.

honesty_kindness.reason: Providing counseling, helplines, and crisis support to people under financial and emotional strain is a caring public-service measure.

news.overall: Only Lean Left coverage was provided, and none of the five headlines names the Farmers First Act of 2025, so no bill-specific framing can be reliably described. The headlines cover adjacent rural and federal-program themes, with a Montana campaign angle, a Malawi drought piece, global health aid, rural health and Medicaid funding, and VA cuts. label: H.R. 4991
title: Disarming Felons Act
one: Adults who, at ages 15 to 17, were found to have committed an act that would be a felony for an adult would be barred from owning or possessing a firearm, and it would be illegal to sell or give them one.
summary:
Federal law already bans certain groups from having guns, such as people convicted of felonies, and bans selling guns to them. This bill adds one more group. It covers adults who, when they were 15, 16, or 17, were found to have committed "juvenile delinquency" (a youth court finding of wrongdoing) for an act that would have been a felony if an adult had done it.

If the bill became law, two things would change. First, those adults could not legally possess a firearm. Second, anyone selling or giving a gun to them would be breaking the law if they knew or had reasonable cause to believe the person fell in this group. That second part comes from how the existing sale rule is written.

The bill is short and only adds these two lines to the law. It does not set an end date for the ban. It also does not say how it would treat sealed or expunged (erased) youth records, and it does not create a way to get gun rights back. It does not name a start date, so it would likely take effect when signed. Penalties are not written in this bill. Existing penalty rules for these gun laws would probably apply, but the bill text itself does not say so. Youth records are often confidential, so it is unclear how a seller or the background-check system would find out about them.

label: H.R. 5041
title: Smith River National Recreation Area Expansion Act
short_title: Smith River National Recreation Area Expansion Act
one: The bill would extend the Smith River National Recreation Area into southwest Oregon and protect about 24 creek segments there as Wild and Scenic Rivers, while requiring a study of the added area's waters, plants and animals.
summary:
This bill would grow the Smith River National Recreation Area, now in California's Six Rivers National Forest, into Oregon. A new map dated January 23, 2023 would set the added land. The bill would also give 24 stream segments in the North Fork Smith River watershed in Oregon "wild river" status under the Wild and Scenic Rivers Act. That status is the most protective river class. It generally blocks dams and keeps the rivers free-flowing. The bill also changes how part of the Smith River in California and Oregon is described and classed.

Within 5 years, the Forest Service would have to study the new area. The study would cover streams, wetlands, lakes, plants (including Port-Orford-cedar), animals, fungi and algae. It would then have to change its management plans to fully protect what it finds. Parts of the Oregon area would be managed as roadless, meaning no new roads. The Kalmiopsis Wilderness would stay under wilderness rules.

The bill would let the government buy land, not only accept donations. It would direct the government to acquire the 555-acre Cedar Creek Parcel, but only if Oregon's State Land Board approves and money is available. It keeps firefighting and forest-health thinning allowed. It says nothing in the bill reduces tribal rights. The Forest Service would also seek agreements giving tribes access for cultural activities. Oregon's state and local governments would get the same roles that California's now have. The bill gives no cost estimate.

who: Residents and communities in southwest Oregon (Curry County area) and northern California near the Smith River

stage.last_action: Introduced in House

water.reason: Designates 24 North Fork Smith River stream segments as wild rivers, which generally blocks dams and keeps the rivers free-flowing, and requires protection of streams and wetlands.

transparency.reason: Requires a public study and management plan changes for the new area, which adds government accountability, though the bill does not clearly add new disclosure or public-comment mechanisms.

people_over_profit.reason: Blocks new roads and dam development in the added area, limiting extractive commercial uses in favor of conservation and recreation, though it keeps firefighting and thinning allowed.

local_say.reason: Gives Oregon state and local governments the same roles California's now have, but it does not clearly expand local input and it adds federal management over new land; the effect is mixed or unclear.

honesty_kindness.reason: Affirms tribal rights, seeks agreements for tribal cultural access, and directs a land acquisition conditioned on state approval, which reflects good-faith dealing with tribes and landowners.

label: H.R. 5054
title: Freedom From Union Violence Act of 2025
short_title: Freedom From Union Violence Act of 2025
one: The bill rewrites the federal Hobbs Act so that violence or threats of violence used to obtain property count as extortion even when done for a union goal, while leaving minor, non-patterned incidents during peaceful picketing to state and local prosecutors.
summary:
This bill changes a federal crime law called the Hobbs Act, which bans robbery and extortion that affect trade between states. Extortion means getting property from someone by force, threats, or fear. In 1973, in a case called United States v. Enmons, the Supreme Court ruled that violence by union members during a strike was not extortion under this law, because the goal (better pay or conditions) was not "wrongful."

This bill would undo that result. It says that when force, violence, or fear of force or violence is used to get property, it counts as extortion without having to prove the goal was "wrongful." Threats that do not involve force or violence still have to be "wrongful" to count. The bill also says that a labor dispute or a legitimate business or labor goal does not stop federal prosecution, and that overlap with state law does not either.

The bill also adds a carve-out. Conduct is not covered if it is a side effect of otherwise peaceful picketing during a labor dispute, involves only minor injury or minor property damage (or threats of those), and is not part of a pattern of violence or coordinated violent activity. Those cases could be prosecuted only by state and local authorities. The penalty in the text is up to a $100,000 fine, up to 20 years in prison, or both. The bill says it does not change the Clayton Act, Norris-LaGuardia Act, National Labor Relations Act, or Railway Labor Act.

who: Union members, strikers, and picketers
Employers and businesses facing labor disputes
Federal prosecutors and the FBI
State and local prosecutors and police
Anyone targeted by threats or violence tied to a labor dispute

benefits: Could give federal prosecutors a tool to charge serious violence or coordinated intimidation tied to labor disputes.
Could better protect workers, business owners, and bystanders from serious violence during strikes.
Keeps a written carve-out so minor, isolated incidents at peaceful pickets stay with state and local authorities.
concerns: Could expose strikers and union members to federal felony charges with up to 20 years in prison, which may discourage strikes and organizing.
Terms like 'minor,' 'incidental,' 'pattern,' and 'coordinated' are not defined and could be argued over in court or applied unevenly.
Serious violence is already a crime under state law, so critics may see the federal change as aimed at unions more than at filling a gap.
The change is not limited to unions: removing 'wrongful' for force or violence applies to extortion cases generally.
Could shift power in labor disputes toward employers if threatened with federal charges.
imp.cost: No funding or cost estimate is given in the text. Costs would be federal investigation and prosecution time and possible added incarceration costs. No Congressional Budget Office estimate was provided.
unknowns: How courts would read 'minor' injury or damage and 'pattern' or 'coordinated' violence.
How often federal prosecutors would use the new reach, and against whom.
Whether the Supreme Court's Enmons reasoning would be re-argued under the new wording.
I could not compare the exact wording with current law beyond the CRS summary, so some small wording changes (such as the fine amount) may not be reflected here.

stage.last_action: Introduced in House

crs:
Freedom From Union Violence Act of 2025
This bill broadens the scope of conduct that constitutes extortion under the federal criminal statute commonly known as the Hobbs Act. The Hobbs Act prohibits robbery or extortion affecting interstate commerce.
Currently, an extortion offense includes obtaining property of another through the wrongful use of force, violence, or fear. Typically, Hobbs Act violations are investigated by the Federal Bureau of Investigation and prosecuted by the U.S. Attorney's Office.
In 1973, in 
United States v. Enmons
, the U.S. Supreme Court held that the use of violence by union members during a strike did not constitute extortion under the Hobbs Act because its purpose —to achieve legitimate union objectives—was not wrongful.
This bill eliminates the requirement that the use of force, violence, or fear of force or violence to obtain property must be wrongful. The bill specifies that the use of fear not involving force or violence must still be wrongful.
Finally, the bill exempts from the Hobbs Act prohibition conduct that (1) is incidental to peaceful picketing during a labor dispute, (2) consists solely of minor bodily injury or property damage, and (3) is not part of a pattern of violent conduct or of coordinated violent activity. A violation involving exempted conduct is subject to prosecution by state and local authorities.

life.reason: Expanding federal extortion coverage to violence used to obtain property gives prosecutors a tool against serious violence tied to labor disputes, which somewhat protects people from harm.

people_over_profit.reason: Exposing strikers to federal felony charges could weaken workers' leverage in disputes, which tends to favor employers' profit interests over workers.

local_say.reason: Carving out minor incidents for state and local prosecution keeps some local control, but expanding federal prosecution for strike-related conduct shifts decisions toward federal authorities.

The coverage provided centers on procedural setbacks rather than the bill's substance, and the second headline's link to this bill is not clear from the text given. one: Designates the Peter J. McGuire Memorial and Gravesite in Pennsauken, New Jersey, as a National Commemorative Site and lets the Interior Department partner with and fund groups that run education programs there.
summary: This bill would honor Peter J. McGuire, a 19th-century labor leader who helped found the American Federation of Labor and the carpenters' union, and who proposed Labor Day. label: H.R. 5070
title: Federal Police Camera and Accountability Act
short_title: Federal Police Camera and Accountability Act
one: Requires federal law enforcement officers to wear and use body cameras and put video cameras in patrol cars, with rules on when to record, how long to keep footage, who can see it, and a ban on facial recognition.
summary:
This bill would make federal law enforcement officers wear body cameras. They would have to turn on both video and audio when responding to a call or starting a stop with a member of the public. They could not turn the camera off until the stop ends and they leave. Officers would have to tell people they are being recorded. In a home without a warrant or in non-emergency situations, officers would have to ask the occupant if they want the camera off. Crime victims and anonymous tipsters would get the same offer. There are exceptions, including for undercover work, risks to informants, national security, military police, protective details, and school grounds.

Footage would be kept 6 months and then deleted. Footage involving force or a complaint would be kept at least 3 years. People filmed could view footage. The public could request footage, with limits, and it could not be withheld just because it is a law enforcement record when an officer's conduct is under review. Cameras could not use facial recognition. Patrol cars would get in-car cameras, with recordings kept at least 90 days. Officers who break the rules could face discipline, and courts would presume in favor of defendants or plaintiffs when evidence was not captured or was destroyed. The Government Accountability Office (GAO, a congressional watchdog) would study training, pursuits, and use of force. The Attorney General would write the rules within 6 months. The text does not give a cost or a start date for the requirements.
does: Requires federal law enforcement officers to wear body cameras with a wide field of view.
Requires video and audio recording when responding to a call or starting an enforcement or investigative stop, until the stop ends and the officer leaves.
Requires officers to tell people they are being recorded.

Requires officers to offer to turn off the camera for occupants of private homes (without a warrant or in non-emergencies), crime victims, and anonymous reporters. The offer and answer must be recorded first.
Bans using body cameras to gather intelligence on First Amendment speech, association, or religion, to record unrelated activity, or to use facial recognition or biometric surveillance.

Exempts some situations: risk to informants or undercover officers, serious national security risk, military police, Army CID, protective details, and school grounds (unless there is an imminent threat).
Keeps footage 6 months, then deletes it. Footage of force or complaints is kept at least 3 years, and some people can request 3-year retention.
Lets subjects, parents or guardians, next of kin, officers, superiors, and certain defense counsel inspect footage.

Allows public requests for footage. Release can require subject permission for some footage. Footage of deaths, shootings, or grave injuries must be released within 5 days if approved. It bars withholding footage just because it is a law enforcement record when an officer's conduct is under review.
Allows blurring of faces or voices to protect privacy, safety, or fair trials, while keeping the original.
Bars officers from reviewing footage of force or complaint incidents before completing initial reports and interviews, except to address an immediate threat.
Requires agencies to take custody of cameras after deadly force or criminal-investigation incidents and copy the data.
Bars the government from using footage recorded in violation of the Act as evidence against members of the public.
Requires in-car cameras in all federal patrol vehicles, with at least 10 hours of recording capacity and 90-day retention.
Requires discipline and rebuttable (challengeable) legal presumptions favoring defendants and plaintiffs when officers fail to record, tamper with footage, or destroy it.
Requires agencies to post their body camera policies online.
Orders a GAO study within 18 months and Attorney General regulations within 6 months.
who: Federal law enforcement officers and their agencies
Members of the public who interact with federal officers, including suspects, victims, and bystanders
Crime victims and anonymous tipsters, who can ask for the camera to be turned off
Families of people injured or killed in encounters with federal officers
Defense lawyers, civil plaintiffs, journalists, and others who request footage
The Attorney General, the Department of Justice, and GAO
Taxpayers, who would fund the equipment and storage

stage.last_action: Introduced in House

crs:
Federal Police Camera and Accountability Act

This bill establishes requirements for federal law enforcement officers to wear body cameras and for federal law enforcement agencies to install video cameras in patrol cars.

local_say.reason: Public footage requests and the right of people filmed to view footage give community members more ability to check federal policing in their area.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill funds federal equipment and storage with no corporate bailout or ratepayer-funded tax break involved.

label: H.R. 509
title: Western Hemisphere Nearshoring Act
one: Offers cheaper government loans, moving-cost financing, 15 years of duty-free trade treatment, and a special tax break to companies that move factories from China to Latin America or the Caribbean, and tells the U.S. to pursue trade and nuclear-reactor-sale talks with those countries.
summary:
This bill tries to get companies to move their factories out of China and into Latin America and the Caribbean. It does this with several kinds of help. First, the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation (DFC, a government development bank) must put at least 10% of its financing money toward paying moving, worker-training, and building costs for these companies. It must also cut the interest rates on their loans. Second, the President must give these companies duty-free (no import tax) or similar treatment for goods they make in the region, for 15 years. Third, the bill creates a special tax rule letting these companies write off 75% of the cost of new equipment and buildings right away, for property placed in service before 2038.

Companies must create jobs in the new country, must not be controlled by China, Russia, or another adversary, and must keep their assets in the region. State-owned companies can't qualify. The Commerce Secretary must find the help won't hurt U.S. jobs. Tariffs collected on Chinese goods go into a trust fund to cover the lost revenue.

The bill also tells the U.S. Trade Representative to start trade talks with countries in the region that lack a trade deal, if they curb migration, reduce reliance on China, and allow a Taiwan commercial office. It allows talks on selling nuclear reactors on the same terms. Cuba and Venezuela are excluded unless the State Department certifies major democratic and human rights steps.
does: see list
who: see list

stage.last_action: Introduced in House

crs:
Western Hemisphere Nearshoring Act
This bill provides assistance for corporations to relocate operations from China to Latin America or Caribbean (LAC) countries and specifies actions to expand trade and nuclear energy agreements with LAC countries. 
Specifically, the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation must use at least 10% of its funding to finance moving, workforce development, and facility construction costs associated with such relocations. Tariffs collected by the United States on goods manufactured in China shall be used to fund such assistance. The President must provide duty-free or other preferential treatment for goods and services produced in a LAC country by a corporation that received relocation assistance under this bill.
A corporation must meet certain conditions to receive these benefits, including creating sufficient jobs in the LAC country and guaranteeing that the corporation will not be controlled by China, Russia, or other foreign adversary government. State-owned enterprises are not eligible. 
Additionally, the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative must start trade negotiations with each LAC country that does not have a free trade agreement with the United States if the country meets certain conditions (such as reducing economic reliance on China). The President is authorized to start negotiations with a LAC country for the sale of nuclear reactors if these same conditions are met and the sale does not threaten U.S. national security. 
Neither Cuba nor Venezuela qualify as a LAC country unless the Department of State certifies that the country has taken certain actions, including holding free and fair elections.

people_over_profit.reason: Large subsidies, interest-rate cuts, duty-free treatment, and a 75% expensing tax write-off mainly benefit corporations' bottom lines, with worker protections limited to job-creation conditions.

no_bailouts.reason: It directs DFC financing at reduced interest rates, duty-free treatment, and accelerated tax write-offs to specific companies, which are targeted corporate subsidies and tax breaks paid for by taxpayers and tariff revenue.

news.overall: Across the three groups, none of the headlines directly covers the Western Hemisphere Nearshoring Act, so this analysis reflects adjacent trade coverage rather than the bill itself. The Center group has the most directly relevant item (Mexico-U.S. trade talks), while Lean Left coverage is broad and global, and Lean Right has only one thin article focused on a chip rule carve-out. Evidence for every group is limited to headlines only, with no article text or descriptions provided.

label: H.R. 5092
title: District of Columbia Police Home Rule Act
short_title: District of Columbia Police Home Rule Act
one: The bill would remove the President's power under the DC Home Rule Act to take emergency control of Washington, DC's police department.
summary: Under the District of Columbia Home Rule Act, passed in 1973, DC residents elect a mayor and council to run local affairs. One part of that law, section 740, lets the President take over control of the city's Metropolitan Police Department in certain emergencies. This bill would delete that section entirely. It would also remove the matching line from the law's table of contents. Nothing else in the Home Rule Act would change. If the bill became law, the President would no longer have this specific emergency power over DC police, and the city's elected government would keep control of its police. The bill text does not say what the section 740 power currently requires, such as time limits or reporting rules. It also does not say whether the President could use other legal powers, such as the National Guard, in an emergency. Those powers are outside this bill and would stay as they are. The bill was introduced on September 2, 2025 by Delegate Eleanor Holmes Norton, who represents DC in the House but cannot vote on final passage. It has been referred to the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee. No start date is given, so it would take effect when signed into law.

label: H.R. 5093
title: District of Columbia National Guard Home Rule Act
short_title: DC National Guard Home Rule Act
one: Moves control of the District of Columbia National Guard's administration from the President to the Mayor of DC, giving DC the same kind of authority over its Guard that governors have in the states.
summary: Right now, the President of the United States is the commander-in-chief of the DC National Guard. Governors command the Guard in their own states, but DC residents and their elected mayor do not. This bill would change that. It would replace "President" with "Mayor of the District of Columbia" in the old 1889 law that organizes the DC militia. The Mayor would become commander-in-chief of the DC Guard. The Mayor would appoint and retire commissioned officers, call the Guard to duty, and convene general courts martial (military trials). The bill also changes many places in federal military law (Titles 10 and 32 of the U.S. Code) where "the commanding general of the DC National Guard" now acts like a governor. The Mayor would take over those roles, such as consenting to certain active-duty orders, appointing the top Guard officer (the adjutant general) and a fiscal officer, and running programs like the Challenge youth program. It would also add DC to the definition of "State" for one federal assistance section, and it removes a line in the Home Rule Act that kept the Guard outside the DC government's control. The bill does not say when it would take effect. It also does not spell out in the text how it would affect the President's power to call out the Guard for national purposes, as with other states' Guards. It has only been introduced and sent to a House committee.

Members of the DC National Guard

label: H.R. 51
title: Washington, D.C. Admission Act
one: The bill would make most of Washington, D.C. the 51st state ("Washington, Douglass Commonwealth") with two Senators and one House member, while keeping a small federal "Capital" district around the Capitol, White House, Supreme Court and National Mall.
summary: This bill would turn most of the District of Columbia into a new state called "Washington, Douglass Commonwealth." Residents would elect two Senators and one Representative with full voting power, and the non-voting Delegate seat would end. A small area around the U.S. Capitol, the White House, the Supreme Court, the National Mall and nearby federal buildings would stay out of the state. It would be called the "Capital" and remain the seat of the federal government. The new state would use the constitution that D.C. voters approved in 2016, and current D.C. laws would carry over. Because the state would get a House seat, the House would permanently grow to 436 members. For a transition period, the federal government would keep running some services, such as the public defender service, courts funding, parole supervision, prosecutors, U.S. Marshals, and some prison housing. Each of these would end once the state certifies that it has its own laws and funding in place. Federal pensions and benefits already promised would continue. The bill would let people living in the Capital vote absentee in the state where they last lived. It would also set up fast-track congressional votes on a constitutional amendment to repeal the 23rd Amendment, which gives D.C. electoral votes for president. An 18-member commission would advise on the transition. The state could not tax federal property unless Congress allows it. If a court strikes down the admission section, the rest of the Act would also be invalid.

crs:
Washington, D.C. Admission Act
This bill provides for the establishment of the State of Washington, Douglass Commonwealth, and its admission into the United States.
The state is composed of most of the territory of the District of Columbia (DC), excluding a specified area that encompasses the U.S. Capitol, the White House, the U.S. Supreme Court building, federal monuments, and federal office buildings adjacent to the National Mall and the U.S. Capitol. The state may not impose taxes on federal property except as Congress permits.
The bill provides for the DC Mayor to issue a proclamation for the first elections to Congress of two Senators and one Representative of the state. The bill eliminates the office of Delegate to the House of Representatives.
The bill applies current DC laws to the state. DC judicial proceedings and contractual obligations shall continue under the state’s authority. The bill also provides for specified federal obligations to transfer to the state upon its certification that it has funds and laws in place to assume the obligations. These include maintaining a retirement fund for judges and operating public defender services. 
The bill establishes a commission that is generally comprised of members who are appointed by DC and federal government officials to advise on an orderly transition to statehood.

transparency.reason: Gives D.C. residents full voting representation in Congress (two Senators and a voting Representative) in place of a non-voting Delegate, increasing their formal say in federal lawmaking and making the government more accountable to them.

local_say.reason: Converts D.C. into a state with elected Senators and a voting Representative, and lets residents govern their own courts, laws, and local services once federal transition duties end.

label: H.R. 510
title: Regulatory Cooling Off Act of 2025
one: Requires most final federal agency rules to wait 6 months (instead of 30 days) before taking effect, lengthens public comment to at least 60 days, adds posting and notice requirements, and makes it easier to sue agencies in more courts.
summary:
When a federal agency, such as the EPA or the FDA, writes a new rule, it usually must let the public comment first. After the rule is final, it normally can't take effect for at least 30 days. This bill would change that in several ways.

First, the public would get at least 60 days to comment on a proposed rule. Second, the waiting period before a final rule takes effect would grow from 30 days to 6 months. Third, agencies would have to send each final rule to the congressional committees that oversee the issue at least 6 months before it takes effect. They would also have to post final and proposed rules on their own websites at least 24 hours before publishing them in the Federal Register (the government's daily journal of rules), and publish a notice on the day a rule actually takes effect.

The bill also changes where people can sue an agency over a rule. A lawsuit could be filed in the plaintiff's home district or in any district where the agency has an office. Finally, it changes the Congressional Review Act, the law that lets Congress cancel new rules. Big rules that now wait 60 days would wait 6 months, unless Congress passes a measure approving them.

The bill does not say whether existing exceptions to the waiting period, such as emergencies, would still apply. It does not edit those parts of the law.

who: Federal agencies that write rules (for example, environmental, health, safety, and consumer agencies)
Members of the public who comment on proposed rules

People who sue agencies over rules, and the federal courts that hear those cases

benefits: A 60-day minimum comment period gives the public, local groups, and small organizations more time to review and respond to proposals.
Posting rules on agency websites 24 hours before publication, and publishing a notice on the effective date, adds some transparency.
Sending rules to Congress earlier could improve oversight of agencies by elected officials.
Letting people sue in their home district could make court challenges cheaper and easier for ordinary people and local communities.
A longer runway could give businesses, small businesses, and local governments more time to prepare for compliance.
concerns: A 6-month delay on rules could slow protections for clean air, clean water, food and workplace safety, and public health.
The longer delay and the Congress-approval condition for major rules could give regulated industries more time to lobby against or block rules, which could favor corporate interests over the public.
Broader court venue could also let industry groups choose favorable courts to challenge rules, and could encourage forum shopping (picking a court expected to rule a certain way).

The requirement to send a rule to Congress 6 months before it takes effect, combined with the 6-month delay, could make it hard for agencies to act quickly in emergencies, unless existing exceptions still apply.
Longer delays may raise agency workload and costs and slow changes that relieve burdens on people (such as rules that loosen restrictions), if those are not exempt.
imp.cost: No cost estimate or funding provisions are in the text. Costs could come from agency administrative work and more litigation. The delayed benefits or savings from rules could also have economic effects, but none are quantified here.
unknowns: Whether existing exceptions in section 553(d) (such as good cause or interpretive rules) would still apply. The bill does not change them, but I could not see the full existing statute in the material provided.
How the Congressional Review Act changes would work in practice, especially the phrase 'unless the Congress enacts a joint resolution or other measure explicitly approving the rule.'
How emergency or deadline-driven rules set by other laws would be handled.
The number of cosponsors and whether a committee will take up the bill.
No Congressional Research Service summary or cost estimate was available.

life.reason: Lengthening the effective-date delay from 30 days to 6 months and adding a 6-month congressional pre-review could slow health, safety, and environmental protections that save lives, though the bill does not explicitly repeal any protection.

water.reason: A longer delay before final rules take effect could postpone new clean water standards and enforcement, though the effect is indirect and depends on which rules are delayed.

air.reason: A 6-month waiting period and congressional pre-review could slow EPA clean air rules from taking effect, though the bill does not weaken any standard itself.

transparency.reason: Longer comment periods, 24-hour advance website posting, effective-date notices, and earlier delivery of rules to Congress all give the public and lawmakers more visibility into agency rulemaking.

people_over_profit.reason: Longer delays and a congressional-approval condition for major rules give regulated industries more time and more venues to lobby against protections, which tends to favor corporate interests, though the public also gets longer comment periods.

local_say.reason: A 60-day minimum comment period and the ability to sue in one's home district make it easier for local people and communities to participate and challenge federal rules.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill does not provide subsidies, bailouts, or ratepayer-funded tax breaks, so it does not touch this value.

honesty_kindness.reason: The bill's provisions on procedure do not clearly advance or undermine honesty or kindness.

news.overall: Only one outlet group (Lean Left) is represented, with six headlines from two outlets (New York Times and Politico), so no cross-perspective comparison is possible. The headlines are short and descriptions are empty, so the evidence on how the bill itself is characterized is limited; the framing is inferred mainly from titles.

label: H.R. 5112
title: Tipped Worker Protection Act
one: The bill would phase out the lower "tipped" minimum wage so tipped workers get the full federal minimum wage, and it adds new rules to stop employers from keeping tips, hiding service charges, or imposing tip pools without worker votes.
summary:
Right now, employers can pay tipped workers a lower cash wage (the federal floor is $2.13 an hour) as long as tips bring them up to the regular minimum wage. This bill would end that system in steps. In the first year after enactment, the minimum cash wage for tipped workers would be $3.60 an hour. Each year after, it would rise by $1.50 until it reaches the regular federal minimum wage (currently $7.25). At that point, tipped workers would be paid the full minimum wage by the employer, and tips would be extra.

The bill also sets new tip rules. Employers could not keep tips, and managers and supervisors could not take any part of them. Employers could not use tips to pay credit card processing fees. Tip pools (where tips are shared) would only be allowed if at least 51 percent of non-supervisory workers vote for them, after at least 30 percent ask for a vote. Joining a pool would have to be voluntary, and workers could not be punished for how they vote.

Mandatory service charges would have to be explained to customers and workers, including how much goes directly to workers. Any part promised to workers must be paid to them promptly. A charge described as optional could not be added unless the customer asks. Those worker-directed charges would also count as tips for an employer Social Security tax credit. Penalties for misusing tips would be expanded. The bill's text does not include cost estimates.
does: Raises the minimum cash wage for tipped workers to $3.60 an hour in year one, then by $1.50 each year until it equals the regular federal minimum wage.
who: Tipped workers such as restaurant servers, bartenders, and other service staff

stage.last_action: Introduced in House

transparency.reason: It requires service charges to be explained to customers and workers, bars employers from describing a charge as optional when it is mandatory, and sets voting rules for tip pools, which makes tip handling more visible to workers and customers.

people_over_profit.reason: It raises the cash wage employers must pay tipped workers, bars employers and managers from keeping or taking tips, and bars using tips for card processing fees, shifting money from business operations toward workers.

honesty_kindness.reason: It stops employers from keeping or skimming tips, requires honest disclosure of mandatory service charges, and blocks charges that are misleadingly labeled optional.

label: H.R. 5122
title: NASA Talent Exchange Program Act
one: Lets NASA swap employees with private companies for 3 months to 3 years, with ethics, conflict-of-interest, and reporting rules attached.
summary:
This bill would let NASA set up a program to temporarily trade workers with private companies. A NASA employee could work at a company, or a company's employee could work at NASA. Both the company and the worker must agree. Each assignment would last at least three months and normally no more than two years. It could run up to three years if NASA decides the mission needs it. A single NASA employee could not spend more than three years total on these assignments.

A written agreement would cover each assignment. NASA employees would have to return to government service for twice as long as their assignment, or repay the costs. Company workers sent to NASA would stay on their company's payroll. They would be treated as federal employees for many ethics, conflict-of-interest, and liability laws. They could not see the home company's trade secrets. They also could not do "inherently governmental" work, meaning core decisions that only the government should make. The company could not bill the government for those workers' pay. No more than 2% of NASA's civil service workforce could be on assignment at once.

NASA would have to build a system to manage conflicts of interest. It would also have to send Congress yearly reports. These would name the companies, positions, and pay grades involved. The Government Accountability Office (GAO, Congress's watchdog) would review the program within three years. The bill does not say who pays the salary of NASA workers sent to a company.

Bars company-paid workers' pay from being charged to the government through contracts.
Requires yearly reports naming companies, positions, and pay grades, plus a GAO review that can recommend limits.
Caps participation at 2% of the workforce and bars use of the program to dodge workforce limits or contractor rules.

Rules rely on NASA's own policies and certifications, which may be hard to enforce or check.
The bill does not say whether taxpayers keep paying the salaries of NASA staff working at private firms, which could amount to a subsidy to those firms.
The reports go to congressional committees. The bill does not say they must be made public.

Whether the yearly reports will be public.

What the official cost would be, since no CBO estimate exists yet.
