transparency.reason: Reports go only to Congress and do not have to be made public, and the bill leaves unclear who pays NASA staff salaries at companies, which limits public visibility into the arrangement.

people_over_profit.reason: Company employees and NASA staff moving between firms and the agency could give companies insider access and influence over federal decisions, which may favor corporate interests over the public.

no_bailouts.reason: Taxpayers may end up paying NASA salaries for staff working at private firms, which could function as an indirect subsidy, and the bill does not clarify this.

label: H.R. 5147
title: WIRELESS Leadership Act
one: Sets national deadlines for local and state governments to decide on cell tower and small-cell applications, automatically approves applications that miss the deadline, limits fees and local rules, and bars local regulation based on radio-frequency health or environmental concerns.
summary:
This bill changes federal communications law to speed up approval of cell towers, antennas, and small cell equipment. It keeps the basic idea that cities, counties, and states decide where wireless facilities go. But it adds strict rules on how they decide.

Local governments would have firm deadlines. These run from 60 days for small equipment on an existing structure to 150 days for other large facilities. The clock covers all local proceedings together. A local moratorium (a pause on new applications) would not stop the clock. If a government misses the deadline, the company can send written notice, and the request is then treated as approved with no further local action.

Any denial would have to be in writing, backed by substantial evidence, and made public the same day it is issued. Local governments could not treat providers differently, and could not block or effectively block wireless service. They could still set objective, reasonable engineering, safety, and appearance rules. They could not regulate based on the environmental effects of radio-frequency emissions if the facility meets Federal Communications Commission (FCC) limits.

Fees would have to be set in advance, made public, and based on actual, reasonable costs. Anyone harmed by a local decision or delay could sue within 30 days, or ask the FCC to review it. The FCC would have 120 days to rule. The bill text does not say how environmental, historic, or community review would fit into these deadlines.
does: placeholder
who: placeholder

stage.last_action: Introduced in House

crs:
Winning the International Race for Economic Leadership and Expanding Service to Support Leadership Act or the WIRELESS Leadership Act
This bill imposes limits on state and local review and regulation of requests to construct wireless telecommunication facilities.
Specifically, states and localities must grant or deny requests to place, modify, or construct personal wireless service (PWS) facilities by a specified deadline. This deadline varies based on the nature of the request and the proposed facility. If a state or locality fails to act on a request within that timeframe, the request is deemed granted. On the day a decision to deny a request is made, the state or locality must publish the decision and provide it to the requesting party.
Further, the bill expands an existing prohibition on unreasonable discrimination in the regulation of such requests. Under the bill, any discrimination among PWS facilities or communications service providers is prohibited. For example, a state or locality may not grant preferential or exclusive use of facilities to a particular provider or class of providers. However, states and localities may establish objective, reasonable, and nondiscriminatory engineering standards, safety requirements, or aesthetic requirements.
Finally, the bill establishes requirements for fees imposed by states and localities for consideration of a request. For example, such fees must be (1) competitively neutral, technology neutral, and nondiscriminatory; (2) established in advance and publicly disclosed; and (3) based on actual and direct costs to the state or locality.

life.reason: Shortened review clocks and deemed-approval rules may leave little time for environmental, historic, or community review, and RF-emission concerns are largely removed from local consideration.

transparency.reason: Denials must be in writing, backed by substantial evidence, and published the same day, and fees must be published in advance.

people_over_profit.reason: Deemed-approval and binding deadlines give wireless providers faster approvals and limit local leverage over company-proposed facilities, favoring provider speed over community review.

local_say.reason: Local governments lose much of their power over siting: deadlines are firm, moratoria do not stop the clock, missed deadlines mean automatic approval, and RF-based objections are barred.

label: H.R. 5151
title: Quiet Communities Act of 2025
one: The bill would bring back the EPA's Office of Noise Abatement and Control to research noise pollution, help states and towns fight it, and study aircraft noise, with $25 million a year authorized for five years.
summary:
This bill would restart an office inside the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) that deals with noise pollution. That office, called the Office of Noise Abatement and Control, has not had funding since 1982. Congress says that has left noise programs across the country dormant, even though the EPA is still legally responsible for enforcing the noise rules already on the books.

The restarted office would give states technical help and grants to build noise control programs. Those grants could cover equipment for local communities. The office would also research how noise affects mental and physical health, track noise levels over time, and create public education materials, training, and workshops. It would set up regional help centers that work with colleges and private groups. It would also review how well the 1972 Noise Control Act has worked.

The EPA would also run a special study of aircraft noise. Outside scientists would look at how the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) measures noise, at what noise level health problems begin, and at whether airport noise programs work. A report with recommendations would be due to Congress within 2 years.

The bill also updates the grant section of the 1972 Noise Control Act and repeals a 1970 noise law. It says the office should favor approaches that rely on state and local action, market incentives, and teamwork with other agencies. It authorizes $25 million per year for fiscal years 2026 through 2030. "Authorizes" means Congress would still have to actually provide the money in a separate spending bill.

transparency.reason: The bill requires public education materials, a public noise-level tracking effort, and a congressional report on FAA noise methods and airport programs.

label: H.R. 5152
title: BOP Release Card ID Act of 2025
short_title: BOP Release Card ID Act of 2025
one: Requires the federal Bureau of Prisons to give departing U.S.-citizen prisoners a REAL ID-standard photo ID card valid at least 18 months, to be accepted for many federal benefit programs and to help them get state IDs.
summary:
This bill would require the Bureau of Prisons (BOP), which runs federal prisons, to hand a photo ID card to each U.S. citizen leaving federal custody. The card would have to meet the federal REAL ID security standards. The BOP would have 180 days after the bill becomes law to start issuing the cards. Each card would stay valid for at least 18 months after the person is released.

The bill would also make many federal agencies and programs accept the card as proof of identity. These include Social Security, Medicaid, Medicare, SNAP (food assistance), TANF (cash assistance), and programs at the Education, Housing and Urban Development, and Veterans Affairs departments. It would also cover federal probation and pretrial services, the D.C. offender supervision agency, and entry into federal buildings.

The BOP director would have to negotiate with each state so the card can be used to get a state ID. The director would report on that progress to the House and Senate Judiciary Committees each year, starting one year after enactment. Within one year, the Attorney General would also issue guidance to states that want to issue similar release cards to people leaving state prisons. The bill does not say how much this would cost, and it does not replace the BOP's existing duty to plan for prisoners' release. It does not cover non-citizens.

one: Changes how often the Manufacturing USA program must update its strategic plan from every 3 years to every 4 years, so it lines up with the National Strategy for Advanced Manufacturing.
summary:
Manufacturing USA is a network of institutes where government, companies, and universities work together on new manufacturing technology. Under current law, the program's strategic plan (a planning document that sets goals and priorities) must be updated at least every 3 years. A separate document, the National Strategy for Advanced Manufacturing, must be updated every 4 years. Because the two cycles do not match, the timing can be awkward.

This bill changes the program's update schedule to at least once every 4 years. The goal stated in the bill is to match the national strategy's cycle so the program better reflects national priorities. It also makes small wording changes in nearby paragraphs so that references to the plan include the new update requirement. The bill was introduced on September 4, 2025, by Rep. Luz Rivas (D-CA) with one cosponsor, Rep. David Rouzer (R-NC), and was sent to the House Science, Space, and Technology Committee. It has not moved further. The text does not say when the change would take effect beyond becoming law.

label: H.R. 5159
title: Nationwide Right to Unionize Act
one: The bill would repeal the part of federal labor law that lets states ban contracts requiring workers to join or pay a union, which would end state "right-to-work" laws.
summary: Federal labor law lets employers and unions agree to a contract rule that workers covered by the union contract must support the union, usually by paying dues or fees, to keep their jobs. These are called "union security" agreements. Right now, Section 14(b) of the National Labor Relations Act lets each state ban those agreements. About half the states have used that power to pass "right-to-work" laws. This bill is just one operative sentence. It repeals Section 14(b). If it became law, states could no longer ban union security agreements for workplaces covered by that Act, which covers most private-sector employers. Employers and unions in those states could then negotiate these agreements, as they already can in other states. The bill does not force any employer or union to adopt such an agreement. It only removes the state ban. The bill text does not say when it would start, and it does not add other rules, funding, or penalties. The title talks about a "right to unionize," but the bill does not change the right to form or join a union. It only changes whether states can bar union-security clauses. Outside the bill text, existing court rulings limit what unions can require of workers who object to joining. Those rulings are not changed by this bill. Because there is no CRS summary yet, this reading relies on the short bill text.

label: H.R. 5165
title: Go Pack Go Act of 2025
one: Lets TV subscribers in 13 northwestern Wisconsin counties, who now get Minnesota-market stations, choose to receive Wisconsin network stations instead of, or in addition to, their assigned local stations.
summary: Some Wisconsin counties near the Minnesota border are placed in TV markets based in another state, so cable and satellite customers there often see Minnesota news, weather, and sports instead of Wisconsin programming. This bill would let customers in 13 named Wisconsin counties (Ashland, Barron, Bayfield, Burnett, Douglas, Dunn, Florence, Iron, Pierce, Polk, Sawyer, St. Croix, and Washburn) pick what they get for each TV network. They could choose the local-market station their provider must already carry, a Wisconsin station from a neighboring TV market, or both. The bill applies to counties that have no same-network station of their own in Wisconsin. If a customer picks only the Wisconsin station, that counts as meeting the provider's duty to carry a local station. The bill also changes some copyright and broadcast-rule details so these Wisconsin signals do not use up satellite limits, do not need the usual cable permission deal, and are treated as "significantly viewed" (a rule that lets certain out-of-market stations be carried). Satellite companies only have to do this where it is technically feasible, as decided by the FCC. The bill does not say when it would start or what it would cost, and the text does not describe how it affects local stations' finances.

crs:
Go Pack Go Act of 2025
This bill requires cable and satellite television providers to make Wisconsin-based television programming available to subscribers in counties assigned to out-of-state television markets.
U.S. counties are assigned to geographic television markets, and television providers are generally required to provide subscribers with programming local to their assigned market. Counties on state borders are sometimes assigned to out-of-state markets; subscribers in those counties often receive out-of-state programming (e.g., out-of-state news and sports).
Under the bill, a cable or satellite television provider must offer subscribers in specified Wisconsin counties with the choice of (1) programming local to the subscriber's assigned market that the provider is currently required to retransmit, (2) Wisconsin-based adjacent-market programming, or (3) both.
The bill also establishes that the provision of Wisconsin-based programming to subscribers who have elected it fulfills certain statutory coverage obligations applicable to providers.

transparency.reason: Customers get a clearer, direct choice over which stations they receive, though the bill does not add public reporting or disclosure requirements.

people_over_profit.reason: Subscribers gain a choice over what they receive, which somewhat shifts control from providers and broadcasters toward viewers, though carriers may still face added compliance costs.

local_say.reason: Residents of 13 named Wisconsin border counties gain a direct say in which in-state stations they receive, reflecting their state and community ties.

news.overall: Only one Lean Left outlet with two headlines was provided, and neither headline clearly addresses the Go Pack Go Act, so the evidence is too limited to describe how this bill is framed. No other perspective groups were supplied for comparison. Descriptions were also not included, so framing is inferred only from headline wording.

label: H.R. 5170
title: CABLE Leadership Act
one: Requires local cable franchising authorities to approve or deny a new cable franchise request within 120 days, or the request is automatically approved.
summary: Today, a cable company that wants to offer service in a town or county usually needs a "franchise," which is a permission agreement from the local government (the "franchising authority"). This bill would put a strict clock on that process for new franchise requests (not renewals). The local government would have 120 days after getting a complete request to say yes or no. If it misses the deadline, the request is automatically treated as approved. The clock covers all local steps combined, and a local moratorium (a pause on considering requests), whether official or informal, cannot stop the clock. If a local government says no, it must do so in writing, back the decision with substantial evidence in a written record, and release it publicly and to the applicant the same day. The bill also defines a "complete" request. A request counts as complete once the applicant takes the first step the locality requires, unless the locality sends a written notice within 30 days naming the missing information and citing a public rule that requires it. If no such notice arrives, the request is treated as complete and received the day after that 30-day period ends. The bill does not mention broadband build-out terms, community service requirements, or fees, so how those would interact with automatic approval is not addressed in the text.
does: Sets a 120-day deadline for local governments to approve or deny a complete request for a new cable franchise.
Treats the request as automatically granted if the local government misses the deadline.
Makes the deadline cover all local proceedings together.
Bars moratoriums, formal or informal, from pausing the clock.
Requires denials to be written, backed by substantial evidence in a written record, and released publicly the same day.
Defines a request as complete after the applicant takes the first required step, unless the locality sends a detailed written notice within 30 days of missing items citing a public rule.
who: Cable and video service providers seeking new franchises
City, county, and other local franchising authorities
Residents in areas where new providers might enter
Local officials and staff who review franchise requests
Consumers who may gain or lose competition and service choices

stage.last_action: Introduced in House

transparency.reason: Requiring written denials, a written evidentiary record, and same-day public release makes local franchise decisions more visible to residents.

people_over_profit.reason: Automatic approval and a firm deadline favor new cable companies' ability to enter markets quickly, though the bill does not address consumer prices or service quality.

local_say.reason: Local governments lose the ability to pause or deny requests on their own timeline, since missing the 120-day deadline automatically grants the franchise and moratoriums cannot stop the clock.

news.overall: Only one Lean Right article is provided, and its description is empty, so the evidence is very limited. No comparison across perspectives is possible from this input. Coverage from Lean Left, center, or other outlets would be needed to assess how the bill is framed across the spectrum.

label: H.R. 663
title: To oppose the permitting of deep seabed mining and exploration for deep seabed mining, and for other purposes.
short_title: Oppose Deep Seabed Mining Permitting Act
one: The bill would direct the President to have U.S. representatives at international bodies push for a pause on deep seabed mining permits and exploration, and oppose funding for it, until international rules are in place and certified as protective of the ocean.
summary: This bill is about mining the deep ocean floor for minerals. It starts with a list of findings from Congress. These say scientists think deep seabed mining poses major risks, such as killing unique species, creating large clouds of sediment, adding noise pollution, possibly contaminating food fish, and harming the ocean's ability to store carbon. It also says we don't yet know enough about the deep sea to judge the full risks. The bill then states the "sense of Congress," which is a non-binding opinion. That opinion is that no deep seabed mining should happen in international waters until the International Seabed Authority (the UN-linked body that oversees the international seabed) adopts a full, binding set of rules based on solid science. The one binding part is an instruction to the President. The President must tell U.S. representatives at international organizations the U.S. belongs to or observes to use the country's voice, vote, and influence to call for a moratorium (a pause) on permitting deep seabed mining and exploration. They must also oppose investment, financing, or other support for it. This continues until the President certifies to Congress that the International Seabed Authority has issued regulations that are based on scientific consensus and effectively protect the marine environment. The President must also send Congress a report describing those regulations. The bill does not create a domestic ban or change U.S. law on permits.
does: Lists congressional findings about the environmental risks of deep seabed mining and the gaps in scientific knowledge.

States a non-binding sense of Congress that no deep seabed mining should occur in international waters until the International Seabed Authority adopts a full, binding, science-based regulatory framework.
Directs the President to instruct U.S. representatives at relevant international organizations to call for a moratorium on permitting and exploration for deep seabed mining.
Directs U.S. representatives to oppose investment, financing, or support for deep seabed mining and exploration.

Ends that duty only after the President certifies to Congress that International Seabed Authority regulations exist, are informed by scientific consensus, and effectively protect the marine environment, and submits a report on them.
Requires the report to describe the regulations, the scientific consensus on risks, and how the rules protect the marine environment.
who: Companies that want to explore or mine the deep seabed, and their investors
Marine ecosystems and deep-sea species
Fishing industries and coastal communities, including Indigenous peoples who depend on the ocean
The President and U.S. diplomats at international organizations
The International Seabed Authority and its member nations
Industries that depend on minerals found on the seabed, such as batteries and electronics

stage.last_action: Sponsor introductory remarks on measure. (CR E86-87)

life.reason: It directs U.S. diplomacy to seek a moratorium on deep seabed mining until science-based protections exist, which would help shield deep-sea species and ecosystems from mining harm.

water.reason: By pausing deep seabed mining and its sediment plumes and noise, it would help keep ocean water clean, though it does not directly regulate water quality.

air.reason: It supports protecting the deep ocean's ability to store carbon, a modest indirect benefit to air quality and climate.

transparency.reason: It requires the President to report to Congress with a certification and a description of the regulations and scientific consensus, giving lawmakers and the public more information.

people_over_profit.reason: It directs the U.S. to oppose investment and financing for deep seabed mining, placing environmental protection ahead of company mining interests, though it does not directly address profit margins.

no_bailouts.reason: It directs U.S. representatives to oppose financing and public support for deep seabed mining, which limits government backing for these projects.

news.overall: Evidence from this group is limited to two headlines with no article descriptions, so framing can only be inferred from titles. The New York Times item frames the issue as a legal challenge to a government action, while the NPR item takes a more ocean-environment angle that is only loosely connected to the bill. Neither piece's text is available to show how the coverage treats the bill's merits.

label: H.R. 664
title: American Seabed Protection Act
one: Bans new federal permits for deep seabed mining and for hardrock mining on the Outer Continental Shelf (except scientific research) and orders a National Academies study of the environmental effects of such mining.
summary:
This bill would stop the U.S. government from issuing licenses, permits, or other approvals for two kinds of ocean mining. The first is exploring for or commercially recovering minerals from the deep seabed, which is the ocean floor beyond national boundaries that current law lets U.S. companies seek permits for. The second is exploring for, developing, or producing hardrock minerals (such as metals) on the Outer Continental Shelf, the underwater lands off U.S. coasts that the federal government manages. Permits for scientific research would still be allowed.

The bill also tells the Commerce Secretary, working through NOAA, to try to make a deal within 90 days with the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine. The Academies would do a broad study of how this mining could affect ocean life, habitats, sediment clouds, the ocean's ability to store greenhouse gases, fishing, recreation, fish farms, undersea cables, and Indigenous peoples and cultures. The study would also estimate greenhouse gas emissions from mining and look at alternatives, like recycling, substitute materials, and cleaner land-based mining. NOAA would send a report on the findings to key House and Senate committees.

The bill begins with findings that say scientists have raised serious concerns about deep seabed mining and that there is not enough information to judge its risks. It does not set a deadline for the study or give a dollar amount.
does: Bars any license, permit, or authorization for deep seabed exploration or commercial recovery, overriding the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act.
Bars any authorization for exploration, development, or production of hardrock minerals on the Outer Continental Shelf, overriding the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act.
Allows permits for scientific research activities.
Directs the Commerce Secretary (through NOAA) to seek an agreement within 90 days with the National Academies for a comprehensive environmental study.
Requires the study to cover ecosystems, species recovery, carbon storage, sediment plumes, fisheries, recreation, aquaculture, subsea infrastructure, Indigenous peoples, and greenhouse gas emissions.
Requires the study to assess alternatives such as recycling, substitute materials, and less harmful land-based mining.
Requires a report on the findings to the House Foreign Affairs and Natural Resources Committees and three Senate committees.
who: Companies seeking U.S. permits for deep seabed or offshore hardrock mining
Commercial and recreational fishers and fish-farm operators
Coastal communities and Indigenous peoples tied to marine resources
Marine species and ocean ecosystems
NOAA and the Department of Commerce
Subsea cable and infrastructure developers
Industries wanting minerals for batteries and electronics, and those pursuing domestic mineral supply

stage.last_action: Sponsor introductory remarks on measure. (CR E86-87)

life.reason: Bars permits for deep seabed and offshore hardrock mining, which removes a threat to marine species and ocean ecosystems while a study of impacts is commissioned.

water.reason: Blocking seabed and offshore hardrock mining avoids sediment plumes and contamination that could degrade ocean water quality, though it does not directly regulate water pollution in general.

air.reason: The study would examine greenhouse gas emissions from mining and the ocean's carbon storage, and the bill halts a new mining activity that would add emissions.

transparency.reason: Requires a National Academies study with a report to multiple House and Senate committees, making findings on this mining available to Congress and the public.

people_over_profit.reason: Blocks mining permits that would benefit companies seeking seabed minerals in favor of protecting fishers, coastal communities, and ecosystems.

local_say.reason: Stops federal approvals for Outer Continental Shelf mining off coasts, giving coastal communities more say over nearby offshore activity, though it is a federal ban rather than a local vote.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill neither provides corporate subsidies nor ratepayer-funded tax breaks, so it does not touch this value.

honesty_kindness.reason: Findings and a comprehensive study of risks reflect a commitment to evidence-based disclosure of potential harms to people and Indigenous communities.

label: H.R. 8424
title: Promoting Access to Local Agriculture Act of 2026
short_title: Promoting Access to Local Agriculture Act of 2026
one: Directs USDA to create a single application (or shared-information system) and standard technology so small direct-selling farmers and ranchers can more easily accept SNAP, WIC, senior farmers market, and GusNIP benefits.
summary:
Farmers who sell directly to shoppers, such as at farmers markets, often have to fill out separate applications for each federal food assistance program they want to accept. They also may need different equipment for each one. This bill would tell the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) to make that easier.

First, USDA would build either a single application farmers and ranchers could use to apply to SNAP (food stamps), WIC (nutrition aid for women, infants, and children), the Senior Farmers' Market Nutrition Program, and the Gus Schumacher Nutrition Incentive Program (which helps people buy more fruits and vegetables). Or, USDA would build a system that shares a farmer's information between programs, so approval in one program automatically counts as pre-qualified for the others.

Second, USDA would set up a streamlined way for these farmers to process benefits with standard technology, such as one device or one mobile app.

Third, the bill changes the SNAP law so USDA must make sure equipment and systems that states or their partners provide are right for the seller. For farmers markets and other direct-to-consumer markets, that includes wireless or mobile equipment.

USDA must report to Congress on progress within one year. The bill gives no dollar amounts for funding.
does: Requires USDA to set up a streamlined vendor application for direct-marketing farmers and ranchers across SNAP, the Senior Farmers' Market Nutrition Program, WIC (including its farmers' market program), and GusNIP.
Lets USDA choose between a single application or an information-sharing system that treats a farmer approved in one program as prequalified for the others.
Requires USDA to create a streamlined way to process benefits using standardized technology, like a single device or mobile app.

Amends the SNAP law so USDA must ensure equipment and systems offered by states or their partners are appropriate for the entity, including wireless or mobile tools for farmers markets and direct-to-consumer markets.
Requires a progress report to House and Senate agriculture committees within one year of enactment.
Applies GusNIP only 'as practicable' to the streamlining activities.
who: Farmers and ranchers who sell directly to consumers (farmers markets, farm stands)
SNAP, WIC, and senior nutrition program participants
Low-income shoppers who want fresh local food
USDA and state agencies that run these programs
Equipment and payment technology vendors
Local communities and food economies

stage.last_action: Introduced in House

crs:
Promoting Access to Local Agriculture Act of 2026
This bill directs the Department of Agriculture (USDA) to establish a streamlined process for farmers and ranchers to provide benefits under certain federal nutrition programs. These programs include the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP); the Senior Farmers Market Nutrition Program (SFMNP); the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC); and the Gus Schumacher Nutrition Incentive Program (GusNIP).
Specifically, USDA must establish a streamlined application process for farmers and ranchers to apply to be vendors under the nutrition programs, including by developing a single application for the programs or an information sharing system. USDA must also develop a streamlined process for these vendors to use standardized technology to process program benefits (such as a single piece of equipment or a mobile application).
Further, USDA must ensure that the program benefit processing equipment and systems made available by a state agency are appropriate for the entity. For example, this includes ensuring wireless or mobile processing equipment and technology systems are appropriate for farmers markets and other direct-to-consumer markets.

people_over_profit.reason: Streamlined applications and standardized payment tools reduce paperwork and cost burdens for small direct-sale farmers relative to large vendors' compliance capacity, modestly favoring independent producers.

honesty_kindness.reason: Making it easier for low-income shoppers and seniors to use benefits at farmers markets and for small farmers to participate supports fair, accessible access to nutrition programs.

label: H.R. 9968
title: Opening Programs to Organic Farms Act
short_title: Opening Programs to Organic Farms Act
one: Requires the USDA to study and publicly report on barriers that organic and organic-transitioning farms face in USDA programs, then give three yearly progress updates.
summary: This bill does not create new programs or hand out money. It orders the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) to study why certified organic farms, and farms thinking about switching to organic, have trouble using USDA programs. The USDA would have 180 days after the bill becomes law to send a report to the House and Senate agriculture committees and post it on its website. The report would look at programs for conservation, loans, disaster aid, crop insurance, exports, marketing, technical help, rural development, data collection, buying food for government use, and organic certification cost-sharing. It would include data where possible on how many organic farms apply, are approved or denied, how much funding they get, where they are, and why they are denied or don't take part. It would also look at specific problems such as eligibility rules, payment rates, paperwork, crop insurance prices, how disaster losses are valued, and whether USDA staff know enough about organic farming. It would assess the need for organic training for field staff. The USDA must describe the steps it plans to take and suggest any law changes Congress should consider. For three years after, it must post yearly updates on progress and remaining barriers.
does: Requires a USDA report to Congress within 180 days of enactment, also posted publicly on the USDA website.

Directs USDA to assess barriers to organic farms in conservation, credit, disaster aid, risk management, export, market development, technical assistance, rural development, data, procurement, and certification cost-share programs.
who: Certified organic farmers
Farmers considering transitioning to organic
USDA agencies and field staff (FSA, NRCS, RMA, Rural Development, FAS)
House and Senate agriculture committees
Consumers and rural communities that rely on organic food production
Taxpayers (modest cost of preparing reports)

stage.last_action: Introduced in House

transparency.reason: It requires a public USDA report to Congress and on the agency website, plus yearly public updates for three years, shedding light on program barriers for organic farms.
